0.title: Romans
0.overview:
Martin Luther called the letter to the Romans "the chief part of the New Testament and the very purest gospel." John Calvin wrote that "when anyone understands this Epistle, he has a passage opened to him to the understanding of the whole Scripture." Martyn Lloyd-Jones preached 366 sermons on it over some thirteen years and still felt he had not exhausted it. Romans is not one letter among many; it is the theological heart of the New Testament, the fullest and most systematic exposition of the gospel that God ever moved a human pen to write.

Paul wrote to a church he had never visited, in the capital of the empire, at the height of his apostolic ministry — probably from Corinth around AD 57. His purpose was not merely to introduce himself before a planned visit to Spain. It was to set before these believers, Jew and Gentile alike, the full panorama of the gospel: the universal guilt of humanity, the righteousness of God revealed in Christ, justification by faith alone, the transforming work of the Spirit, the sovereign purposes of God in election and in the mystery of Israel, and the shape of the redeemed life in the world. No letter covers more ground. No letter has changed more lives.

The structure follows the gospel's own logic. Chapters 1–3 establish the diagnosis: all humanity — pagan, moralist, and Jew — stands guilty before the righteous God, with no resources of its own to secure acquittal. Chapters 3–5 announce the remedy: the righteousness of God given freely through faith in Jesus Christ, who bore the wrath we deserved. Chapters 6–8 trace the fruit: union with Christ, death to sin, life in the Spirit, adoption as children, and the unshakeable security of those whom God has called. Chapters 9–11 address the mystery: if Israel is the covenant people, why has Israel largely rejected its Messiah? And chapters 12–16 show what the gospel-transformed life looks like in home, church, city, and empire.

Who were the Christians in Rome? No apostle founded the church. Luke lists visitors from Rome in the Pentecost crowd (Acts 2:10), and the gospel probably reached the capital through Jewish believers like them. Some years before this letter Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2), and for a time the congregations were largely Gentile. When Jewish believers returned after his death, they came back to churches whose leaders and habits had changed. That tension between Jewish and Gentile Christians lies behind much of the letter, especially chapters 9–11 and 14–15 (cf. 1:7).

And what of the New Perspective on Paul? Since the 1970s scholars such as E. P. Sanders, James Dunn and N. T. Wright have argued that first-century Judaism was not a religion of earning salvation; that works of the law means chiefly the marks that set Jews apart, such as circumcision, the food laws and the Sabbath; and that justification is mainly about who belongs to God’s people. They are right that the unity of Jew and Gentile is a real concern of Romans (3:29–30; 15:7), and that Judaism has sometimes been described unfairly. But the more likely reading is the Reformation one. Paul’s charge in 1:18–3:20 is not that Jews kept Gentiles out but that all have broken God’s law and stand guilty before him, so that every mouth may be stopped (3:19). Justification answers that guilt. It is God’s verdict of acquittal, given freely to the ungodly (4:5) on the ground of Christ’s blood (5:9). Belonging to God’s people follows from that verdict; it is not what the verdict means.

We will draw on the great Reformed interpreters of this letter: Calvin's magisterial commentary, Luther whose reading of 1:17 unlocked the Reformation, Lloyd-Jones whose fourteen volumes remain the richest English-language treatment, John Stott whose Message of Romans is a model of accessible depth, Timothy Keller's Romans for You, and scholars Douglas Moo and Thomas Schreiner. Come expecting to be undone and remade. Romans has that effect on everyone who takes it seriously.

1.title: The Gospel and the Wrath of God
1.overview:
Romans 1 opens with one of the most carefully crafted sentences in ancient literature — a single Greek sentence spanning seven verses, in which Paul introduces himself, his gospel, and his Lord with the precision of a theologian and the ardour of a man in love with what he believes. By the time the chapter ends, the same pen that wrote of the gospel as "the power of God for salvation" has traced the terrifying arc of divine wrath against human idolatry. These two things belong together: the good news is only truly good when the bad news is truly bad.

The movement of the chapter is deliberate. Paul establishes the gospel (vv. 1–17), then demonstrates the need for it (vv. 18–32). The power of God for salvation is proportionate to the depth of human lostness — and that depth, as Paul will show, is vertiginous. The world Paul describes in vv. 18–32 is not ancient history; it is every human culture that has suppressed the knowledge of the God it cannot stop knowing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Paul, the Gospel, and the Grace of Apostleship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's opening sentence is a controlled explosion of theology. In seven verses he identifies himself as a slave of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God — a gospel promised in the Old Testament Scriptures, concerning God's Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh and declared to be the Son of God in power by the resurrection from the dead. Every phrase is a chapter of theology waiting to be unfolded. This is not a man warming up; this is a man who knows exactly what he believes and why it matters.

The word that unlocks everything is euangelion — gospel. It meant, in the first-century Roman world, the proclamation of good news, typically the accession of a new emperor or a great military victory. Paul seizes the word and repurposes it entirely. The great news is not that Caesar has triumphed; it is that Jesus Christ, Son of God, Lord, has been raised from the dead and now reigns over all things. This is a message with empire-shaking implications — which is precisely why Paul is eager to preach it in Rome itself.

The address of grace and peace — "to all those in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints" — is not a formality. It is a theological declaration. These people, in the capital of pagan power, are loved by God. They are called. They are saints — not by virtue of their moral achievement but by virtue of their union with Jesus Christ who is holy, and who has made them holy in him. Before Paul preaches a word of gospel to them, he speaks a word of gospel over them. This is the Pauline method: ground identity before applying imperatives.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pre-Pauline Gospel

One of the most important features of Romans 1:1–4 is Paul's insistence that the gospel he preaches was "promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures." The gospel is not a Pauline invention or a Gentile innovation — it is the fulfilment of Israel's own scriptures. Jesus is the descendant of David (2 Samuel 7), declared Son of God by resurrection (Psalm 2). Calvin saw in this the unity of the two testaments: the Old Testament is the gospel in promise; the New Testament is the gospel in fulfilment. Any reading of the Old Testament that does not find Christ there has missed its point.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's designation of himself as a doulos — slave — of Christ Jesus was shocking in a world where slavery was degradation. He inverts the social order: the highest dignity available to a human being is not freedom but bondage to Jesus Christ. Now: In an age that prizes autonomy above all things, the Christian claim that the best possible life is one of radical submission to Christ still provokes the same offence — and still offers the same liberation to those who discover that the lordship of Christ is the only yoke that is easy and the only burden that is light.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul introduces himself in three phrases: “a servant of Christ Jesus” (he belongs entirely to Christ), “called to be an apostle” (he did not volunteer; he was stopped on the Damascus road), and “set apart for the gospel of God” (one purpose governs his life).

Slave. Most Bibles say “servant”, but doulos means slave, and a slave in Rome was not an employee but property — legally a thing. He owned nothing, had no right to his own time, body or plans, could not refuse, and was often named by the man who bought him. And this letter was going to Rome, where perhaps a third of the population was enslaved and the church met in houses. When it was read aloud, there were slaves in the room, and almost certainly slave-owners. Into that room the greatest missionary in history introduces himself by the legal status of the lowest person present — the one word in Roman vocabulary that meant a man belongs entirely to someone else. Yet a Jewish reader heard something else too: “servant of the LORD” is one of the great Old Testament titles — Moses, Joshua, David, the prophets, and above all the Servant of Isaiah. In one word Paul makes the lowest rung of Rome’s ladder and the highest title in Israel’s Scriptures the same rung. That is the shape of the whole gospel he is about to explain.

What does it ask of you? A slave does not own his own time, and the quickest way to find what you believe about ownership is to listen to yourself when a day is interrupted: “my morning”, “my weekend” — and the resentment when someone spends it for you. That reaction is information about who you think holds the deed. One guard, because this image has been used to injure people: Paul is describing ownership, not exhaustion. His Master ordered a sabbath, told his workers to come away and rest, and slept through a storm. A church that quotes this verse to squeeze more work out of a tired person has understood neither the slave nor the Master.

Called. The adjective klētos appears three times in seven verses: Paul is “called to be an apostle”; the readers are “called to belong to Jesus Christ” (v. 6) and “called to be saints” (v. 7). Paul has no special word for his own vocation and an ordinary one for everyone else’s. Neither he nor you volunteered or was consulted.

Set apart. There is an irony Paul could not have missed. The name “Pharisee” most likely means “separated one”, a movement devoted to separation from everything that might defile, and Paul had been an expert. God keeps the verb and reverses the direction: he is no longer set apart from people but for a message, which sends him straight to the Gentiles he had spent decades avoiding (Galatians 1:15; Acts 13:2). Nothing about him was wasted; it was requisitioned. That is worth hearing if you suspect that other people have callings and you have a routine. Paul’s assignment is not yours, and you should not manufacture a dramatic one. But if you belong to Christ, you were called in exactly the sense he was, and the parts of your history you think unusable are the parts God is most practised at requisitioning.

And when Paul describes what the Son of God did, he uses the same word: Christ “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7) — the form of a slave. The title is not beneath Paul, because it was not beneath his Lord.
verseByVerse.note: “Servant” translates the ordinary word for a slave, one wholly owned by his master. Paul wrote Romans from Corinth, probably around AD 57, before taking the collection to Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: before you were born I consecrated you

verseByVerse.quote: which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel is not a novelty. God “promised [it] beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures”, and it concerns his Son, “descended from David according to the flesh.” As Calvin saw, the Old Testament is the gospel promised; the New is the gospel arrived.

An answer to “it’s new”. In the first century Christianity looked like a novelty, and Rome respected age and distrusted new religions. The charge was easy: a sect barely twenty-five years old, gathered round an executed provincial. Paul replies that the gospel is the oldest thing in the world; what happened outside Jerusalem was not the start of something but the keeping of something.

A promise kept over centuries. A promise is only as good as the one who makes it, and the waiting is the test. God said he would crush the serpent’s head, and millennia passed. He swore to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed in his offspring, and the family went down to Egypt and was enslaved for four centuries. He told David a son of his would reign for ever, and the dynasty collapsed, the city burned, and the line dwindled to a carpenter in a village nobody respected. At every point it would have been reasonable to think the promise had lapsed. Then it did not. So if you are waiting on God for something he has said — a child who has walked away, a marriage you cannot see mending, a wrong unaddressed for years — the point is not that your wait will be short. It is that God’s delays run to centuries and he has never yet failed to arrive. That is not soothing, but it is solid: the waiting proves only that we are not the ones who set the timetable.

Christ in the Old Testament. Paul preached out of a book his hearers already owned; every sermon in Acts expounds the Old Testament. So any reading of it that does not find Christ there has missed the point. The two-thirds of your Bible you find hardest is not the run-up to the gospel; it is the gospel in promise. On the Emmaus road Jesus, “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets… interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27).

“Descended from David according to the flesh.” God’s Son entered a genealogy, a family whose history can be traced — and if you have read it, you know what is in it: David arranging a man’s death to hide adultery, Solomon ending in idolatry, Manasseh filling Jerusalem with innocent blood; a foreign widow, a prostitute in Jericho, and kings the Bible itself calls evil. That is the family the Son of God joined, and not at a distance; he took their flesh. And it means Christianity is not a set of timeless principles any thoughtful person might discover. It is a report of something that happened to a particular man in a family whose records survive — which is why it could be false, and why, if it is true, it is not merely inspiring but binding. The long silence between promise and fulfilment was never God losing interest; it was God taking the time to become one of us.

parallels.desc: the promised son of David

verseByVerse.quote: and was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The resurrection is God’s public verdict on Jesus: he “was declared to be the Son of God in power… by his resurrection from the dead.” The Son who lived in weakness and humiliation was openly declared Son in power.

Declared, not made. This verse has long been used to argue that Jesus became the Son of God — a man promoted or adopted at the resurrection. The sentence itself answers that. Verse 3 says the gospel is “concerning his Son, who was descended from David”: the Son is the one who did the descending. He was already the Son before there was a genealogy to enter. What changed at the resurrection was not the Son but the public record. A verdict does not create the fact it announces: a man wrongly convicted and later cleared was innocent all along, and the court has finally said so. The world had reached its verdict on Jesus, written over his head in three languages, and sealed it in a grave. God overturned it in public. Peter put it as a straight contradiction: “God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified” (Acts 2:36).

Why it matters for you. Paul will later say Christ was “raised for our justification” (4:25). If the Father reversed the verdict on the Son in public, the verdict on everyone joined to him is reversed with it. The empty tomb is God’s receipt: the debt was accepted as paid, and he said so by opening the grave.

“According to the Spirit of holiness.” Paul has just said “according to the flesh” (v. 3); now he balances it. In ordinary human descent Jesus is David’s son; in the realm of the Spirit he is declared God’s Son in power. Both are true of one person. And the same Spirit lives in believers: “he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you” (8:11).

“Our Lord.” After titles of enormous height, Paul lands on a possessive. Kyrios was the word the Greek Old Testament used for God’s name, and the word the empire demanded people use of Caesar; Paul claims both. Yet a slave writing to a house church in the capital calls him “our Lord”, as if he belongs to them.

A test. What would you say if someone told you tomorrow that they had found Jesus’ body? Not whether you could refute it — whether it would matter. If your faith is mainly a set of values and a hopeful way of life, the news would be sad but survivable. Paul’s faith would not survive it for an hour: “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins… we are of all people most to be pitied” (1 Corinthians 15:17, 19). He staked everything on an event that a corpse could disprove. The resurrection is not a happy ending tacked onto the story of a good man. It is the Father standing up in the courtroom of the world, after the sentence was carried out and the body sealed in rock, and announcing that the accused was his Son all along.

parallels.desc: you are my Son

verseByVerse.quote: ...through whom we have received grace and apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith for the sake of his name among all the nations, including you who are called to belong to Jesus Christ... — Romans 1:5-6
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through Christ, Paul received “grace and apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith for the sake of his name among all the nations” — and the Roman Christians are among those nations, “called to belong to Jesus Christ.”

“Grace and apostleship.” Paul almost certainly means the grace that consisted in being made an apostle — and remember who is writing. The man commissioned to preach had been arresting preachers. He held the coats at Stephen’s stoning and went to Damascus to drag Christians back in chains. He never got over it: “I am the least of the apostles… because I persecuted the church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:9–10). The commission was not a reward after the pardon; the commission was the pardon. God did not only forgive the persecutor; he handed him the message and sent him to the people he had been hunting.

“The obedience of faith.” The grammar allows several readings: the obedience that consists in faith (believing is the first act of obedience), the obedience that flows from faith, or obedience to “the faith”. Paul would probably be puzzled by our need to choose, and the decisive clue is where he puts the phrase: at the very beginning of the letter and again at the very end (16:26). It brackets everything between. And that matters if you have worried about faith and works. This letter insists more than any other that we are justified by faith apart from works — and it opens and closes by calling for obedience. Paul saw no tension. Faith is not a substitute for obedience, and obedience is not faith’s wage; faith is the first thing God commands and the root from which everything else grows. That is why faith is not passive. It costs nothing to admire Jesus or agree that the gospel is probably true. This asks you to stop underwriting your own life.

“For the sake of his name.” Not for the nations’ sake or the church’s growth, though God loves both, but for his name. That exposes our motives. Think of someone you long to see come to Christ, and ask why. Most reasons are decent but partial: that they would be happier, stop frightening us, bring peace to the family. Now the harder version: if that person came to faith but never thanked you, never joined your church, never became easy to be with, and their life stayed as hard as it is now — would you still count it everything you prayed for? If you hesitate, that is not cause for shame; it is simply the place where Paul’s motive and ours are not yet the same, and it is worth praying about.

“All the nations” — “including you.” This echoes God’s promise to Abraham that “in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed” (Genesis 22:18) — the promise made beforehand in the Scriptures (v. 2). Paul’s travels are the means by which an oath sworn to a childless herdsman two thousand years earlier is being kept, on real roads, by a tentmaker. And then: “including you”. The Roman Christians are not spectators of this mission; they are what “all the nations” looks like when the plan becomes a room with people in it. And they are “called to belong” — not to achieve or understand or be useful, but to belong. The greatest missionary ever names the ends of the earth as his parish and then tells a few dozen believers meeting in borrowed rooms in a hostile city that they are not watching the story; they are the evidence that it is true.

parallels.desc: the obedience of faith

verseByVerse.quote: To all those in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. — Romans 1:7
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul addresses “all those in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints”, and greets them with “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” Before any argument, the gospel comes as gift.

Who was in the room. Some years earlier the emperor Claudius had expelled the Jews from Rome — which is how Priscilla and Aquila came to be in Corinth (Acts 18:2). The Jewish believers, including many founders, were gone, and for several years the Roman churches were Gentile. Then Claudius died, the edict lapsed, and the exiles came home to churches that had learned to function without them, with other leaders and other customs. Hold that in mind and much of this letter stops being abstract: Jew and Gentile equally guilty and equally justified; the ache over Israel (chapters 9–11); the warning to Gentiles not to be arrogant toward the broken branches; the strong and the weak in chapter 14. Paul is writing into a church with a seam running through it. And the first thing he does is address them all with one description: loved by God, called, saints. Not founders and newcomers, returned and established — one greeting over one church.

Saints. Church usage has made the word mean exceptional Christians, mostly dead, formally recognised, in stained glass. In the Old Testament holiness belongs first to things: the holy place, garments and vessels. A bowl in the tabernacle was not a better bowl; it was a bowl set aside for God and no longer available for ordinary use. So when Paul calls a room of tradesmen, slaves and immigrants “saints”, he is describing what has happened to them, not their record. That has a practical consequence. If holiness were your achievement, you would have to keep proving it, and every failure would put your status in question. If it is a designation, failure contradicts what you are rather than disproving it. That is how Paul writes to the most disorderly church he knew — lawsuits, drunkenness at the Lord’s table, a man sleeping with his stepmother — and still calls them saints (1 Corinthians 1:2). He does not withdraw the word to rebuke them; he rebukes them on the strength of it: be what you are.

“Loved by God.” The participle is passive, and it decides how the whole letter is read. There is a way of being a Christian that is really auditioning: you believe God loves you, but roughly in proportion to how the week went. Ask yourself: does God love me more today than this time last year? If the honest answer is yes, because you have been doing better, the love has become a wage. Paul rules that out. They were loved before they did anything, and the letter will say it plainly: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (5:8). The love was at full strength at the worst possible moment; it has nowhere to grow to.

Grace and peace. “Grace” plays on the standard Greek greeting (chairein), and “peace” is the Jewish shalom. Writing to Greeks and Jews eyeing each other across a room, Paul opens with both. Grace is the favour no one was owed; peace is what it produces once the war is over. The order never reverses: no one has found peace and then gone looking for grace. And notice “God our Father” — said at the door, before the argument begins. The God who is about to spend a chapter and a half describing his wrath is introduced to these people, by name, as their Father.
verseByVerse.note: “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people — all believers. The church at Rome was not founded by Paul; he had never been there.

parallels.desc: visitors from Rome at Pentecost

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Paul's Longing and His Debt to All
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having established his gospel and his greeting, Paul opens his heart. He has prayed for the Roman Christians unceasingly. He has longed to visit them. He has been prevented — more than once. This passage is often passed over quickly on the way to the theological fireworks of vv. 16–17, but it deserves careful attention: it shows us what a gospel-shaped pastor looks like. Paul's longing is not merely strategic (Rome as a missionary base) but personal. He wants to see them, to be mutually encouraged, to share with them some spiritual gift.

The phrase "I am under obligation" (v. 14) — literally "I am a debtor" — is startling. Paul does not feel that preaching the gospel to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish, is above and beyond the call of duty. He feels indebted to them. They have a claim on him. The grace that was lavished on him on the Damascus road was not for his private enrichment; it was for their benefit. He owes them what he received for free. This is the logic of all gospel ministry: grace received creates obligation discharged.

"I am not ashamed of the gospel" (v. 16) — the understatement implies the opposite: he is eagerly proud of it, itching to proclaim it in Rome's very centre. Rome was the most intimidating platform imaginable: the seat of empire, the crossroads of civilization, the city that had crucified the Lord of the gospel. And Paul cannot wait to get there.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pastoral and Missionary Logic of Paul

Romans 1:8–15 reveals that Paul's missionary strategy is inseparable from his pastoral affection. He does not view the Roman church as an audience for his theology or a resource for his mission; he views them as beloved brothers and sisters in whom he longs to rejoice. Reformed missiology has always insisted that mission and church are inseparable — the mission proceeds from the church, through the church, and for the establishment of the church. Paul's eagerness to visit Rome exemplifies this: he is not a lone-ranger evangelist but an apostle embedded in the body of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's sense of debt to all people — Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish — erased every cultural and social hierarchy. The gospel belonged to no class or culture. Now: The contemporary church is perpetually tempted to preach a gospel shaped for those who are already culturally similar to us. Paul's "debtor" language is a rebuke: the gospel is owed to every person in our reach, regardless of whether they seem like likely converts or comfortable neighbours.

verseByVerse.quote: First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed in all the world. For God is my witness, whom I serve with my spirit in the gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I mention you
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul begins by thanking God for the Roman Christians, “because your faith is proclaimed in all the world”, and swears that he prays for them constantly. He had been serving Rome on his knees for years before he arrived.

Thanks first. This is Paul’s settled habit, even in letters to churches about to be told hard things. The Corinthians were tolerating incest and getting drunk at the Lord’s table, and he still opens by thanking God for them. The one exception is Galatians, where he goes straight to “I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you” (Galatians 1:6). When Paul omits the thanksgiving, something is seriously wrong. Here it is present, warm, and first. And it is offered “through Jesus Christ”: Paul cannot even say thank you on his own account. People with no standing cannot simply address the throne, so even gratitude travels through the Mediator. Every “thank you, Lord” before a meal is carried by the same blood that carried the thief into paradise.

What he thanks God for. Not their numbers, generosity, organisation or strategic position, but their faith, which was being talked about across the world. Rome was the hub of the empire; travellers, traders, soldiers and slaves carried news out along every road, and something about these believers had got into the traffic. If people two countries away were talking about your church, what would they have heard? That it is large, well run, has good music, or holds the right line on a contested question? All of that can be true of a church whose faith is not what is being reported.

The oath. “God is my witness” — why swear to something as ordinary as praying for people? Because they had no way of checking, and reason to wonder. Paul had never been to Rome, did not found the church, and was openly hoping to use it as a base for a mission further west (15:24). Someone could easily conclude that the famous apostle’s interest was strategic. So he calls God to witness what no one else could verify: that for years, unseen, they had been on his list. And the word for his service, latreuō, is temple language — priestly worship. A former Pharisee applies it to talking about Jesus in rented rooms, workshops and prisons. He is not saying his work is like worship; it is the real thing, and the altar has moved outdoors.

“Without ceasing.” This phrase intimidates honest readers, so be clear what it does not mean. Paul made tents, argued in synagogues, sailed, wrote, ate and slept. The phrase means something regular and unremitting: these people never dropped off his list. A reader who takes it as a demand for continuous verbal prayer will conclude within a week that he cannot pray at all — the opposite of what it was written to produce. But there is a test in it. What fills your praying? For most of us, situations — the diagnosis, the interview, the money — and when the situation resolves, the subject disappears. Paul’s prayer was populated by people, most of them absent; in chapter 16 he greets some two dozen by name in a city he had never visited. And the Romans had no idea any of this was happening until the letter was read aloud. The same is probably true of you: somewhere an old woman, a friend from a church you left, or a parent mentions your name to God with a regularity you know nothing about, and some of what has held you up was never yours to see.

verseByVerse.quote: always in my prayers, asking that somehow by God's will I may now at last succeed in coming to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul keeps asking “that somehow by God’s will I may now at last succeed in coming to you.” He wants it intensely and submits it entirely to God.

“Now at last” is the sound of a long wait. He has often intended to come and been prevented (v. 13), and later says, “I have longed for many years to come to you” (15:23). A plan he believed was right, for the best reasons, had been blocked repeatedly for years, and he was still asking.

What he does not do. He does not decide the door is shut and stop asking. He does not conclude the desire itself was wrong — ambition dressed as mission — and that maturity means wanting nothing. Nor does he force it, overriding obstacles by determination. He keeps wanting it, keeps asking, and leaves the timing with God. That combination is rarer than it sounds. Most of us manage desire without submission, which is impatience, or submission without desire, which is resignation wearing a pious face. And “somehow by God’s will” is not the disclaimer “if it be your will” often becomes — attached in advance so that nothing has really been asked and nothing can fail. Paul asks for the specific thing, plainly and repeatedly, then submits the outcome. James says the same to people making business plans: “you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that’” (James 4:15). We are creatures who do not know if we will be alive on Thursday, and a plan that forgets that is not confident, just unrealistic.

When delays do not feel like providence. Most delays feel like a door closing for no reason: the job that went to someone else, the treatment that did not work, the years waiting for a child, the ministry you were sure God gave you that quietly failed. Paul did not always know what his delays were for. When the Spirit stopped him entering Bithynia (Acts 16:7), he was given no explanation; only later did a man from Macedonia appear in a dream. Often the meaning comes afterwards, and sometimes not in this life at all. So the honest form of this doctrine is not “every delay has a reason you will be shown”, but that the delays are not random and not neglect. The proof is in your hands. If Paul had reached Rome when he first wanted to, he would have preached there, and we would almost certainly not have this letter. The greatest exposition of the gospel ever written exists because a man could not get to the city he wanted and had to write instead.

And when the prayer was answered, it was in a form he had not asked for. He reached Rome as a prisoner, after arrest, two years in custody and a shipwreck, chained to a soldier at the empire’s expense (Acts 27–28). He got the city, not the itinerary. Acts ends with him welcoming all who came, “proclaiming the kingdom of God… with all boldness and without hindrance” (Acts 28:31) — remarkable words for a man under guard, and exactly what this prayer had asked for. You may be asking for something good, for the right reasons, and getting only closed doors. This verse does not promise the door will open on your terms. It promises that the one keeping it closed has not stopped listening.

verseByVerse.quote: For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you — that is, that we may be mutually encouraged by each other's faith, both yours and mine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul longs to visit “that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you” — and then corrects himself: “that is, that we may be mutually encouraged by each other’s faith, both yours and mine.” Even the apostle expected to receive from those he served.

A sentence that breaks. He starts confidently, everything flowing one way, from apostle to church. Then he hears himself, and “that is” is the sound of a man stopping mid-flow for a better sentence. He does not delete the first version; he lets us watch him revise it. The greatest theologian in church history heard a note of condescension in his own words and corrected it before the full stop. And it cost him something. Paul had seen the risen Christ and wrote Scripture; the Roman believers were tradesmen, slaves and immigrants, some only a year or two in the faith, and they could teach him nothing about justification. But he does not say he needs their knowledge. He says he will be encouraged by their faith — and faith is not expertise. A frightened woman still trusting God after a bad year has something the most learned person in the room cannot produce by knowing more. He can only watch it and be strengthened.

Both directions. If you are usually the one who teaches, leads, hosts or fixes, notice Paul’s picture of a strong Christian: not someone with no needs, but someone who knows he has them and says so to people less impressive than himself. If you are newer or quieter and think you are there only to receive, the apostle to the Gentiles was looking forward to being helped by people exactly like you. The body of Christ has no passengers, and also no one who attends only to give.

A test. When did you last tell another Christian plainly that you needed their help — not a general “please pray for me”, but the actual thing? If you cannot remember, you are living in a posture Paul refused, probably at a cost you have stopped noticing: the loneliness of the person everyone assumes is fine. Usually the reason is not humility, but that needing help means giving up being the one everyone depends on.

“Some spiritual gift.” Paul is not describing a technique for transferring a supernatural endowment, and he blurs the direction anyway by saying it will run both ways. He is deliberately vague — “some gift” — because he does not yet know what these people will need, and he trusts God to supply it when he arrives. That is a healthy model: go, be present, and expect God to provide the particular good you cannot specify in advance. And the strengthening comes through faith, theirs and his. So the currency of Christian encouragement is not cheerfulness, advice or competence, but someone in front of you still trusting God. That is why sitting with a believer who is suffering well can leave you steadier than a conference, and why the person who thinks a hard life leaves them nothing to offer has misunderstood what the church runs on.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented), in order that I may reap some harvest among you as well as among the rest of the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has often planned to come to Rome “(but thus far have been prevented)”, hoping to “reap some harvest among you as well as among the rest of the Gentiles.” His long absence was not indifference.

Correcting an impression. “I do not want you to be unaware, brothers” is a formula Paul uses when correcting something his readers might get wrong (11:25; 1 Thessalonians 4:13). Someone in Rome had surely noticed that the apostle to the Gentiles had worked the Mediterranean for twenty years without visiting the largest Gentile city on earth — and drawn an unflattering conclusion: he does not think we matter, or he avoids a church he did not found. Paul does not say he was too busy, though that was true. He says he was prevented, a word that puts someone behind the obstacle. The two accounts of the same year are very different to live inside. “I never got round to it” leaves you the manager of a life that is not going well. “I was prevented” leaves you a servant whose Master has other arrangements.

Harvest. Paul hopes to reap a harvest, not merely teach or hold meetings. Harvest is slow — no one reaps the week he sows. It is not manufactured — a farmer can plough, sow and water but cannot make one seed germinate: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6). And it is seasonal, which is why years of prevention did not mean the work was lost. A field not yet visited is not a field abandoned; it is a field not yet ripe. That matters to anyone sowing and seeing nothing: the parent who has prayed for a son for eleven years and watched him drift further away; the teacher of teenagers who seem to absorb nothing; the Christian at work, kind and honest for a decade and never once asked why. Scripture is honest that often “one sows and another reaps” (John 4:37). But the growing is not your department, and the absence of visible fruit in June says nothing about what is happening underground.

Even in a healthy church. The Roman believers’ faith was famous across the empire (v. 8), yet Paul still expects a harvest there — more conversions and growth. A healthy church is not a finished one. A building is completed and then maintained; a field is never finished, and is either being worked or going back to weeds.

So think of the situation you have privately written off: the relative who will never believe, the colleague too far gone, the part of your character you have decided is just how you are. Ask not when you stopped trying, but when you stopped expecting. The difference between Paul’s years of frustration and resignation is not only that he kept working, but that after all that time he was still planning a harvest in a city he had never seen.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “brothers” can include sisters in the church.

verseByVerse.quote: I am under obligation both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish. So I am eager to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome. — Romans 1:14–15
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I am under obligation both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish. So I am eager to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome.” “Greeks and barbarians” meant everyone: the cultured Greek-speaking world and everyone else, whose languages sounded to Greek ears like “bar-bar”. The gospel has no cultural prerequisites.

In debt to strangers. Paul does not say he is willing, burdened or available. He says he is a debtor — ledger language for a man who owes something not yet paid. How do you come to owe people you have never met, borrowed nothing from and never wronged? There are two ways to owe a man money. You can borrow from him, which Paul had not. Or someone can hand you a sum to deliver to him, so that you owe a stranger money that was never yours until it reaches his hand. That is Paul’s position. On the Damascus road he was given a message addressed to the nations, and from then on they had a claim on him — not because they earned it, but because what he had been handed was theirs.

That turns evangelism the right way up. If the gospel is my possession, telling someone is generosity, and generosity is optional and can wait until I feel equipped or they seem receptive. If the gospel is a delivery, none of that applies. A courier does not congratulate himself for handing over a parcel, nor decide the recipient looks unlikely to appreciate it. The only question is whether it arrives.

The whole field. “Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish”: two pairs, each covering everyone from opposite ends — the two groups a preacher instinctively avoids for opposite reasons. The sophisticated frighten us because they can argue and we fear we would lose; the unsophisticated bore or embarrass us or seem unpromising. Paul owes both; the church does not choose its creditors. The modern failure is usually not contempt but sorting: we build churches for people culturally like us and then find our gospel quietly shaped to fit them. So name the last five people you have spoken to about Christ, or would consider speaking to. How many are recognisably a version of you? If the list is uniform, the problem is not courage but an unconscious decision about who the message is for.

A guard. A debt can be preached in a way that crushes: if every conversation you did not have is a debt in arrears, a sensitive Christian can be flattened. But Paul feels not guilt but eagerness; the debt has become a desire. And he is one man who cannot reach Spain and Rome in the same year. Your debt is to the people God has actually put within your reach — the ones whose names you know, whose kitchens you sit in, who work at the next desk — not to the whole world. The post of apostle to the Gentiles is already filled.
verseByVerse.note: Greeks thought of all non-Greek speakers as “barbarians.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–17 — The Theme: The Righteousness of God by Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two verses. The entire letter in miniature. Everything Paul will argue across sixteen chapters is compressed here with the density of a diamond. "I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written: 'The righteous shall live by faith.'" This is the thesis statement of Romans, and it is the sentence that changed the world.

Martin Luther, tormented by the phrase "the righteousness of God" — understanding it as the terrifying standard by which God condemns sinners — wrestled with it until the light broke. "At last," he wrote, "meditating day and night...I began to understand that the righteousness of God is that by which the righteous lives by a gift of God, namely by faith. And this is the meaning: the righteousness of God is revealed by the gospel, namely, the passive righteousness with which the merciful God justifies us by faith. Here I felt that I was altogether born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates." The Reformation began in these two verses.

The gospel is power — not advice, not inspiration, not a moral framework, but the very power of God actively at work to save. It is power for salvation — not merely forgiveness of past sins, but the complete rescue of a human being from the dominion of sin and death and the wrath of God, and the restoration of that person to the full flourishing of life in God. And it is for everyone who believes — the one condition, the one instrument, the one hand that receives what God freely gives: faith.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Righteousness of God: Attribute or Gift?

Reformed exegesis has understood "the righteousness of God" in Romans 1:17 as a righteousness that originates with God and is given by God to the believing sinner — what the Reformers called iustitia aliena, an alien righteousness, a righteousness that is not our own. Luther's breakthrough was recognising that this righteousness is not the demanding standard that condemns but the gracious gift that saves. This is the doctrine of imputation: Christ's perfect righteousness is credited to the account of the believing sinner, so that God can be simultaneously just (the sin has been punished in Christ) and the justifier (the sinner is declared righteous). Calvin called this the "wonderful exchange" — Christ takes our sin; we receive his righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Luther's discovery of Romans 1:17 broke the back of a system of salvation by merit and religious performance that had enslaved Western Christendom for centuries. The Reformation was, at its heart, a rediscovery of these two verses. Now: Every generation re-erects the system of merit that the gospel demolishes. Every human heart, left to itself, believes it must earn its standing with God. Romans 1:16–17 is the permanent, repeatable antidote: the gospel is not something you do; it is something done for you, received by faith, given by the merciful God who justifies the ungodly.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. — Romans 1:16
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.” The negative implies real temptation to shame; Paul’s confidence rests not on bravado but on what the gospel is.

What there was to be ashamed of. Crucifixion was a deliberately degrading death, reserved for slaves, rebels and the lowest criminals; Roman citizens were normally exempt by law. Cicero argued that the very word should be kept away not only from a citizen’s body but from his thoughts, eyes and ears. Polite people did not discuss it, and Paul’s message for the capital of that world centres on a Jewish provincial executed that way. Scratched into plaster on the Palatine Hill in Rome, a century or two later, someone drew a figure on a cross with a donkey’s head and a man beside it raising his hand, with the words “Alexamenos worships his god.” To confess this gospel in Rome was to be the person everyone found faintly ridiculous. And Paul had private reasons too: run out of Philippi after a beating, hurried out of Thessalonica by night, politely dismissed in Athens, arriving in Corinth “in weakness and in fear and much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3). He has felt the pull repeatedly and decided where he stands.

“The power of God.” Paul does not say the gospel is true, reasonable or beautiful, though it is all three. He says it is the power of God for salvation — not a description of something powerful happening elsewhere, but the instrument God uses to do it. That is why ordinary preaching, and ordinary Christians saying ordinary things about Christ, keep producing results out of all proportion to the people involved. (One correction: preachers sometimes say this word gives us “dynamite”. The arrow points the other way — Nobel named his explosive after the Greek word. Paul’s word means effective might, power that accomplishes, not a blast.)

“To the Jew first and also to the Greek.” The only condition is faith: “everyone who believes”. “First” is a matter of sequence, not rank: the promises came to Israel, the Messiah came as Israel’s king, the preaching began in Jerusalem. Does it mean the church must take the gospel to Jewish people before others? Some read it as a standing priority in mission. The more likely reading is that it describes the order of salvation history, which Paul’s practice followed — the synagogue first, then the Gentiles (Acts 13:46). It does not put one people ahead in the queue. But it forbids the opposite error: Paul’s “heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved” (10:1), and a church that left Jewish people out of its witness would have forgotten whose promises it is preaching. In a Roman church divided between Jews and Gentiles, Paul settles what mattered most: one power, one condition, two peoples, one door.

Where shame lives. Almost no one reading this will be interrogated about Christ. Shame is quieter: the sentence begun and not finished; the disclaimer attached in advance — “I’m not really religious, but…”; the vague, edited account of your Sunday given to a colleague on Monday so that it will not invite a follow-up question. Watch for the edit this week. And the answer is not to work up more nerve. The verse gives an argument: I am not ashamed because it is the power of God. Confidence grows in the person who has seen it work — someone written off who became a Christian, a friend held together through what should have destroyed him.

And the deepest reason Paul can write this: Jesus “endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God” (Hebrews 12:2). Paul refuses to be ashamed of something his Lord was willing to be shamed for, and a servant has no ground to be more fastidious than his Master. No army carried this message and no philosophy underwrote it; it travelled the trade roads in the mouths of slaves, weavers and dockhands, and within three centuries it had emptied the temples of the empire that crucified its subject.

verseByVerse.quote: For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, 'The righteous shall live by faith.' — Romans 1:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the gospel “the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, ‘The righteous shall live by faith.’” Received by faith from first to last: not faith to begin and works to keep it going, but faith all the way.

Which “righteousness of God”? Everything turns on this phrase, and there are three readings: God’s own perfect righteousness, the standard he is; God acting to put things right; or a righteous standing God gives to people who have none. For a guilty person, the first would not be good news at all — it would restate the problem more clearly.

Luther. Martin Luther was a monk who took sin seriously enough to be broken by it. He fasted, kept vigils and confessed for hours until his confessor lost patience, and found no peace, because he knew the standard and he knew himself. For him this was the worst sentence in the Bible: more of God’s righteousness was the one thing he could not survive. He later admitted he had hated the phrase. Then it broke open. He saw that the righteousness revealed in the gospel is not the standard God demands but the standing God gives — not the righteousness by which he condemns but the righteousness with which he clothes — and he wrote that he felt “altogether born again” and had entered paradise “through open gates.” The Reformation came out of that sentence.

An alien righteousness. The Reformers called it iustitia aliena — alien in the sense of belonging to someone else. It is not produced in you but credited to you, as a sum is entered into an account that did not earn it. Christ’s obedience is counted as yours; your sin was counted as his and dealt with at the cross. Calvin called it the wonderful exchange. It is the only arrangement that lets God be “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (3:26): the debt really paid, not waived; the guilty really acquitted, not excused. And it “is revealed” — present tense. Every time the gospel is preached, the curtain goes back again.

Two tests. The merit system was not a medieval problem solved in the sixteenth century; it is the default setting of the human heart and reassembles itself in every generation, including in churches that would sign every Reformation confession. So: if you were asked tonight why God should accept you, what rises first — not what you would say in a Bible study? If it includes “I try”, “I have been”, or “at least I never”, your account is being kept in your own name. The gospel’s answer contains no information about you at all. And watch what happens to your sense of acceptance after you sin badly. If it drops and slowly recovers over a few days of doing better, you have discovered what you are living on. An alien righteousness does not fluctuate: the bad days do not lower the balance any more than the good days raised it.

Habakkuk. The prophet was not enjoying a settled faith; he was watching injustice go unanswered and being told the answer would come in a form he would not like, on a timetable he would not choose. Into that God said, “the righteous shall live by his faith” (Habakkuk 2:4) — a life held up by trusting God rather than by seeing results. So the faith that receives a righteousness you did not earn is the faith you go on living by afterwards, in the dark. Luther spent years trying to give God a righteousness God would accept, looking at the wrong side of the transaction. The gospel announces a righteousness from God, and the only hand that can take it is one that has stopped trying to make its own.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “from faith for faith” can also be rendered “beginning and ending in faith,” and the quotation “The one who by faith is righteous shall live.”

parallels.desc: the righteous shall live by his faith

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–32 — The Wrath of God and the Ruin of Idolatry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having announced the gospel, Paul immediately establishes why it is necessary. The gospel is good news only against the backdrop of very bad news — and the bad news Paul now delivers is as stark and unsparing as anything in Scripture. God's wrath is being revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men who suppress the truth in unrighteousness. The problem is not ignorance; it is suppression. Humanity knows God — knows him through creation, through conscience — and actively holds that knowledge down, refusing its implications, fleeing from its demands.

The structure of vv. 18–32 is a three-stage description of idolatry's logic and its consequences. First, the knowledge of God is suppressed (vv. 18–20). Then, God is exchanged for idols — images of creatures replacing the uncreated Creator (vv. 21–23). Then, God gives them up — three times that terrible phrase appears (vv. 24, 26, 28) — abandoning them to the sexual and moral dissolution that is both the consequence and the judgment of their idolatry. The wrath of God is not primarily a future event; it is a present reality, operating through the structure of a moral universe that reaps what it sows.

This passage is not a description of the worst of humanity — the serial killers and tyrants. It is a description of normal human culture operating without the restraining grace of God. The Rome to which Paul wrote would have recognised itself in these verses. So would every culture in every age. So would every human heart that is honest enough to look clearly at itself.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Wrath of God

Reformed theology has insisted, against every attempt to soften or allegorize it, that the wrath of God is real, personal, and active. It is not merely the impersonal outworking of a moral law (as C.H. Dodd argued), nor a primitive metaphor for natural consequences. It is the holy, settled, righteous opposition of the living God to everything that contradicts his character. Leon Morris showed definitively that in both Testaments, divine wrath is personal and purposeful — God's moral revulsion at sin, expressed in active judgment. The gospel is only fully good news when this wrath is fully real: Christ bore the wrath we deserved (3:25), and those who are in Christ are saved from the wrath to come (5:9).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's description of idol worship in vv. 22–23 — exchanging the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal creatures — described the Roman religious world exactly. The pantheon of Rome was populated by humanised gods and deified emperors, all of them creatures rather than Creator. Now: The idols have changed shape but not substance. We exchange the glory of God for the image of the successful career, the perfect family, the autonomous self, the entertained mind. Every idol is a creature thing promoted to Creator status — and Paul's analysis of the consequences (futile thinking, darkened hearts, moral dissolution) maps precisely onto what happens when any created thing is made to bear the weight only God can carry.

verseByVerse.quote: For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s first subject after his thesis is the bad news: “the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth.” The gospel is good news only against this background. The wrath is present, not only future, and its cause is not ignorance but suppression.

Not temper. Rome’s gods were famous for temper — capricious, easily offended, dangerous because unpredictable. If that were what Paul meant, the right response would be caution, not repentance. God’s wrath is not a mood. It is his settled, personal opposition to everything that ruins what he has made. It has no flare-ups and no bad days. It is the form love takes when it faces what is destroying its object; the parent who feels nothing on learning what was done to their child has not achieved serenity but stopped loving. Some have argued that “the wrath of God” in Paul is not an attitude in God at all but an impersonal process by which sin produces bad results — no one is angry; the machinery simply grinds. It does not survive the sentence. The wrath is revealed “from heaven”, the language of a throne; and the whole letter culminates in a cross that would be unnecessary if the problem were mismanaged consequences. If no one is angry, no one needed to die.

Ungodliness and unrighteousness. The first is the vertical failure, a wrong relation to God; the second the horizontal, a wrong relation to people. The order is deliberate: the rest of the chapter argues that the second always grows out of the first. Every item in the list at the end — envy, gossip, ruthlessness, broken promises — comes as a consequence. Society does not have a morality problem; it has a God problem, of which the morality is the symptom.

“Suppress.” The word means to hold something down by force — an action, not a condition. Think of holding a football under water in a swimming pool. Anyone can do it, but never for a moment does it happen by itself; the ball pushes up the whole time, and the instant your attention wanders it surfaces. That is Paul’s picture of unbelief: not an empty space where knowledge of God never arrived, but continuous effort to keep down something that keeps rising. Think of the moments when the pressure slips: at a graveside, when the usual explanations go thin; holding a newborn; somewhere so beautiful that you wanted to thank someone and there was no one to thank; three in the morning after bad news. Something surfaces — the sense that there is Someone, that you are known — and it is usually pushed back down within the hour. Paul’s claim is that the pushing is the whole story. No one is short of evidence; we are all working very hard.

A guard. The next fourteen verses have been used as ammunition more than almost any other passage. But the wrath is against the ungodliness of “men” — humanity, with no subgroup named. Paul is not describing a class of people his readers are safely distinct from, and as soon as the list ends he turns on the reader who has been enjoying it: “Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges” (2:1). If you finish this chapter feeling vindicated about someone else, you have read it as Paul expected, not as he intended.

Two revelations. In verse 17 God’s righteousness “is revealed”; in verse 18 his wrath “is revealed” — same verb, consecutive sentences. And there is one place where both were revealed at once. At the cross God’s wrath was displayed more terribly than in any judgment ever recorded, and it fell on the only man who never held the truth down. God put him forward as the propitiation (3:25), so that his people are “saved by him from the wrath of God” (5:9). That is why a Christian can read this verse without terror. The wrath is real and personal — and it has already landed somewhere, and that somewhere was not you.

verseByVerse.quote: For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has shown it to them. For his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What can be known about God is plain to all people, because God has shown it: “his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse.” This is general revelation: creation, as Calvin put it, is a theatre of God’s glory.

How much creation tells you. Paul is careful, and we often are not. He names two things: God’s eternal power and divine nature — that there is a God, immeasurably powerful, of a different order from everything he made. That is what a sunrise says. It does not say that God is merciful, that he has a Son, or that there is forgiveness for what you did. Creation gives enough light to know you are answerable, not enough to be saved — which is why Paul spends his life on roads and ships, and later asks, “How are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard?” (10:14). General revelation closes the mouth; only the gospel opens the door.

“Clearly perceived.” The unseen is plainly seen, as when you say you can see someone is exhausted: you see a face and read it. No one has watched a hand write a letter and observed a mind, yet only a fool would say the mind is unevidenced. The world works like handwriting. And this becomes something to check in yourself. Think of the last thing that genuinely stopped you: a night sky with no streetlights, music that went through you before you decided anything about it, the face of someone you love while they sleep, the fact that there is something rather than nothing. The response in the moment was not neutral observation; it was closer to awe, and awe responds to a someone. That reflex, Paul says, is the knowledge of God arriving. Then notice what you usually do with it thirty seconds later.

“Without excuse.” This is often heard as a claim that everyone secretly believes and is lying. It is a courtroom word: having no defence to offer. Paul is not saying no one is honestly confused, but that when the case is heard, no one will stand up and say the evidence was insufficient and God must concede. It is about what will be sayable on the last day.

Two guards. First, this is no licence for contempt. If this passage has ever made you feel superior in an argument, you have used a truth about the human race as a weapon against one member of it. The suppression it describes is yours too; it is why you can know God is real and still live for stretches of a week as though he were not. Second, for the anxious reader: this passage does not teach that people are condemned for what they could not have known. They are answerable for what they actually had, and God judges according to the light given (2:12); “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Genesis 18:25).

Can anyone be saved without hearing of Christ? Some Christians hold that God may save people who respond in faith to the light they have in creation, though they never hear the gospel, appealing to God’s justice and to believers outside Israel such as Melchizedek and Job. The more likely answer is no. Creation makes people answerable, but Paul never says it saves them, and he argues that saving faith depends on hearing the gospel (10:14); “there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). No one will be condemned for not believing a message he never heard; he will be judged for his sins against the light he had (2:12). That is why Paul’s answer to this question is not speculation but mission: “how are they to hear without someone preaching?” So the person who says he sees no evidence is standing inside it as he says so. Creation is God’s own voice, everywhere, all the time, and the human race’s remarkable achievement is not failing to hear it, but becoming so good at talking over it.

parallels.desc: the heavens declare the glory of God

verseByVerse.quote: For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools.” The fall described here is first a fall of worship: refusing to honour or thank the God they knew.

Not honouring him as God. This does not mean failing to praise loudly, but declining to give God his proper weight in the actual running of a life. It is possible to hold a correct belief in God and never let it cost a decision — to arrange your week, money, ambitions and bedtime exactly as you would if he were not there. That is not atheism; the Bible treats it as worse, because it knows and does not weigh.

Not giving thanks. This chapter ends in murder and malice, and the first item on the charge sheet is failing to say thank you. That looks like a category error until you see what gratitude is: admitting you received something you did not produce. And nothing about you was produced by you — not the lungs working without your attention, the intelligence you use to argue about God, the century you were born in, your parents, a country not at war, or the fact that you exist at all. Thanklessness is not rudeness; it is a claim about ownership: what I have, I hold by right, and owe no one for. No one has ever genuinely thanked God for something he believed he had earned.

You become what you worship. “Became futile” uses a word whose family, in the Greek Old Testament, is the standard term for idols — the vanities, the nothings. Jeremiah’s pun carries the indictment: they “went after worthlessness, and became worthless” (Jeremiah 2:5). The Psalms give the mechanism: idols “have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see… Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them” (Psalm 115:5, 8). Worship is not a transaction with an object but a transformation you undergo. Bow to something blind and deaf and you go blind and deaf — which is exactly what Paul reports: minds emptied, hearts darkened. And “were darkened” is passive: this is the first tremor of the phrase that will sound three times in the rest of the chapter — “God gave them up.” The lights did not fail; they were turned down in judgment. And a dark room is the one place where you cannot tell how dark it has become.

“Claiming to be wise.” The claim is the evidence of the folly. Paul is writing to the capital of a civilisation with law courts, aqueducts, libraries and four hundred years of philosophy, where serious men carried food to statues. He is not against learning — he is the most educated writer in the New Testament and quotes pagan poets when it suits him. The folly is not a shortage of information but a first-rate mind with its worship pointed at something that cannot bear the weight.

A test. You cannot usually see your own idol directly. But if we become like what we worship, look at what you are becoming and read backwards. More anxious and grasping over five years? You are probably worshipping something that can be taken from you. Harder, quicker to contempt? Something that requires hardness to keep. Exhausted and unable to rest? Something that never says “enough, well done”. Your character is sworn testimony about your worship, and unlike your doctrine it cannot be edited before submission. And that is why idolatry is a tragedy, not merely an offence: you will get what you chose. What you chose has no mouth to speak your name and no ears for anything you say to it in the dark, while the God you set aside is the only one in the transaction who could ever love you back.

parallels.desc: they went after worthlessness

verseByVerse.quote: and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul names what idolatry is: a trade. People handed over “the glory of the immortal God” and took in exchange images of things that die — men, birds, animals, creeping things. They shrank God to a size they could handle.

An exchange is chosen. Exchanged is the hinge of the chapter. An exchange is not a loss. It is a deal you make on purpose, because at the moment of the trade you prefer what you are getting. So Paul is not describing people who drifted or were misled. He is describing a swap somebody wanted. And look at the terms: on one side the weight and splendour of the God who cannot die; on the other, not even the creatures but images resembling them — copies. The trade runs from the living God to a picture of a lizard, and Paul lets the sentence make the argument.

The staircase only goes down. Man, then birds, then four-footed animals, then creeping things. Idolatry never levels out. Whatever a person puts in God’s place begins as something fairly impressive — a career, a cause, a person you admire, the self you are working towards. It does not stay there. The thing you serve keeps asking a little more and giving a little less, and the man who set out to be excellent at his work ends up unable to get through a meal without his phone. Nobody sets out to worship a creeping thing. The staircase does it for them.

Israel did it too. Paul is using Israel’s own words. Within weeks of hearing God at Sinai the nation made a calf: “They exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox that eats grass” (Psalm 106:20). Jeremiah: “But my people have changed their glory for that which does not profit. Be appalled, O heavens, at this” (Jeremiah 2:11–12). So Paul is not indicting pagans from a safe distance. He describes the human race in the language of Israel’s worst failure — which is what makes chapter 2 possible. The people with the true revelation did it faster and with less excuse.

What it looks like now. An idol is any created thing given the job that belongs to God. The question is not whether you own a statue. It is what you have quietly required a creature to do for you — make you feel significant, keep you safe, tell you that you turned out well after all. Created things can carry a great deal, but not that. A career cannot forgive you. A marriage cannot take away your shame. A child was never designed to be the meaning of a parent’s life, and a child handed that job will feel its weight long before either can name what has gone wrong.

A test. Take something you value and ask what losing it would do to you. If it went tomorrow — the job, the reputation, the health, the person — would you be grieved, or finished? Grief is what you feel when you lose a great gift. The floor giving way is what you feel when you lose a god. Then ask: what do I reach for first when I feel small? Not what I believe in — what I reach for. That reflex is worship.

The way back. This verse describes the race, not only you, and Paul is not building to “try harder not to do it.” The exchange is reversed when the glory that was traded away comes looking for the people who traded it: God “has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). They wanted a god they could look at. God gave them his Son, with a human face.

parallels.desc: they exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts to impurity, to the dishonoring of their bodies among themselves, because they exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever! Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“God gave them up.” This is the first of three times (vv. 24, 26, 28). God’s wrath here is not lightning. God hands people over to what they already want, and what they want ruins them. Verse 25 names the root: they “exchanged the truth about God for a lie” and served the creature instead of the Creator.

What “gave them up” means. The verb is a strong one — to hand over, as a court hands a prisoner to the jailer. So this is not God losing interest. It is a sentence. But notice what they are handed over to: “the lusts of their hearts.” Nothing is injected from outside. God “tempts no one” (James 1:13). He lifts the restraint that had been holding an existing desire in check, and lets the person have himself.

How it feels. That is more frightening than fire from heaven, because from the inside it feels like nothing. No announcement. If anything it feels like freedom: the resistance is weaker, the inner argument that once took an hour takes a minute and then stops happening. You do not feel a hand come off your shoulder. You only notice, if at all, that you move more easily than you used to.

A test. Is there something that used to trouble your conscience and no longer does? Not something you thought through, repented of, or honestly came to see differently. Something that simply went quiet — a habit that once cost you a bad evening and now costs nothing; a way of speaking about your wife or a colleague that would have embarrassed you five years ago; a compromise at work that no longer feels like a decision. If you can name one, do not be relieved that the discomfort has gone. The discomfort was the restraint. Bring it back into the light today.

The sentence fits the sin. In verse 21 they refused God honour; here they are given up to “the dishonoring of their bodies.” Withhold from God the weight that is his and you do not keep it for yourself; you lose your own. “Among themselves” adds the last turn: no outside power does this to them. It is what they do to one another once nothing holds them back.

The lie. The Greek has “the lie,” not just any lie. It was first told in a garden: “you will be like God” (Genesis 3:5). Every idolatry since is a variation on it. Today it is rarely held as a theory. It is lived as the reasonable conviction that you are the best judge of what your life is for. And they “worshiped and served” — two verbs. Worship is not only what you revere but what you serve: what you arrange your hours around, what gets first call on your energy and the last word in your decisions. Check your diary and bank statement. They are less polite than your conscience and better informed.

The doxology. In the middle of the darkest paragraph he ever wrote, Paul cannot say “the Creator” without stopping to bless him: “who is blessed forever! Amen.” This tells you two things. God is not diminished by being exchanged — idolatry does not injure God; it destroys the idolater. And the man writing this list is a worshipper, not a prosecutor. Anyone who recites Romans 1 with relish has the content and has missed the author.

The hope. Paul uses the same verb twice more in this letter. Jesus “was delivered up for our trespasses” (4:25), and God “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (8:32). God handed sinners over to what they chose; then he handed his Son over to what they deserved. The second handing-over is the answer to the first, which is why this sentence has never been the last word about anyone willing to have it lifted.
verseByVerse.note: “Gave them up” means God handed them over to what they chose — his judgment working through their own desires.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason God gave them up to dishonorable passions. For their women exchanged natural relations for those that are contrary to nature; and the men likewise gave up natural relations with women and were consumed with passion for one another, men committing shameless acts with men and receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now gives one example of being “given up.” Men and women exchanged natural sexual relations for relations with their own sex. His argument is that idolatry causes sexual disorder, not the other way round. When the creature’s relationship to the Creator is turned upside down, everything downstream is disordered too. The “due penalty” is already present in the distortion itself.

Why this example. Many readers arrive at this passage already wounded, so it needs to be taken slowly and in the right order. Paul’s argument is that idolatry is an exchange — the creature put where the Creator belongs. He chooses a case where the exchange is visible in the created order itself, so that the shape of the sin matches the shape of the idolatry. He is not ranking sins.
