The list ends a few verses later with envy, gossip, boasting and disobeying parents, under the same verdict.

What Paul teaches. Say it plainly, because vagueness here is its own unkindness. Paul regards these acts as contrary to how God made men and women. He grounds that not in the customs of his day but in creation — which is why his word is nature, and why the passage reaches back past Moses to Genesis. The church has read him this way for two thousand years.

The other reading. Many now hold that Paul had in mind the exploitative forms common in his world — men using boys, sex with slaves, temple prostitution — or people acting against their own natural desires; and that nature means only custom, so committed same-sex partnerships were not in view. But the text does not bear this out. Paul says the men “were consumed with passion for one another,” which describes mutual desire, not one party exploiting another, and he says nothing about age, payment or force. He includes women in v. 26, whom the explanation about boys cannot cover. And nature points back to the creation of male and female (Gen 1:27; 2:24), the ground Jesus himself gives for marriage (Matt 19:4–6). The rest of Scripture speaks with one voice (Lev 18:22; 1 Cor 6:9–11; 1 Tim 1:10). The church’s historic reading stands.

A description of the race, not a diagnosis of a person. The sentence is corporate throughout — they, humanity in the dock — tracing what happens to a civilisation that lets go of God. It does not say that a fifteen-year-old who finds he is attracted to other boys got there by personally trading God for an idol, and anyone who tells him so has gone beyond what Paul wrote. Nobody chooses what they find themselves wanting. Every person is answerable for what they do with it — and that is true of every desire in this chapter, including the more socially convenient ones.

Temptation is not sin. Our Lord “in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). An unwanted desire, however persistent, is not itself guilt. A same-sex-attracted Christian who has spent years refusing to act on it is not failing at holiness. He is doing it — a harder version than most of his congregation is asked to do. He is not in a category of his own. He is a Christian saying no to something he wants, which is the ordinary work of every believer, and it costs him more.

The real burden is often loneliness. The church asks such a brother or sister, in effect, for lifelong celibacy without the supports that have made celibacy bearable for anyone who managed it: deep friendship, a household to belong to, a place at someone’s table on ordinary Tuesdays, people who notice when they are ill. A church that preaches this passage is obliged to be the family it is asking people to do without. Ask yourself who in your church that would mean inviting this month.

For the parent. Someone reading this was recently told something by a son or daughter and has not slept properly since. Two things are true together: you may hold what you believe, and you may keep your child. It is not compromise to go on eating together, to be at the birthdays, to be the one they ring when something goes wrong. Nothing here tells you to withdraw your affection, and the Gospels show whose houses your Lord sat in. The relationships that survive are the ones through which anything true can travel later.

The trap Paul sets. Paul knows the warm feeling a religious reader gets here — not one of those — and he springs the trap three sentences later: “Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things” (2:1). Anyone who has used these verses as a weapon has walked into it.

Such were some of you. Paul lists the sexually immoral, adulterers, men who practise homosexuality, thieves, the greedy, drunkards, revilers and swindlers, and then tells the Corinthians: “And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11). The first Christians read such lists as a description of the people sitting next to them, and of themselves. The past tense was their whole hope, as it is ours.

verseByVerse.quote: And since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God gave them up to a debased mind to do what ought not to be done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third “gave them up.” Because they “did not see fit to acknowledge God,” God handed them over to “a debased mind” — a mind that can no longer judge rightly — so that they do “what ought not to be done.” The mind that would not think about God loses the ability to think straight about what matters.

The wordplay. “Did not see fit” and “debased” come from the same root (see the note). They tested God and marked him rejected; God tested them and marked them rejected. The verdict they passed on him became the verdict passed on them.

A debased mind is not a stupid one. The word was used of a coin or metal that failed the test — it looks right and weighs right, but it is not good currency. So this mind still reasons, argues, builds bridges, writes laws and wins prizes. Its horsepower is untouched. What has gone is its ability to reach the right conclusion about anything that matters. That is why highly sophisticated societies have organised atrocities with excellent paperwork. Intellect was never the safeguard. It is a tool, and it works just as hard for a lie.

What they refused. Not knowledge of God — verses 19–20 settled that they had it. They would not keep him in view, would not let him remain a live consideration. That is not lecture-hall atheism. It is practical atheism, open to people who would tick the right box on a survey: God is not denied, just not consulted, and the mind quietly reorganises itself around his absence.

The chapter comes full circle. It began with the mind: “they became futile in their thinking,” and “claiming to be wise, they became fools” (vv. 21–22). It ends with the mind handed over. The organ used to commit the crime is the one confiscated. It takes a mind to argue yourself out of what you know; the punishment is that God stops preventing the argument from succeeding.

Their own standard. “What ought not to be done” uses the language of the Stoic moralists, who spoke of actions fitting for a rational creature. The charge is not only that pagans broke Moses’ law, which they never had. They fall short of the standard their own best thinkers set.

A test anyone can run. Everyone still has a list of things that ought not to be done — including people who will tell you morality is a social construct. Watch what happens when one is done to them: the promise broken, the confidence betrayed, the credit taken by someone else. Nobody is a relativist about being wronged. That instant outrage is an appeal to a law by someone who has just denied there is one. It is the last working instrument in a debased mind, and the reason no one will be able to say the standard was never known.

The cure. Paul answers with the same word eleven chapters later: “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect” (12:2). Testing there is the very thing the mind of 1:28 can no longer do. The condition is real and it is reversible. But you cannot reason your way out of a broken way of reasoning using the faculty that is broken. It takes a voice from outside, applied over years — which is what Scripture is for. So read it daily, let it argue with you, and expect your judgment to change. The new mind is one more thing God hands over.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay: because they did not “see fit” (edokimasan) to acknowledge God, he gave them up to a “debased” (adokimon, literally “unfit”) mind.

verseByVerse.quote: They were filled with all manner of unrighteousness, evil, covetousness, malice. They are full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, maliciousness. They are gossips,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The vice list begins. People are “filled with all manner of unrighteousness” — not brushed by it but saturated, like a vessel with no room left. The list runs from inner dispositions (covetousness, malice) to sins against others (envy, murder, strife, deceit), and ends this verse with “gossips.”

No dividing line. Anyone can read murder and feel safely excluded. Then the sentence carries on to envy, strife, deceit — and arrives, with no change of tone, at gossips. Paul puts the sin that ends a life and the sin that runs in the car park after the service into one catalogue, on purpose. There is no point in this chapter where the serious sins stop and the acceptable ones begin.

Filled. The word is passive. A person handed over to himself does not stay level; he fills up. Sin is not a stain that stays where it lands. It is a liquid that finds every space in the container.

An ordinary week. Take the items one by one and you have an ordinary week in an ordinary office: wanting what a colleague has and being unable to be glad for him; carrying on an argument for the pleasure of winning; the small deceit that makes you look better than the facts; the ill-will you would never act on but enjoy holding. These are not the sins of monsters. They are the sins of people who are pleasant to have lunch with — which is why this chapter is more dangerous to its readers than it first looks.

Covetousness. The settled resentment that someone else has what you should have had. It is the one commandment invisible from outside: you can keep all the others in public and break this one continuously in a room by yourself. That is why it flourishes in respectable people, and why Paul calls it idolatry (“covetousness, which is idolatry,” Colossians 3:5).

Gossip. The Greek word sounds like what it describes — a whisperer, a low voice behind a hand. Gossip makes a person who is not in the room smaller, at no cost to the speaker. It produces a warm feeling of closeness between the people talking, paid for with someone else’s reputation. It is often accurate, which is its best disguise, and usually spoken in a tone of concern, which is the disguise under that one.

A test. Think over the last three conversations you had about someone who was not present. Would you have said it in the same words if they had walked in halfway through? And what were you hoping the listener would think — about them, or about you? Most gossip is not about the absent person at all. It is a way of arranging myself favourably in someone’s mind, using a friend as material. If one of those conversations fails the test, go back to the listener and set the record straight.

Why the list is so long. Paul is not enjoying himself. He needs every reader to reach chapter 3 unable to plead anything, so that “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (3:23) lands as a description, not an insult. The list is long because it has to reach everybody. The word gossips was put there for the respectable reader who had been nodding along.

verseByVerse.quote: slanderers, haters of God, insolent, haughty, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, foolish, faithless, heartless, ruthless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list goes on: slanderers, “haters of God,” insolent, haughty, boastful, “inventors of evil,” disobedient to parents, and finally “foolish, faithless, heartless, ruthless.” Hatred of God is the root made explicit. The list ends not in violence but in coldness — love itself switched off.

Haters of God. Almost nobody owns this phrase. You will find people who doubt God or resent the church; you will look a long time for someone who says he hates God. What does it look like from inside? A sense that God is a rival — that his claims and your happiness pull in opposite directions, so every command feels like something taken from you rather than something kept safe for you.

A test. When you learn that something you enjoy is out of bounds, watch the first reaction, before the one you would say aloud. Sorrow at being in the wrong — or irritation at being interfered with? And when a moral claim you had assumed turns out not to apply to you after all, is the feeling relief? Relief at being released from an obligation to God is the tell. Nobody feels relief at being released from the love of someone they actually love.

Inventors of evil. Invention is a glory — the image of God in a creature who makes things. Here it is conscripted. People apply imagination, effort and real ingenuity to finding wrongs nobody had thought of yet. Every tool the race has made has been improved for harming people, usually within a generation. You can see it early: no child needs lessons in finding the sentence that will hurt a sibling most. Cruelty is inventive on its own. Kindness has to be taught.

Heartless, faithless. “Heartless” is the Greek word for family affection — the love between parent and child that needs no persuading — with a negative in front: without natural affection. The collapse goes so deep that it takes out the one love nobody has to be talked into. Its neighbour, “faithless,” describes someone who does not keep an agreement: whose signature means nothing, who says he will be there and is not.

From the cosmos to the kitchen. The chapter opened in the heavens, with God’s eternal power seen in everything made. It ends in a house: a child who cannot rely on a parent, a promise never meant to be kept, a table where nobody feels much any more. That is where the damage is finally measured.

A guard. Someone will reach heartless and go cold, because they have felt nothing for months — a mother who cannot find the love for her baby everyone said would come, a man numb at his father’s funeral, someone so exhausted or depressed that affection will not switch on. That is not what Paul describes. He describes a hardness that is chosen, defended and finally preferred. Numbness that grieves you is not hardness of heart; it is a symptom, and your distress is the proof. The people in this verse are not distressed. If this is you, tell your pastor and your doctor; it is not a verdict on your soul.

Who the witnesses are. Most of these items are invisible to colleagues and obvious to the people you live with. So do not ask whether they apply. Ask who the jury is. On heartless, ruthless and faithless it is not the people who see you for an hour on a Sunday. It is the ones who see you on a Tuesday evening when you are tired and nobody is watching. Ask one of them, and listen.

verseByVerse.quote: Though they know God's righteous decree that those who practice such things deserve to die, they not only do them but give approval to those who practice them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The indictment ends at its worst point. People know God’s verdict — that such things deserve death — and they not only do them but applaud others who do them. Doing wrong is bad; celebrating it, knowing it is wrong, is a deeper darkness.

They still know. Count the times knowledge has appeared: what can be known about God “is plain to them” (v. 19); “although they knew God” (v. 21); “they did not see fit to acknowledge God” (v. 28); now, “though they know God’s righteous decree.” Not one of these is a charge of ignorance. The human problem is not a shortage of light but what is done with it. Even at the bottom, the knowledge is still there.

“Deserve to die.” This sounds disproportionate to a modern reader. But Paul is not proposing a penalty for anyone to carry out. He is stating what these things weigh, and he will explain why: “the wages of sin is death” (6:23). Wages, not a punishment invented from outside. If God is the source of life, a settled turning away from him has only one end. Calling it a sentence is God telling the truth about where the road goes.

Why applause is worse than the act. Three practical reasons. A man who does wrong and knows it is still at war with himself, and that war is the last thing standing between him and ruin; approval ends the war and dismantles what might have called him back. Approval costs nothing — you can give it from an armchair, endlessly. And approval recruits: doing wrong damages you; applauding it produces more of it in others, the difference between having an illness and being a carrier. A society is not destroyed by the presence of sin; every society has plenty. It is destroyed when it begins to praise it.

Small and silent. Don’t look only for loud public endorsement, which lets almost everyone off. Approval is mostly small: the laugh you gave because not laughing would be awkward; the anecdote passed on because it was entertaining. Above all, we consume as entertainment behaviour that would appal us in our own street — and watching for pleasure is not neutral. It is a small vote, cast repeatedly, for more of it.

A guard. Not every silence is approval. Sometimes speaking would be self-righteous, sometimes it is not your business, sometimes you must earn the right to be heard. Paul is not asking you to object to everything. The line falls where your silence does work you would be embarrassed to admit — where you said nothing not from wisdom but because you wanted to be liked.

A test. Name something you would be ashamed to be caught doing and are perfectly happy to be entertained by others doing. Then ask what the difference is. Paul’s answer is that there is not much of one, and that the second is the one he chose to end on. Change the habit, starting with what you choose to watch this week.

He does not stop here. The next words are “Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges” (2:1). The reader who has been shaking his head at the world is exactly the one the next sentence is waiting for. The chapter ends with everyone deserving death, and the letter was written because its author knew Someone who died in their place.

They are full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, maliciousness. They are gossips,<sup>30</sup>slanderers, haters of God, insolent, haughty, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents,<sup>31</sup>foolish, faithless, heartless, ruthless.<sup>32</sup>Though they know God’s righteous decree that those who practice such things deserve to die, they not only do them but give approval to those who practice them.

2.title: God's Impartial Judgment
2.overview:
Chapter 1 ended with a catalogue of Gentile vice that a first-century Jewish reader would have heard with satisfaction, nodding along at the depravity of the pagan world. Chapter 2 turns without warning on that same reader: "Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges." The trap is sprung. The person who condemns the sins of others while practising the same things is not morally superior to the Gentile; he is, Paul argues, in an even more culpable position — because he knows better.

Paul's target in chapter 2 is not the pagan but the moralist — specifically, the Jewish moralist who believes that covenant membership and religious privilege provide a buffer against divine judgment. They do not. God's judgment is impartial: He renders to each according to his works, to Jew and Gentile alike. The Gentile who has only the law of conscience will be judged by that; the Jew who has the law of Moses will be judged by that. In either case, the verdict will be the same: all fall short.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — God's Righteous and Impartial Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The rhetorical brilliance of Romans 2:1 is breathtaking. Paul has spent fifteen verses describing the moral ruin of the Gentile world — and now he wheels on the approving reader: "Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things." The knife Paul had been pointing at the Gentile he now turns on anyone who imagines that moral judgment of others places them above judgment themselves.

The principle Paul establishes is foundational: God's judgment is according to truth (v. 2), according to works (v. 6), without partiality (v. 11). These three principles together demolish every form of religious self-satisfaction. "According to truth" means God sees through performance to reality. "According to works" means the whole life is the evidence, not merely the religious moments. "Without partiality" means no ethnic or covenant privilege exempts anyone from accountability before the Judge of all the earth.

Verses 14–15 introduce the remarkable teaching about the conscience as a moral witness — Gentiles who do not have the Torah nonetheless "show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness." This is Paul's doctrine of moral general revelation: human beings are not morally blank. The conscience, however distorted by sin, retains something of the moral law written at creation. This is why all human beings, without exception, will have no excuse on the day of judgment.

Two things in this section deserve naming here, because they are easily lost between the principles. The first is verse 4, the warmest sentence in the passage and the most often misread: the riches of God’s kindness and forbearance and patience are not evidence that he does not mind. They are “meant to lead you to repentance”. Every day on which judgment does not fall is not indifference; it is an invitation still being held open — and Paul’s charge is that we presume on it, reading the delay as a verdict already returned in our favour. The second is verse 16, which tells us when this happens and who conducts it: “on that day when, according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus”. The Judge is not a principle but a person with a face, and the material to be weighed is not the record other people can see but the secrets. Which is the most frightening sentence in the chapter, or the most freeing — since for those who are his, the one who will weigh what nobody else knows about them is the one who died for it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgment According to Works

Romans 2:6–11 appears to teach salvation by works — "to those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality, he will give eternal life." Reformed exegesis has understood this as describing the principle of judgment (God will judge the whole life) rather than the means of salvation (which is faith alone). The person who truly seeks God from the heart will be given — by grace — the faith that produces the works that evidence genuine conversion. Works are the evidence of salvation, never its ground. Paul is not contradicting 1:16–17; he is establishing the standard of divine judgment that makes grace necessary for everyone.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish confidence in covenant privilege — circumcision, Torah, temple — as a buffer against divine judgment was a live pastoral issue in Paul's day. Many Jews believed that while Gentiles might face judgment, the covenant people were secure by virtue of their membership. Paul demolishes this with surgical precision. Now: The equivalent today is the nominal Christian who trusts in baptism, church membership, or moral respectability as a substitute for genuine faith and repentance. Paul's word is the same: God is not impressed by religious credentials. He is looking for the transformed heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things. We know that the judgment of God rightly falls on those who practice such things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul turns on the reader who agreed with chapter 1. If you condemn others for these things, you condemn yourself, because you do the same things. God’s judgment, unlike ours, falls “rightly” — by the truth, without the exemptions we grant ourselves.

The trap. Paul spent fifteen verses on idolatry, sexual chaos, envy, gossip and family breakdown, knowing exactly what a religious reader does with such a passage: he agrees, warmly. And every nod establishes in his mind that he is the kind of person who can tell the difference. Then therefore arrives, and the paragraph he has been applauding turns out to be a mirror. The address changes too. Chapter 1 was plural — they. Now it is singular: “O man.” Paul rounds on one imagined listener, as lecturers of his day did, and nobody can pass this verse on to someone else. It is addressed to the person holding the letter.

“The very same things.” The obvious protest is: I have never done what that man did. Paul means the same basic disorder, not an identical list. But the mechanism works in all of us daily. We judge others by their actions and ourselves by our intentions. Another man is short with his child — he is impatient; I am short with mine — I had a hard day. He didn’t reply because he is unreliable; I didn’t because I was busy. Same act, two headings, filed automatically before any conscious dishonesty, which is why it is so hard to catch. Jesus gave the permanent picture: the speck in your brother’s eye and the log in your own (Matthew 7:3–5). The log is in the eye — lodged in the very organ you are using to look at him. That is why the man with the worst vision is usually the most confident about what he sees.

A test. Take the last ordinary thing you did wrong and describe it in one sentence, in the words you would use if your brother-in-law had done it. Most of us find we have two vocabularies for sin and know which to reach for. A second probe: notice which sins make you angry out of all proportion. The disproportion is often information — the fury is at something nearer home.

A guard. Paul is not forbidding moral judgment. He has just made severe ones, and later he tells churches to deal with sin. Jesus does not stop at the log either: “first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye” (Matthew 7:5). The speck still comes out. What changes is the order — and a man who has just removed a log from his own eye handles other people very differently.

The kindness in it. Paul is not scoring a point. He is moving a man out of the one position from which the gospel cannot be received. Everything this letter offers is for the guilty; grace has nothing to say to the innocent, and self-approval is a locked door. “You have no excuse” sounds like the end of the argument. It is the first moment the reader becomes eligible for anything.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you suppose, O man — you who judge those who practice such things and yet do them yourself — that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul names two errors of the religious moralist. He assumes he will escape judgment, and he mistakes God’s patience for approval. But God’s kindness is not indifference. It is “meant to lead you to repentance.”

The unspoken assumption. “Do you suppose… that you will escape?” Nobody says that aloud. It is an assumption beneath the beliefs, and Paul drags it into daylight so the man hears it in his own voice. And the logic is strange: he condemns a thing in others, does it himself, and expects a different outcome. He has quietly made himself the exception, with no argument at all — just a sense that his case is different.

Kindness, forbearance, patience. Three words stacked. Kindness is God’s active goodness, not mere tolerance. Forbearance is holding back what could justly be done. Patience is literally “long temper,” the opposite of a short fuse. This is not a God who does not notice. He notices, is entitled to act, and does not — yet.

What presumption sounds like. It rarely sounds defiant. It sounds reasonable: “It can’t be that serious, or something would have happened by now.” “I’ve done this for six years and my life has improved.” “God knows what I’m like and has made his peace with it.” Each argues from silence and treats a stay of execution as an acquittal. A prisoner whose appeal is pending is not free because the corridor is quiet.

Kindness has a destination. It is “meant to lead you” — God’s goodness is not a backdrop but an agent at work on you. The mercies you enjoy are not evidence the subject is closed. They are the means by which it is being reopened.

A test. Think of the good things of the last year — the recovery, the friendship, the provision, the disaster that didn’t happen. What did they produce in you: gratitude, a softening, movement toward God? Or a quiet confidence that the account is in order? The same kindness does both, depending on the man it lands on. Sun softens wax and hardens clay. Thank God specifically for one of them today and ask what he means by it.

A guard. Someone will read this and conclude they have used up their allowance and the offer has expired for them. Read it again. It is not a warning that kindness is running out but a complaint that it is being wasted — and you cannot waste what has stopped being given. That this frightens you is proof the kindness is still at work, because it is exactly what a hardened man does not feel. Presumption is comfortable. It does not lie awake.

Where it leads. The destination is not the dock but repentance — home. God waited out the golden calf, the judges, the kings, the stoned prophets and four hundred silent years, and went on waiting while men sharpened the charges against his Son (cf. 2 Peter 3:9). He is slow not because he is indifferent but because he means to bring home everyone he came for.

parallels.desc: slow to anger

verseByVerse.quote: But because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath when God's righteous judgment will be revealed. He will render to each one according to his works:
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hard, unrepentant heart is not just failing to earn credit; it is storing up wrath for “the day of wrath,” when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed. On that day God “will render to each one according to his works” — works as the evidence of what the heart really is.

A treasury. Paul has been using banking language. Verse 4 spoke of the “riches” of God’s kindness. Verse 5 says you are literally treasuring up wrath — the verb Jesus used: “lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven” (Matthew 6:20). So this is not a man drifting toward a bad end. He is making deposits, daily. Everyone is building a treasury; the question is what goes into it.

Hard. Hardness is not a mood but a condition, like a callus. Nobody decides to grow one. It forms slowly under repeated friction, and its whole function is to stop you feeling what happens at that spot. That is why hardness is almost impossible to diagnose from inside: the symptom is the loss of the sensation that would have reported it.

Impenitent. When did you last actually repent — not feel bad, not resolve to do better, not endure the sick feeling of being caught? Scripture separates these in one week: Judas was sorry enough to die of it, and Peter “wept bitterly.” Only one came back. The difference is not the amount of feeling. Remorse is about me — what I have lost, how I look. Repentance is about God — I agree with him about the thing, and I turn. Remorse can be intense and leave a man exactly where it found him.

A test. Take something you know is wrong in your life and ask what has actually happened about it in six months. Has anything changed, in some observable direction? Or only a cycle of failure, discomfort and a private promise nobody expects you to keep? A repenting heart moves. A regretting heart circles and mistakes the circling for movement because there is so much feeling in it. If it is circling, name it to God and to one other person this week.

Revealed. The word keeps returning: God’s righteousness revealed (1:17), his wrath revealed (1:18), and now his righteous judgment revealed. Everything hidden is on a schedule to be uncovered. Nothing is being lost; it is being kept.

“According to his works.” Paul is quoting his Bible (Psalm 62:12; Proverbs 24:12), and David puts it beside something else: “to you, O Lord, belongs steadfast love. For you will render to a man according to his work” (Psalm 62:12). Steadfast love and exact recompense in one breath. And “each one” — not nations or groups, nobody graded on a curve or lost in the crowd. Unnerving, and the only arrangement that could be just.

Works and faith. Judgment by works and justification by faith answer different questions. Works are evidence produced in court, not payment made at the counter. A tree is not made alive by its fruit, but at harvest the fruit is inspected. And the balance can be changed — not by improving your deposits, which is the one remedy that cannot work, but by being credited with an account that was never yours (see 1:17; 3:21–26).

parallels.desc: you will render to a man according to his work

verseByVerse.quote: to those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality, he will give eternal life; but for those who are self-seeking and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, there will be wrath and fury.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two destinations. To those who patiently keep doing good, seeking “glory and honor and immortality,” God gives eternal life. To the “self-seeking” who obey unrighteousness rather than the truth come “wrath and fury.” Sin here is not weakness but allegiance — a rival master willingly served.

The difficulty. State it honestly. Paul says the gospel saves “everyone who believes” (1:16) and that a person “is justified by faith apart from works of the law” (3:28). Here he says God gives eternal life to those who persist in doing good. Taken alone, that teaches salvation by works. Either Paul contradicts himself within two chapters, or we have misread what the sentence is doing.

The standard, not the means. From v. 2 to v. 16 Paul is describing how God’s court works — impartially, by truth, by the whole life. He states the law’s own terms at full strength because his argument needs everyone to agree the standard is fair before he shows that nobody meets it. The verdict comes at 3:23: “all have sinned.” Verses 7–8 state the principle; chapter 3 gives the finding. The offer is genuine. Anyone who lived an uninterrupted life of patient well-doing really would receive eternal life. It is like a scholarship for candidates with a flawless record: the terms are honest, the money is real, and nobody collects — not because the committee is dishonest.

What a Christian life looks like. There is a second thing here. Look at the words: “patience” — endurance under weight, staying at it — and “seek” — not having arrived, but oriented. Paul is describing a direction, not a spotless record. And both groups are seeking. The question the last day puts to a life is what it was after. Wanting glory, honour and immortality is not condemned; it is the right ambition. The second group’s fault is not that they wanted much but that they wanted it for themselves and settled far too cheaply.

A test. Don’t audit this month. Draw a line through the last five years. Is there anything you now hate that you used to excuse? Anything you now do that once seemed impossible? Is God more to you than he was, or less? A car that stalls often is still going somewhere; a car revving in neutral is not, however loud. Paul says “patience” because he expects interruptions. The question is the direction of travel.

A guard. If you read verse 7 and conclude you fall short of it, you read it correctly — the man who thinks he qualifies has misread it. Verse 7 is a mirror, and the letter goes on to tell you who kept these terms. Christ endured patiently, did good without a break, sought his Father’s glory, and never once obeyed unrighteousness. What he earned is given to people who plainly did not. So the works here are real and they matter, but they are never the currency. Your patient well-doing is not the payment for eternal life. It is the evidence it has already been given to you.

verseByVerse.quote: There will be tribulation and distress for every human being who does evil, the Jew first and also the Greek, but glory and honor and peace for everyone who does good, the Jew first and also the Greek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul repeats the two outcomes in reverse order: “tribulation and distress” for everyone who does evil, “glory and honor and peace” for everyone who does good — “the Jew first and also the Greek” both times. Being first in privilege means being first in accountability.

Said twice, on purpose. Verses 7–8 ran good then evil; verses 9–10 run evil then good. Read either way and you reach the same two outcomes and the same phrase, “the Jew first.” Paul does not want to be misheard.

Narrow space. “Tribulation” is pressure, crushing under weight. “Distress” literally means a narrow place — hemmed in, no room to turn. The end of a life without God is not pictured as a distant fire but as a closing in. And that is the shape sin takes even now. Every temptation presents itself as enlargement — more freedom, more experience. Then watch what it delivers over twenty years. The drinker’s world shrinks to one room and one bottle. The bitter woman’s life organises itself around a single grievance she cannot put down. The pornography habit that promised variety leaves a man unable to look at his own wife properly. The world gets smaller. Final judgment is this, continued, with the restraints gone.

Glory, honour, peace. Against that: peace — for a Jewish reader, shalom, everything in its proper place and working; and glory, which in Hebrew carries the idea of weight and substance. The contrast is expansion against contraction: a life given room to become what it was made for, or one closing in until nothing is left but what it chose.

“The Jew first.” Every Jewish believer knew what first meant: first called, first given the promises and the law. Paul uses the same word about the dock. Amos said it more bluntly: “You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities” (Amos 3:2). Therefore. Election is the ground of the stricter reckoning, not an exemption. Jesus: “Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required” (Luke 12:48).

Who is first today. The person raised in a Christian home who cannot remember not knowing the gospel. The one who has sat under good preaching for thirty years, owns four Bibles and has friends praying for him by name. Each is a mercy, and each is an entry on the account. The most dangerous seat in church is not the back row. It is the one held by someone who has heard everything and been changed by very little.

A test. Recall the last time a sermon or passage really landed — “that is about me, and it is true.” What changed in the seven days after? Not what you felt; what changed by the next Sunday. Do that for the last three times you remember, and you have a fair measure of what your light is doing in you.

If that frightens you. First runs both ways: first in accountability, first in the offer. The gospel has come to you — the very mercy now unsettling you. And the weight of the greater light was carried by the one man who had all of it and wasted none. He was crushed so the narrowing could stop, and what he opens is room.

verseByVerse.quote: For God shows no partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“God shows no partiality.” His judgment does not tilt toward the Jew, the moral, the religious or the respectable. He applies the same standard to everyone — which is why no human advantage counts before him, and why justification has to be by faith.

Lifting the face. The word literally means “receiving the face” — a judge raising the chin of the man before him because he is somebody. Israel’s law forbade it: “You shall not be partial to the poor or defer to the great” (Leviticus 19:15), for God “is not partial and takes no bribe” (Deuteronomy 10:17). Paul is applying the oldest principle in Israel’s law to Israel.

It cuts both ways. First, nothing you bring raises your chin: not lineage, not church since age four, not your giving, competence or reputation. But run it the other way, which is the half seldom preached. If no advantage lifts a face, no disadvantage lowers one. God does not listen more closely to the articulate, the theologically trained, the emotionally stable or the tidy. The woman who cannot pray aloud, the man converted at sixty with a wrecked past, the believer with a criminal record, the one whose mind is slow — none is further down the list, because there is no list. Impartiality terrifies anyone trading on advantage and is the best news in the world to anyone who has none.

Peter learned it the hard way. It took a vision and a journey to a Gentile’s house. His first words there: “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality” (Acts 10:34). He was watching a wall come down he had thought was load-bearing.

In church. James applies the same word to Sunday morning: the man with the gold ring is told “You sit here in a good place,” the poor man “You stand over there” (James 2:1–4). A church that receives faces does what its Judge has never done. Today it is rarely about seats. It is who gets followed up after missing three weeks, whose name is remembered, which visitor is introduced to someone and which gets a handshake at the door.

A test. Think of your last two conversations at church. What could those people do for you — professionally, socially, or in how they made you feel about yourself? When did you last seek out the person who can do nothing for you and whose company is hard work? Do it this Sunday.

Not indifference. Impartiality does not mean God has no particular love for particular people; chapter 8 says the opposite. It means no consideration of status moves the bench. His love is not bought and his verdicts are not steered.

The lifter of my head. God will not raise your chin for anything you bring to court. But he will raise it: “But you, O LORD, are a shield about me, my glory, and the lifter of my head” (Psalm 3:3). Not because the Judge was impressed, but because his Son stood in your place and left nothing on the charge sheet to keep your eyes on the floor.

verseByVerse.quote: For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified. — Romans 2:12–13
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each person is judged by the light he received. Gentiles who sinned without Moses’ law will perish without it; Jews who sinned under the law will be judged by it. And having the law is not enough: “not the hearers of the law” but “the doers of the law” will be justified. Since no one keeps it perfectly, the argument is heading toward a righteousness that must come from outside us.

Judged by the light given. There is mercy here: nobody will be tried for a revelation that never reached him; the tribesman who never heard of Sinai will not be tried by Sinai. But the mercy stops short of where we would like. He is judged by less, and he still perishes. Fewer rules did not mean he kept them.

Hearers. This word would have gone straight through a Jewish reader. Israel’s creed begins “Hear, O Israel,” and every Sabbath the law was read aloud in the synagogues of Rome to people who came to hear it. Hearing was close to the heart of Jewish devotion. Paul says that faithful, lifelong habit will not make one person righteous before God.

Hearing feels like doing. No generation has had easier access to preaching. A Christian with a phone hears more sermons in a month than earlier believers heard in years. And the danger is exact: when a passage lands, something genuinely happens — recognition, conviction, warmth, resolve. It registers as an event. You can have it weekly for thirty years and be unchanged in ordinary life. That is why James says the hearer who does not do is “deceiving” himself (James 1:22). The deception is that agreement feels like obedience.

A test. Listen this week for “Yes, that’s a good point” in your own mouth — after a sermon, a book, or someone telling you the truth about yourself. Notice what it does. It sounds like agreement and works like a full stop. Someone who means to act says, “What do I do about that?” — and a fortnight later someone else can see the difference.

Justified. Verse 13 is the first use in Romans of the verb “to justify,” the word the whole letter turns on. Paul introduces it in a sentence that seems to contradict everything he will build with it. That is deliberate: he wants the standard at full strength before he says who met it.

Who are the doers? Two readings. The majority Reformed reading, taken here: the category is real but, among fallen people, empty — Paul states the principle so that 3:20 can close it: “by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight.” Others point to 8:4, where the law’s requirement is fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit, and see the doers as Christians whose obedience is the Spirit’s gift. That is not a back door to works. But the immediate argument settles the immediate question: Paul is setting a standard so that every mouth may be stopped (3:19).

Two kinds of hearing. Here hearers are not justified; later “faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (10:17). Both are true. One hearing files information and changes nothing. The other is a drowning man hearing where the rope is. That hearing is not the opposite of doing. It is the first thing a man does, and the only kind that has ever justified anybody.

verseByVerse.quote: For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law. They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness, and their conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gentiles without Moses’ law still know right from wrong. When they do by nature what the law requires, they show that “the work of the law is written on their hearts,” and their conscience accuses or excuses them. Paul is not saying they are saved by conscience. He is saying they are accountable.

Christians or ordinary pagans? Some readers, from Augustine to Cranfield, take these Gentiles to be Christians: “written on their hearts” sounds like the new covenant (Jer 31:33), and v. 29 speaks of the Spirit in the heart. That reading is not foolish. But the context points the other way. Paul is still proving that everyone is accountable (1:18–3:20), and he speaks of what Gentiles do “by nature” and of a conscience that accuses or excuses — the moral knowledge every person has, not the new birth. Jeremiah promised the law itself written on the heart; Paul speaks of the work of the law, its demands, known to all. These are ordinary pagans, and their consciences leave them without excuse.

Conscience. The Greek word means “knowing with” — the strange fact that a human being can stand back from himself and pass judgment. You are the only creature that can be ashamed of itself. A dog can fear consequences; it cannot lie awake at four in the morning over something it said in 1998. And Paul pictures a courtroom: a witness testifies, some thoughts prosecute (“accuse”), others defend (“excuse”). It happens daily in people who have never read a Bible, and the court presupposes a law. Even excusing yourself admits there is a case to answer — nobody mounts a defence in a court he thinks does not exist.

A witness, not the judge. Paul says conscience “bears witness.” It gives evidence at a trial run by Someone else. And witnesses can be wrong — shaped by a bad upbringing, a frightening father, a church that taught rules God never made. Conscience is God-given and real, and it is not infallible. Confusing those facts has damaged many Christians.

Two failures, opposite medicine. The first is the conscience that will not stop accusing: believers who confess the same sin nightly for years, who cannot receive assurance without finding a reason it doesn’t apply, who feel guilty on Sunday night without naming any offence. That is often a witness testifying beyond the evidence. Scripture speaks to exactly this person: “whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything” (1 John 3:20). He knows more than your accusing heart, including what his Son has done. Your conscience does not have the last word on you. The second failure is the witness frightened into silence — the “seared” conscience (1 Timothy 4:2). Its horror is its comfort: it is quiet. It is far more common than scrupulosity among people pleased with their spiritual health.

A test. Don’t ask whether you feel guilty; that measures volume, not accuracy. Take the last thing your conscience convicted you of and ask: Can I name the command this broke? If so, that is real conviction, and the answer is repentance, not reassurance. If there is nothing behind it but a feeling of not being good enough, it is a witness without evidence, and you may decline it. Then: Does this drive me toward God or away? The Spirit’s conviction is specific and takes you to the cross. Accusation from the other quarter is vague and always advises you to keep your distance for a while.

Mercy in it. The law was written on your heart before you were converted, through every year you were running. That is why a conversation from twenty years ago can still make you wince. Conscience accused you accurately, and was one of God’s means of bringing you home. Then it was answered — not by your improvement, but by a verdict from a higher bench.
verseByVerse.note: Conscience is the inner sense of right and wrong that God has given to every person.

parallels.desc: I will write it on their hearts

verseByVerse.quote: on that day when, according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the last day God will judge “the secrets of men” — hidden motives, things known only to the person and to God — and he will do it through Christ Jesus. Paul says this is “according to my gospel”: judgment is part of the good news, the guarantee that nothing done in the dark stays hidden forever.

Good news for whom? Judgment is not awkward small print. Ask the woman whose abuser was never charged and kept his job, reputation and pew. Ask the man whose career was destroyed by a lie he could never disprove, or the family whose village was burned by men promoted afterwards. The world told each of them the file is closed. This verse says it is open, the evidence is kept, and a date is set. A universe without judgment is not gentler. It is one where the powerful got away with it permanently and the torturer and his victim end up of equal consequence. It is easy to dismiss God’s wrath from a safe address. Most of the human race has never had one.

Secret good too. Jesus said, “your Father who sees in secret will reward you” (Matthew 6:4). The day uncovers hidden good as well as hidden wrong: eleven years caring for a parent with dementia, unwatched, at the cost of a career; money given quietly by a man everyone thought tight-fisted; prayers at night for someone who never knew. No system recorded them, and none was lost. For many obscure people that day will be the first time anyone sees what they actually did with their lives.

The Judge is human. God judges “by Christ Jesus,” as Jesus himself said: the Father “has given all judgment to the Son” and given him authority “because he is the Son of Man” (John 5:22, 27). The bench is held by one who was poor, exhausted, misrepresented, betrayed by a friend and tried in a rigged court. Nobody will say the Judge did not understand.

A test. Think of one thing that would genuinely surprise the people who think well of you. Not to tell anyone — just notice you didn’t have to search. It came at once, because you have known it all along. That gap between the known you and the actual you is the material of this verse.

For the Christian. If that test left you cold, hear two things. First, your standing on that day is not open. It was settled elsewhere: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (8:1). What is assessed for a believer is his work, not his welcome. Some work will not survive, and Scripture says how that ends: “he himself will be saved, but only as through fire” (1 Corinthians 3:15). Loss, yes; loss of him, never. Second, the Judge will learn nothing new. He has known every secret from the start, without your explanations attached, and went to the cross already holding the complete file. You are not going to be found out. You were found out long ago, and he came anyway.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–29 — The Failure of Israel: Circumcision of the Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now addresses the Jewish interlocutor directly, and the charge he levels is devastating. The Jew who possesses the Torah, who teaches it to others, who relies on it for his identity — does he keep it himself? "You who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?" The indictment is not that the Torah is worthless but that it cannot save those who merely possess and teach it without obeying it from the heart.

The climax of the argument comes in the citation from Isaiah and Ezekiel: "The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you." This is the ultimate indictment. Israel, entrusted with the oracles of God, called to be a light to the nations, had become in its hypocrisy a reason for the nations to despise the God of Israel. The covenant privilege had become a covenant disgrace. Nothing has changed in principle: every generation of the church must face the same charge — does our life commend the God we profess?

The solution Paul gestures toward is one of the most important concepts in the entire letter: "circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter" (v. 29). This is the Old Testament's own vision — Deuteronomy 10:16, Deuteronomy 30:6, Jeremiah 31:33, Ezekiel 36:26 — now being fulfilled in the new covenant. The mark of true belonging to God is not an outward physical sign but the inward transformation of the heart by the Spirit. This will be Paul's great theme in chapters 6–8.

One move in the middle of the section should not be passed over, because it is the sharpest thing in it. At verse 27 Paul does not merely say that circumcision without obedience is worthless. He says that the physically uncircumcised man who keeps the law will judge the man who has the letter, the circumcision, and a record of breaking it. The outsider is called as the prosecution witness. It is the same reversal our Lord made when he said of a Roman soldier that he had not found such faith in all Israel (Matthew 8:10), and it is designed to be intolerable to anyone whose security rests in the marking rather than in the obedience the marking was given to signify.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Purpose and Limits of the Law

Romans 2:17–29 is the first extended treatment of the law's purpose and limits in the letter. Calvin identified three uses of the law: to reveal sin, to restrain wickedness in society, and to guide the redeemed life. Paul is here invoking the first use: the law reveals sin. The Jew who possesses the Torah has a clearer mirror than the Gentile — and therefore a clearer sight of his own failure to meet its demands. The law cannot save; it can only expose the need for a Saviour. This is precisely why chapters 3–4 follow: the righteousness the law demands but cannot provide is given freely in the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish confidence in circumcision as the defining covenant mark was absolute in Paul's day. To question its saving significance was to question the entire structure of Second Temple Jewish identity. Paul does not question circumcision's historical significance; he relativises it entirely: the physical sign points to a spiritual reality, and when the sign is present without the reality, it is worse than useless. Now: The equivalent is any Christian community that trusts in the outward marks of religion — baptism, church attendance, doctrinal orthodoxy, moral reputation — as substitutes for the inward transformation of the heart by the Spirit. Paul's word stands: God looks at the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: But if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law and boast in God and know his will and approve what is excellent, because you are instructed from the law;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul now addresses the Jewish reader directly and lists his genuine privileges: he bears the name Jew, relies on the law, boasts in God, knows God’s will and can tell what is excellent, because he has been taught from the law. Paul does not deny any of it. The question is whether having these things has changed him.

A boast allowed to finish. Verses 17–20 are one long sentence of mounting credentials — you call yourself, you rely, you boast, you know, you approve, you are sure you are a guide, a light, an instructor, a teacher — with no main verb. Paul lets the man talk himself up for four verses. Then verse 21 brings it down with one question: “you then who teach others, do you not teach yourself?”

The name. “Jew” comes from Judah, whose mother named him saying, “This time I will praise the LORD” (Genesis 29:35). Judah means praise. Hold onto that: Paul will end the chapter by saying the true Jew is the one whose praise “is not from man but from God” (v. 29). He is telling a man he has carried a name he has not understood.

Relying. The verb means to rest your weight on something, to lean back on it. That is the wrong posture toward the law, which was given as a path to walk. He has made furniture of it. A path helps only while you keep moving; a chair helps most when you have stopped.

Boasting in God. Careful: that phrase is not sinful in itself. Paul commands it: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31), and uses the same verb of Christians rejoicing in God in 5:11. The fault is not being proud of God but being proud of having God. From inside they feel alike; from outside the difference is obvious. Boasting in God makes a man smaller and warmer. Boasting in having God makes him larger and colder.

A test. When someone asks what you believe, listen to your answer. Do you describe a position — what you hold, what your church teaches, where you stand against those who have it wrong? Or do you describe a Person? Both may be orthodox. Only one sounds like someone who has met him. And: does knowing God make you feel nearer to people who don’t, or further from them?

A trained palate. “Approve what is excellent” is literally “test the things that differ” — the verb used of the mind that refused to test God (1:28) and of the renewed mind that discerns God’s will (12:2). Paul credits this man with real moral discernment. That also removes his last excuse: his problem is not that he cannot see.

Every item is real. To have God’s word, to be taught it from childhood, to discern what matters — these are great mercies; in chapter 9 Paul would give up his own salvation for the people who have them. The modern list writes itself: raised in it, well taught, sound, able to spot error at forty paces, secure in the right tradition. Every line is a gift, and none of them is a pulse.

verseByVerse.quote: and if you are sure that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of children, having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list continues: he is sure he is “a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of children,” because the law gives him “the embodiment of knowledge and truth.” This was Israel’s real calling. The question that follows is whether he lives what he teaches.

All teaching roles. Guide, light, instructor, teacher. He does not describe himself as a worshipper, a servant or a forgiven sinner, or even as someone still learning. He defines himself by his position over people who know less. That is a real spiritual condition: every encounter with truth gets filed under who needs to hear it rather than what it says to me. The Bible stops being a word addressed to you and becomes material.

The teacher’s hazard. This is for anyone who teaches — parents, preachers, elders, Sunday school teachers, the person in the small group who always knows the answer. The danger is not error. It is that your relationship to the truth becomes professional. You read a passage and think it would preach; you hear a sermon and assess it. None of it is dishonest, and all of it puts you beside the word instead of under it.

A test. Take the last passage you studied properly. What did it say to you — not to your class, your children, or the person you are worried about? If you never asked, or the answer takes searching while the application to others came instantly, you have found the condition Paul describes. From inside it does not look like sin. It looks like diligence.

The outline. “Embodiment” means outline or formed shape. Here it is positive: the law really is the outline of what God is like. But Paul uses the same word for people “having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power” (2 Timothy 3:5). Everything depends on whether anything is inside the shape. A man who has the outline of truth and lives outside it has the most impressive kind of emptiness there is.

A real calling. God did say to his servant, “I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6; cf. 42:6). This man is reciting a true vocation and has stopped noticing that a vocation makes demands. That is why verse 24 lands so hard: the nation called to make God known had made him despised.

You teach two lessons. People are not chiefly formed by your instruction. Children from Christian homes rarely leave the faith because the doctrine was wrong; more often they watched it up close for eighteen years and concluded it did nothing. Only one of your two lessons is prepared.

Don’t stop teaching. That is the sensitive conscience’s reflex, and it would be a small disaster. Paul does not tell the man to put the law down; he asks, “do you not teach yourself?” The remedy is to get back under the word: tomorrow, read as a man who needs it, not one who dispenses it, and let the first application land on the one person you can actually change.
verseByVerse.note: Israel had been called to be a light to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: you then who teach others, do you not teach yourself? While you preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three pointed questions expose the gap between teaching and living. You preach against stealing — do you steal? You forbid adultery — do you commit it? You abhor idols — do you rob temples? Paul is not accusing every Jew of these crimes. He is exposing a religion that possesses the law without being changed by it.

The order matters. Stealing is ordinary. Adultery is graver and hidden. Then comes the one that stops a modern reader: “do you rob temples?” It is the most searching of the three.

Robbing temples. Israel was forbidden not only to worship idols but to profit from them: “The carved images of their gods you shall burn with fire. You shall not covet the silver or the gold that is on them or take it for yourselves” (Deuteronomy 7:25). Pagan temples held precious metal, and there was money for anyone willing to handle it and ask no questions. The charge was live: at Ephesus the town clerk defends Paul’s companions as “neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess” (Acts 19:37), using the word for temple-robbers. So the accusation is exact: you denounce the idol at the front and take its silver at the back.

That is our usual form. We rarely do what we condemn. We benefit from it. You don’t spread the gossip; you listen to all of it. You deplore the relative whose harshness keeps the family in line, and you rely on it. You disapprove of how a colleague got the result, and you were glad of the result. You have views about where money comes from, and there are questions about your own you have decided not to ask. None of it feels like hypocrisy, because you really do abhor the idol. You just also take the gold.

A test. Name one thing you criticise in public and profit from in private — not something you do, something you are content to benefit from while your hands stay clean. Most of us find one inside a minute. The first two questions catch the obvious hypocrite; the third catches the rest of us. Then decide what to give up.

The law as a mirror. Calvin distinguished three uses of the law: it shows us our sin, it restrains wickedness in society, and it guides believers. The first is at work here, and his picture for it is still the best: the law is a mirror. It shows the dirt on your face and has never removed any, and nobody blames a mirror for that. This man’s error is not owning a mirror. He has framed it, hung it on the wall, and started showing it to visitors as evidence of how he looks.

A guard. Paul is not saying Jewish people were typically thieves and adulterers. He is arguing in the style of the lecture hall, putting stock charges to an imagined objector. He is a Jew himself, and seven chapters later he would accept being cut off from Christ if it would save his people. Anyone reading these questions with satisfaction has walked back into the trap of 2:1.

Why questions. Paul asks; he does not accuse. An accusation can be argued with, and the conversation becomes about you. A question leaves a man alone with the answer. It is how God dealt with the first man who hid from him — not a list of charges, but “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9). God knew. The question was so the man would have to say it himself.

verseByVerse.quote: You who boast in the law dishonor God by breaking the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The summary verdict: you who boast in the law dishonour God by breaking it. This is worse than an ordinary inconsistency. The law was given so that God’s character would be seen in his people. When they claim it and live against it, the watching world draws conclusions about the God behind it.

The boast. The section opened with a man who boasts in God (v. 17) and ends with a man who boasts in the law — the same verb framing everything between. His problem was never valuing the law too highly. He valued it as a possession rather than a demand, and a possession is something you display.

Dishonour. That is not a synonym for disobeying. Chapter 1 said the race refused to honour God (1:21) and was given up to dishonour (1:24). Now the same idea returns with the religious man in the frame. The pagan dishonours God by worshipping something else. The religious man dishonours him by claiming him loudly and living as though he were not there.

His name attached. A man with no profession who does wrong damages himself. A man who has told everyone he belongs to God and does the same wrong has attached God’s name to it. He has made a statement about what God is like, and people believe it, because a life is more persuasive than a doctrine. That is the logic of the third commandment: taking the Lord’s name in vain is not chiefly swearing. It is carrying his name as though it weighed nothing.

No scandal required. The Christian known at work for being sharp about money. The father whose family go quiet when he comes in. The believer whose neighbours have concluded, without discussing theology, that whatever he has, it doesn’t make him kinder. None of these makes a headline. All are public statements about God by someone carrying his name.

A test. Think of three people who know you are a Christian and what you are actually like — a colleague, a neighbour, an adult child. What would a reasonable person conclude about God if your life were the only evidence? Not what you would want them to conclude; what the evidence supports. Pick one of the three and ask what one change would alter that evidence.

A guard. God’s honour is not fragile. His reputation does not rest on your performance this week. He is no more diminished by being misrepresented than the sun by a bad photograph. What is at stake is what the people around you are shown — the difference between “God is at risk” and “they are being shown something false.”

The deepest answer. Not only that you should represent God better, though you should. The honour we failed to give has been paid in full. One life made no false statement about the Father: “I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4). This letter exists to say that his record is credited to people whose own record reads like verse 23.

verseByVerse.quote: For, as it is written, "The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul quotes the prophets: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Isaiah 52:5; cf. Ezekiel 36:20). When those who claim to know God live like those who don’t, the world concludes that God does not exist, or does not change people, or that his people don’t believe what they say. Hypocrisy is always paid for by God’s name.

What the prophets meant. In Isaiah and Ezekiel the setting is exile. The nations mocked God’s name because Israel had been defeated and deported. Ezekiel gives the taunt: “they profaned my holy name, in that people said of them, ‘These are the people of the LORD, and yet they had to go out of his land’” (Ezekiel 36:20). Paul applies it to a different cause: there, the name suffered because of what happened to God’s people; here, because of what they do. Both rest on the same fact. The world forms its view of God from the people who carry his name, whether they are being crushed or behaving badly. Nobody gets to be a private believer.

Not persecution. When a church covers up child abuse to protect its reputation, when a ministry’s finances turn out to be a private fortune, when a celebrated preacher was a different man off the platform, the contempt that follows is not persecution. It is an accurate response to evidence. Peter draws the line: “let none of you suffer as a murderer or a thief or an evildoer… Yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed” (1 Peter 4:15–16). Being despised for the cross is an honour. Being despised for hypocrisy is a bill.

“Because of you.” Don’t let the headlines carry this verse. Paul writes you — singular. Most people do not form their view of Christianity from scandals. Nobody in your street has met a famous pastor. They have met you. Their working theory of what God does to a person is built from two or three Christians they know, over years, in unguarded moments, and for someone reading this, you are one of them.

A test. Recall the last time your faith was visible to someone who doesn’t share it — a disagreement at work, a contested topic, a moment when you were tired and provoked. Not what you said: what came across? Christ, or your certainty, irritation, need to be right? Few of us have blasphemed God’s name. More of us have made it look uninteresting, brittle or unkind — and nobody argues with a thing they have simply stopped finding attractive.

Ezekiel’s answer. Ezekiel 36 does not stop at the problem. God states his motive — “It is not for your sake, O house of Israel, that I am about to act, but for the sake of my holy name” (36:22) — and then the remedy: “I will sprinkle clean water on you… And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you… And I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes” (36:25–27). That is exactly where Paul goes in v. 29: heart and Spirit. God did not demand that his people repair his reputation. He undertook to repair it himself, by changing them from the inside. The name blasphemed because of us will be honoured because of what he does in us.

parallels.desc: my name is continually despised

verseByVerse.quote: For circumcision indeed is of value if you obey the law, but if you break the law, your circumcision becomes uncircumcision. So, if a man who is uncircumcised keeps the precepts of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Circumcision, the covenant sign, has real value — if you keep the law. If you break it, your circumcision counts as uncircumcision. And an uncircumcised man who keeps the law’s requirements will be counted as circumcised. The sign was always meant to go with the reality it pointed to: a changed heart.

How violent this sounded. Circumcision was a permanent alteration of the body on the eighth day of life, carried to the grave — the one credential a Jewish man could not lose. Paul says it can “become uncircumcision” in the only court that matters. To his hearer that was close to saying the covenant can be voided by conduct.

Moses said it first. Paul is quoting the law, not escaping it: “Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no longer stubborn” (Deuteronomy 10:16). Jeremiah went further: God will punish “all those who are circumcised merely in the flesh… for all these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart” (Jeremiah 9:25–26). Israel was listed among the uncircumcised more than six hundred years before Paul wrote.

The sign is real. Paul begins by granting it: “circumcision indeed is of value.” God gave it. What Paul denies is that it works by itself, regardless of the life attached. A wedding ring is real and given for real reasons, and it has never kept anyone faithful; on the hand of a man having an affair it becomes a lie in metal.

Who is the uncircumcised man? Some take him as hypothetical, like the doers of v. 13: if a Gentile kept the law he would count as circumcised, and 3:9–20 will show no one does. Others take him as real — a Gentile believer whose heart the Spirit has changed, so that the law’s requirement is beginning to be fulfilled in him (8:4). The second is more likely here: in v. 13 Paul sets the standard for all, but here he is moving toward the circumcision “by the Spirit” of v. 29. Such a man’s obedience is not perfect and is not the ground of his acceptance. It is the evidence of a heart God has circumcised.

Today’s version. Few trust in circumcision. Many trust in an event: a decision at camp at fourteen, a signed card, a baptism, a confirmation, a week when everything was clear. It may have been entirely genuine. Paul’s question is not whether it happened but whether what it signified is present now.

Two guards. First, this does not make God’s signs unimportant; nobody should conclude their baptism was a formality. The error is the sign cut off from its reality, and the remedy is to seek the reality, not to despise the sign. Second, some will examine a conversion they barely remember and conclude that no vivid moment means no new life. It does not. Assurance never rested on the quality of your memory of the beginning. Nobody proves he is alive with a birth certificate; he proves it by breathing. A man who cannot date his conversion and loves Christ today is far better off than one with a certificate and no pulse.

A test. What evidence of your Christianity is dated later than your conversion? Not how it began — evidence from this year: a sin you have fought, a prayer you actually pray, love for someone you have no natural reason to love, grief over your own hardness. None needs to be impressive; it only needs to be current.

“Regarded.” The verb means to credit to an account, and it will dominate chapter 4, where Abraham’s faith “was counted to him as righteousness.” Here, on its first outing in this sense, God is crediting an outsider with a standing he does not physically have. The word that will carry the doctrine of justification is introduced in the act of counting somebody in.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he who is physically uncircumcised but keeps the law will condemn you who have the written code and circumcision but break the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reversal is complete. The physically uncircumcised man who keeps the law will condemn the Jew who has the written law and circumcision but breaks it. Greater light refused means greater condemnation.

The courtroom door opens. The man in the dock has been a judge all chapter — of the pagans of chapter 1, of the blind and the foolish. Now a witness is brought in, and it is the last person he expected: the uncircumcised outsider he had been instructing. He does not merely turn out acceptable; he stands up and condemns.

His existence is the verdict. The Gentile does not out-argue anyone. Jesus used the same device: the men of Nineveh and the queen of the South “will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it,” because they responded to less, and something greater is here (Matthew 12:41–42). They make no speech. They simply did with a candle what others would not do with the sun.

He is in your church. Someone near you came to Christ four years ago from a background with no advantages — no Christian family, no teaching, a history that makes yours look sheltered. He mangles theological terms and cannot find the minor prophets. And he prays as though God were in the room, forgives people who really wronged him, gives more than he can afford, and talks about Jesus to his neighbours without apparent difficulty. He is not trying to rebuke anyone. He is a rebuke, and everyone feels it.

Hiding behind credentials. “You who have the written code and circumcision” is literally “you who, through letter and circumcision, break the law.” The possessions are implicated. The code and the mark gave him a reason not to look. A man with no credentials at least knows he has nothing to plead. Give him a credential and you have handed him somewhere to hide.

A test. Think of a believer you find slightly irritating — the enthusiastic one, the new convert whose zeal seems naive, the one whose theology is thin and whose obedience is not. What is the irritation made of? Sometimes it is real discernment. Often it is the discomfort of watching someone do easily what you have stopped doing, and the quickest relief is to find something in them to correct. Instead, ask him to pray with you.

A guard. This does not make ignorance safer than knowledge, and it is no argument for leaving people untaught. The Gentile is commended for keeping the law, not for lacking it. Light is a mercy. The man’s problem was that he had a great deal and it stayed outside him.

For the latecomer. If the insider’s credentials cannot save him, the outsider’s lack of them cannot damn him.
