Everyone who has come late, from the wrong background, with the wrong history and no religious furniture, stands where the man in verse 27 stands — and in this chapter that is the better place.

verseByVerse.quote: For no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly, nor is circumcision outward and physical. But a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter. His praise is not from man but from God. — Romans 2:28–29
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul defines who is truly a Jew. Not the one who is one “merely outwardly,” with a physical mark, but the one who is one “inwardly,” whose heart has been circumcised “by the Spirit, not by the letter.” His praise comes from God, not people. Paul is not inventing this. Moses and the prophets promised that God himself would change his people’s hearts (Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26–27).

Has the church replaced Israel? Some read the verse that way and link it with Philippians 3:3, “we are the circumcision,” where Paul speaks of the whole church. But that is not quite what this verse says. Paul is still speaking to the Jew of v. 17, and he says who is a Jew in the full sense: not everyone with the outward mark, but the one whose heart God has changed (cf. 9:6). He does not erase Israel. In the next breath he asks, “what advantage has the Jew?” and answers, “Much in every way” (3:1–2), and chapters 9–11 still speak of Israel as a people with a future in God’s purposes. Gentile believers belong to Abraham’s family by faith (4:11–12; Gal 3:29); this verse makes a narrower point, that within Israel the outward mark never made anyone God’s.

Spirit and letter. This is not a contrast between the Spirit and God’s law, as if Paul were against the law. It contrasts a written demand that cannot produce obedience with the Holy Spirit, who creates the obedience the law commands. Chapter 8 will open it fully.

The pun. Recall that “Jew” comes from Judah, “praise” (see on vv. 17–18; Genesis 29:35). Paul ends: “His praise is not from man but from God.” The true Jew — the true “Praise” — is the one whose praise comes from God. Paul began by addressing a man who calls himself a Jew and ends by telling him what his name means, and that it is not awarded by the people who can see you.

Not inwardness for its own sake. The contrast is not between external and sincere. A merely private religion is no better than a merely public one; chapters 12–16 are full of visible obedience. The contrast is between what people can see and reward and what God sees and rewards. Circumcision could be checked by others. The circumcision Paul describes has one competent witness.

God does the cutting. The prophets never promised Israel would try harder; they promised God would act. Moses gave command and promise in the same image: “Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart” (Deuteronomy 10:16), and later, “the LORD your God will circumcise your heart” (Deuteronomy 30:6). Between them lies Israel’s whole history and the reason the promise was needed. And circumcision was the one act of obedience nobody performed on himself; someone else held the knife. Nobody has ever circumcised his own heart, which is why it leaves no room to boast. Paul quoted Ezekiel 36’s diagnosis at v. 24; here he gives its cure (see on v. 24).

Today’s marks. People trust in baptism, membership, a family name, doctrinal precision, a reputation for soundness, the fact that they never left. Each is real, and several are God’s gifts. All can be displayed and checked by others, which is exactly why they are unsafe to stand on. The question is not whether you have the mark but whether anything has been cut away.

A test. How much of your Christian life would survive if nobody ever found out about it? Remove the congregation, the reputation, the people who think well of you for it, and ask what would still be there on a wet Tuesday with no one watching. What remains is the part that is “from God.”

For the Christian nobody notices. You will not be asked at the end for the visible things — the platform, the record, the esteem of the sound. The praise in this verse comes from the one who saw all of it: years of quiet obedience nobody thanked you for, sins fought in private, prayers said into an empty room. Paul has spent a chapter removing every commendation people can give, in order to hand you one they cannot give and cannot take back. It will be the first entirely accurate sentence ever spoken about a human life.

parallels.desc: the LORD will circumcise your heart

2.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things.<sup>2</sup>We know that the judgment of God rightly falls on those who practice such things.<sup>3</sup>Do you suppose, O man—you who judge those who practice such things and yet do them yourself—that you will escape the judgment of God?<sup>4</sup>Or do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?<sup>5</sup>But because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed.<sup>6</sup>He will render to each one according to his works:<sup>7</sup>to those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality, he will give eternal life;<sup>8</sup>but for those who are self-seeking and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, there will be wrath and fury.<sup>9</sup>There will be tribulation and distress for every human being who does evil, the Jew first and also the Greek,<sup>10</sup>but glory and honor and peace for everyone who does good, the Jew first and also the Greek.<sup>11</sup>For God shows no partiality.<sup>12</sup>For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law.<sup>13</sup>For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified.<sup>14</sup>For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law.<sup>15</sup>They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness, and their conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them<sup>16</sup>on that day when, according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus.<sup>17</sup>But if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law and boast in God<sup>18</sup>and know his will and approve what is excellent, because you are instructed from the law;<sup>19</sup>and if you are sure that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness,<sup>20</sup>an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of children, having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—<sup>21</sup>you then who teach others, do you not teach yourself? While you preach against stealing, do you steal?<sup>22</sup>You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?<sup>23</sup>You who boast in the law dishonor God by breaking the law.<sup>24</sup>For, as it is written, “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.”<sup>25</sup>For circumcision indeed is of value if you obey the law, but if you break the law, your circumcision becomes uncircumcision.<sup>26</sup>So, if a man who is uncircumcised keeps the precepts of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision?<sup>27</sup>Then he who is physically uncircumcised but keeps the law will condemn you who have the written code and circumcision but break the law.<sup>28</sup>For no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly, nor is circumcision outward and physical.<sup>29</sup>But a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter. His praise is not from man but from God.

3.title: No One Righteous — But Now, Righteousness
3.overview:
Romans 3 is one of the most concentrated pieces of theological argument in the entire Bible. It moves through three distinct but connected moments: the faithfulness of God despite human faithlessness (vv. 1–8), the universal verdict of guilt on the entire human race from the Old Testament's own testimony (vv. 9–20), and then — with the two most beautiful words in the letter — "But now" (v. 21): the announcement of a righteousness from God that is apart from the law, given through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe.

The emotional architecture of the chapter is deliberate. Paul has spent two chapters building the case for universal human guilt — the Gentile guilty through creation and conscience, the Jew guilty despite law and covenant. Now he delivers the verdict that springs from the evidence: no one righteous, not even one. And then, from within the deepest valley of human hopelessness, he sounds the trumpet of the gospel: the righteousness of God has been manifested. The darkness is real. The light is realer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — God's Faithfulness and Human Faithlessness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If Jewish identity and covenant privilege provide no buffer against divine judgment (chapter 2), an obvious question arises: what advantage has the Jew? Was the entire covenant history of Israel pointless? Paul will not allow this conclusion. The advantage is real and great: "they were entrusted with the oracles of God." The Torah, the prophets, the promises — these are not nothing. They are the priceless repository of God's self-revelation and covenant purposes. The problem is not the oracles; the problem is the people who received them.

But what about God's faithfulness? If Israel has been faithless to the covenant, does that mean God's covenant promises have failed? Never, Paul declares — and the energy of his negation (mē genoito — "by no means!", "God forbid!", the strongest possible denial in Greek) is palpable. God's faithfulness is not contingent on human faithfulness. He remains true even when every human being is a liar. The covenant will not fail because the Covenant God cannot fail.

This brief passage anticipates the great argument of chapters 9–11: the apparent failure of Israel to embrace her Messiah does not represent a failure of God's word. His purposes stand. His faithfulness endures. The mystery of Israel's unbelief is not the defeat of God's plan but a part of it — and Paul will unfold that mystery with breathtaking scope later in the letter.

The second half of the section (vv. 5–8) turns to a pair of objections that Paul was evidently hearing in real life, and both are attempts to turn grace into a licence. If our unrighteousness only serves to display God’s righteousness more brightly, is God not unjust to punish it? And if my lie makes his truth more evident, why am I still condemned — why not simply “do evil that good may come”? Paul reports that last slander as something people were actually saying he taught, which tells us how radical his gospel of free grace sounded to its first hearers; no one ever accused the Pharisees of encouraging sin. He does not argue the point here — he refuses it, notes that God could judge nothing at all if the objection held, and reserves the full answer for chapter 6. But the objection itself is a compliment in disguise. A gospel that cannot be misheard as permission is probably not the gospel Paul preached.
verseByVerse.theology:
Divine Faithfulness and Human Failure

The question of whether human sin can thwart God's covenant purposes is one of the deepest in all theology. Romans 3:3–4 gives the Reformed answer: it cannot. God's faithfulness is not a function of human response; it is grounded in his own immutable character. Calvin wrote that God's truth stands firm even against the unfaithfulness of the whole world. This has practical implications for Christian assurance: our standing in the covenant does not rest on our faithfulness but on God's. He who called us is faithful; he will do it (1 Thessalonians 5:24).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish readers would have been relieved by Paul's affirmation of Israel's covenant privileges, but troubled by his insistence that these privileges provide no exemption from judgment. The tension — covenant advantage, yet equal accountability — was genuinely new, though rooted in the Old Testament prophets. Now: Christians face the same tension. The advantages of covenant community — Scripture, sacrament, preaching, prayer — are real and great. They are also not saving substitutes for personal faith and repentance. Privilege and accountability always travel together.

verseByVerse.quote: Then what advantage has the Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision? Much in every way. To begin with, the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If circumcision without obedience counts for nothing, was there any advantage in being a Jew? “Much in every way,” says Paul. Above all, the Jews “were entrusted with the oracles of God” — God’s own words, written down. The gift was magnificent. The problem was how it was received.

Paul answers the objection to himself. He has just dismantled every advantage his people had, and he knows what the reader now thinks: then none of it meant anything. A lesser writer would let that stand rather than complicate a good argument. Paul stops to answer it — the difference between winning a debate and telling the truth. A gift can be genuinely magnificent and still not enough to save the man holding it.

Entrusted. Not owned — entrusted. A trustee does not own the fund; he manages it and will be asked about it. So the advantage is real precisely because it is a trust, and a trust is the one kind of advantage that increases your liability rather than reducing it.

God had spoken. In chapter 9 Paul lists many privileges — adoption, glory, covenants, worship, promises, patriarchs, the Messiah. Here he names only one: God had spoken, and they had it in writing. Every ancient nation had priests guessing the gods’ will from entrails, stars, birds, or the mutterings at Delphi, always open to reinterpretation. Israel alone had sentences — actual words in a known language that could be copied, memorised, checked, argued over and read to a child.

We hold it more fully. You own, in a language you can read, more of God’s speech than Isaiah ever saw, probably in several copies. And chapter 2 applies exactly here: the deposit does nothing for a man who never opens it. Scripture has no category called “owning the word of God.” There is only hearing it and doing it, or hearing it and not.

A test. Over the past month, how many hours did you spend with God’s word — reading, hearing, thinking about it — compared with hours on recreation? Don’t moralise; just get the number. It is the truest measure of what you believe you have been entrusted with. Then set a time tomorrow and keep it.

The problem was never the gift. Everything Paul goes on to say about human ruin comes from a man who has just insisted that what God gave was magnificent. Chapters 1–3 are not the story of a deficient revelation. They are the story of what happened to a priceless deposit in the hands of people like us.
verseByVerse.note: “The oracles of God” are the Scriptures.

verseByVerse.quote: What if some were unfaithful? Does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God? By no means! Let God be true though every one were a liar, as it is written, "That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some Jews were unfaithful. Does that cancel God’s faithfulness? “By no means! Let God be true though every one were a liar.” God keeps his word even when his people break theirs. Their unbelief does not falsify his promises; it shows them more clearly.

A play on words. “Faithlessness” and “faithfulness” share a root, one with a negative in front. Paul sets them side by side so the answer is visible before it is argued. One is a quality of God; the other is merely its absence in somebody else. An absence cannot cancel a substance. Darkness has never put out a lamp.

“By no means!” This is Paul’s strongest negative, used ten times in Romans, always when a conclusion is not just wrong but intolerable. The older “God forbid” is not literal but catches the tone. Paul is not weighing a proposition; he is recoiling from it.

A rule for the Christian mind. “Let God be true though every one were a liar.” Sooner or later what God has said and what you can see will not agree. He says he works all things for good, and you are standing in a hospital corridor. He says he is near the brokenhearted, and you have felt nothing for eight months. One of them has to give, and Paul tells you which. Your eyes, the consensus of everyone, and your own heart at four in the morning are all admitted as evidence — and they lose. Not because your experience is unreal, but because a witness who has been wrong before cannot overrule one who never has.

Not a call to pretend. Paul does not say “let every man be silent.” Half the Psalms tell God exactly what the writer sees. You may say it looks as though he has forgotten you. You may not conclude it. Say all you see; then let his word have the last sentence.

David’s psalm. The quotation is from Psalm 51 — David after Bathsheba, after the adultery, the pregnancy, and arranging for a loyal soldier to die so the husband would not come home. He says: “Against you, you only, have I sinned… so that you may be justified in your words and blameless in your judgment” (Psalm 51:4). He is not defending himself. He agrees with the verdict in advance: when God judges him, God will be right. That is why Paul uses it. Human failure does not damage God’s truthfulness; it displays it. God said what such a man is, and such a man proved to be exactly that.

A test. Think of the last time you were rebuked — by Scripture, a sermon, or someone who loved you enough to say it. Did you come out agreeing with God, or explaining yourself? Most of us explain: the context, the provocation, the tiredness, the other person’s share. Each syllable tries to keep the verdict from being wholly just. David stops arguing and lets God be right about him. Next time, try saying only: “You are right.”

The comfort. If God’s faithfulness depended on ours, every Christian’s assurance would rise and fall with his last fortnight. It does not. “If we are faithless, he remains faithful — for he cannot deny himself” (2 Timothy 2:13). The fixed point in your life is not your grip on him but his character, which was never in your keeping and so never at risk.

parallels.desc: so that you may be justified in your words
all mankind are liars

verseByVerse.quote: But if our unrighteousness serves to show the righteousness of God, what shall we say? That God is unrighteous to inflict wrath on us? (I speak in a human way.) By no means! For then how could God judge the world?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul meets a clever objection: if our sin makes God’s righteousness shine brighter, isn’t it unfair for God to punish us? “By no means!” If that were true, “how could God judge the world?” A God who rewarded sin because it served his glory would not be a righteous judge.

The objection today. It runs: God gets glory from forgiving sinners; no sin, no forgiveness, no glory; so my sin is, in a roundabout way, a service, and God can hardly be furious about the raw material of his reputation. Nobody says it aloud. Many run a version of it quietly — the oldest trick there is, finding a way that what you were going to do anyway turns out useful.

Paul’s method. He flags his own words — “I speak in a human way” — not wanting a blasphemous argument left in the air with his name on it. Then he refuses it. Then, instead of a philosophical rebuttal, he asks: “how could God judge the world?” Everyone in the conversation agreed God will judge. Follow the objection to its end and it abolishes that: if evil that serves God’s glory cannot be punished, and all evil somehow serves it, nothing can be punished. The objector has not found a loophole. He has sawn off the branch he sits on.

Good out of evil does not make evil good. God does bring good out of evil, and he is not thereby implicated in it. Joseph: “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). Both clauses stand. The supreme case is the cross. Peter holds both truths in one sentence: Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God,” and “you crucified and killed” him (Acts 2:23). Nobody at Pentecost heard that as an acquittal.

The modern form. “God can bring good out of this.” “He knows my heart.” “I’ll be a better help to others afterwards.” “My testimony will be all the stronger.” Each is true in its place, and each can be used in advance as a permission slip — the moment it stops being theology and becomes a lie.

A test: watch the tense. Looking back on something you regret and saying God has brought good out of the wreckage — that is faith, and it is what Genesis 50:20 is for. Saying beforehand, while the decision is still open, that God can work anything out — that is the objection of verse 5 in your own voice. The same sentence is worship in the past tense and self-permission in the future.

The comfort. Paul assumes that a God who did not punish evil would be worse, not kinder. A judge who could be talked out of a verdict by a clever man protects nobody. The God who cannot be talked round when the argument favours you also cannot be talked round when it doesn’t.

parallels.desc: shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?

verseByVerse.quote: But if through my lie God's truth abounds to his glory, why am I still being condemned as a sinner? And why not do evil that good may come? — as some people slanderously charge us with saying. Their condemnation is just.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The objection goes further: if my lie makes God’s truth abound, why am I condemned — why not “do evil that good may come”? Some were slanderously claiming Paul taught exactly that. He answers with a verdict: “Their condemnation is just.” Grace is never a licence.

The slander. Notice the aside: “as some people slanderously charge us with saying.” Paul had preached grace so freely — righteousness apart from works, God justifying the ungodly, nothing to bring or pay — that respectable people concluded he must be telling converts that sin no longer mattered. That is a test of preaching. Nobody accused the Pharisees of encouraging immorality. Nobody hears a sermon on trying harder as permission to sin. This charge is only ever brought against grace so free that it sounds dangerous. If your gospel has never been misunderstood in this direction, ask whether it has a condition quietly attached.

How Paul handles it. One clause. No paragraph clearing his name, no appeal for fairness. He corrects the record and returns to the argument, which mattered more than his reputation. Anyone who has been misquoted knows the restraint that takes.

A verdict, not an argument. Some propositions are not debated but refused, because arguing them on their merits concedes they might have some. A man who asks whether it might be good to do evil has not made an error you can correct with information. He has revealed what he wants and dressed it in logic.

The full answer waits. Paul returns to the question in chapter 6: “Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?… How can we who died to sin still live in it?” (6:1–2). The answer needs union with Christ, which he has not explained yet. He cannot show why a Christian won’t want to sin until he has shown what a Christian is. Here he blocks the road; in chapter 6 he shows the country beyond it.

How it really sounds. Nobody thinks, “I shall sin so that grace may abound.” People think, at eleven at night: “This is forgivable.” And it is — that is the trouble. The best doctrine there is gets used, just before the act, to lower its cost.

A test. When you consider doing something you know is wrong, does the thought of God’s forgiveness make it easier or harder? For someone who understands the gospel, it makes it harder. Not fear of punishment — that was settled — but the difficulty of casually doing the thing that killed your friend. If forgiveness is working as a discount, whatever is believed, it is not this gospel.

Grace is a power. “The grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions” (Titus 2:11–12). The men of verse 8 knew about the pardon and had never met the trainer. You cannot argue someone into a household he has not entered.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–20 — No One Is Righteous: The Verdict of Scripture
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul has argued the guilt of the Gentile from creation and conscience. He has argued the guilt of the moralist and the Jew from their own failure to live by the law they possess. Now he seals the case with the testimony of Israel's own scriptures. The catena of Old Testament citations in vv. 10–18 — drawn from Psalms 14, 5, 140, 10, 36, and Isaiah 59 — forms a comprehensive indictment: no one is righteous, no one understands, no one seeks God; their throats are open graves, their mouths full of cursing and bitterness, their feet swift to shed blood, and there is no fear of God before their eyes.

The theological move is masterful. Paul is not importing foreign charges against Israel; he is using Israel's own sacred texts to establish Israel's own guilt. The Torah was given to the Jew; and the Torah says that no one is righteous. Therefore the Jew who trusts in the Torah as a source of righteousness has not read the Torah carefully enough. The law's purpose is not to provide righteousness but to reveal the absence of it: "through the law comes knowledge of sin" (v. 20).

"No one" — the universality is relentless. Not most people. Not unreformed people. Not people without religion. No one. The scope of the verdict prepares for the scope of the remedy: the gospel is for everyone because everyone needs it equally. There are no moral high achievers who need it slightly less. There are no spiritual derelicts for whom it is too late. The ground is completely level: all have sinned, all fall short (v. 23), all are justified freely by grace (v. 24).

And the section closes with a courtroom image worth naming, because it is the most vivid thing in it. The purpose of the whole indictment, Paul says, is “so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be held accountable to God” (v. 19). A stopped mouth is what happens at the end of a trial that has gone badly: the defendant who arrived with explanations has run out of them, and the silence in the dock is the verdict arriving before the judge speaks it. That silence is not the aim of the passage but its precondition — because a man still talking is a man still defending himself, and nobody has ever been justified by grace while he was still presenting a case.
verseByVerse.theology:
Total Depravity

Romans 3:9–20 is the locus classicus of the Reformed doctrine of total depravity. The doctrine does not mean that every human being is as bad as possible, but that sin has corrupted every dimension of human nature — the mind ("no one understands"), the will ("no one seeks for God"), the affections, the speech, the conduct, the very orientation of the soul. No part of the human person is untouched by the fall. This means that the human contribution to salvation is precisely zero: we do not contribute our goodwill, our moral achievement, our religious sensitivity. Salvation is entirely of God from beginning to end. This is why Paul can say in v. 24 that justification is "freely" given — there is nothing in us to which it could be a response.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The catena of psalms and prophets Paul deploys was drawn from Israel's own worship book. These were texts sung in the temple, prayed in the synagogue, memorised by devout Jews. Their application to Israel's own guilt was deeply confrontational — like a church being indicted by its own hymns. Now: The contemporary church sometimes prefers a more optimistic anthropology — emphasising human potential and the image of God while minimising the ravages of the fall. Romans 3:9–20 is the permanent corrective. The doctrine of human depravity is not pessimism; it is realism. And realism about the disease is the precondition for gratitude for the cure.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Are we Jews any better off? No, not at all. For we have already charged that all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin, as it is written: "None is righteous, no, not one;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are Jews better off, then? “No, not at all.” Paul has already charged that “all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin” — not just guilty of sins but under sin as a ruling power. And Scripture agrees: “None is righteous, no, not one.”

Does this contradict v. 2? No. The advantage was real: Israel was entrusted with God’s words. But privilege is not a better verdict. In court, having the law only means being judged by it, and so Jew and Gentile stand together under sin.

A courtroom. “We have already charged” is a prosecutor’s word. Chapters 1–2 were not a survey of human behaviour but the evidence. The reader has been in court since 1:18.

Under sin. Paul says not that all have committed sins but that all are under sin, as a soldier is under orders. Sins are the symptom; Sin is the disease. If the problem is sins, it is a record, and you need a pardon. If it is Sin, it is a power, and you need rescue. Romans says God did both: chapter 3 deals with the first, chapters 6–8 with the second.

“But I know decent people.” Of course. Paul has said Gentiles sometimes do what the law requires (2:14). He means something less visible. A man can be honest, generous, faithful to his wife and admired, and still live his whole life without reference to the God who made him. That is what being under sin looks like in a respectable postcode. Not all chains chafe.

Their own hymnbook. The quotation comes from Psalm 14 (and 53), sung in Israel about the fool and the evildoers. Paul turns it on the people who sang it — like a congregation indicted by its own hymnbook. And he adds “no, not one” to close the last exit, because the mind presented with a universal immediately hunts for the exception, usually itself.

A test. As you read the next verses — throats, tongues, feet, eyes — watch your mind. Most of us start assigning them: this fits my brother-in-law, that describes the country, this is someone at work. That reflex is what chapter 2 exposed. Read vv. 10–18 with one rule: each time you think of someone else, stop and ask where the sentence touches you.

Why Paul does this. Christianity does not think poorly of people. The doctor who tells you the growth is malignant is the only person in the room who is any use to you. Paul is levelling the ground because he is about to build something that will not fit on uneven ground. A few verses on, the word comes back: “all have sinned,” and all are “justified by his grace as a gift” (vv. 23–24). The verdict is total because the remedy is.
verseByVerse.note: Paul strings together quotations from the Psalms and Isaiah to show that all are under sin.

parallels.desc: not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins

verseByVerse.quote: no one understands; no one seeks for God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one understands; no one seeks God; all have turned aside; no one does good. These universal negatives are the basis of what Reformed theology calls total depravity: not that everyone is as bad as possible, but that sin has affected every part of us — mind, will and affections — so that, left to ourselves, we neither understand God nor move toward him.

“But the world is full of seekers.” Pilgrimages, retreats, whole shelves of spirituality, people “on a journey.” How can Paul say no one seeks God? Look at what is sought. People look tirelessly for what God gives — meaning, peace, forgiveness, a sense that life amounts to something, the assurance of being loved. What no one seeks, left to himself, is God on his terms: a God with authority over him, who names his sin, will not be edited, and whose company he cannot leave when it is inconvenient. We look for the benefits, not the Person, and religion is often the most sophisticated way to have the first without the second.

God is the seeker. After the fall, God comes walking in the garden and the man is hiding behind a tree (Genesis 3:8). The Bible is not humanity’s search for God but God’s search for humanity: he calls Adam, comes down to Moses, pursues Jonah across a sea, sends prophet after prophet. Jesus defines his mission the same way: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10). If nobody is searching, somebody has to come.

A test. Think of what you most want God to do for you right now. Suppose he offered it in full — the healing, the restored relationship, the job, the peace of mind — on condition that you would have nothing more to do with him. Would you take it? You know your answer within two seconds. That is the difference between seeking God’s hand and seeking his face. “Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you” (Psalm 73:25).

No one understands. This is not about intelligence. Something is wrong with the faculty itself where God is concerned, which is why brilliant people can weigh the evidence and stay unmoved while an uneducated person grasps the gospel and is transformed. “The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them” (1 Corinthians 2:14). Not just unwilling — not able.

Each his own way. “All have turned aside” is Isaiah’s picture: “All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned—every one—to his own way” (Isaiah 53:6). Nobody follows a common script. Depravity does not produce uniformity. It produces highly individual people going, with great originality, in the same direction.

If you do want God. If his existence is a comfort to you rather than a threat, if you would not take the gift without the Giver, you have just produced evidence that something has happened to you that this verse says does not happen naturally. You did not start the search. As Jesus said, no one can come to him unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). The seeking you are aware of is the far end of a search that began with God. Thank him for it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Their throat is an open grave; they use their tongues to deceive." "The venom of asps is under their lips." "Their mouth is full of curses and bitterness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul strings together lines from the Psalms (5:9; 140:3; 10:7) about speech: the throat an open grave, the tongue deceiving, venom under the lips, the mouth full of curses and bitterness. Speech, made to carry truth and love, has become a chief instrument of harm.

Count the organs. Paul walks down the body: throat, tongue, lips, mouth, then feet (v. 15), then eyes (v. 18). Four of the six are organs of speech. With murder available to him, he gives most of his anatomy to the mouth. Jesus gave the reason: “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matthew 12:34). You can hide your character in most areas for years, but you cannot talk for long without giving yourself away. That is why “on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak” (Matthew 12:36) — the careless ones, because they were not edited.

An open grave. An open tomb gives off the smell of what is inside, and the throat is the passage from a man’s interior to the world. And under the law, anyone who touched a grave was unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16). An open grave contaminated people who only came near. So does sinful speech: it does not stay with the speaker.

A sequence. The throat is the source. The tongue is the method — habitual deceit. The lips are the concealment: a snake’s venom is not visible on the fangs but under them, and by the time you know, it is in you. The mouth is the overflow — cursing and bitterness, when a man stops bothering to hide it.

Venom under the lips. This names speech that is lethal because it is smooth. Not the shouted insult, which announces itself and can be answered. The compliment with a hook in it. The concerned question that plants a doubt and leaves no fingerprints. “I only say this because I care about you,” occasionally true. The accurate remark timed to humiliate in front of others. None would stand out on a recording.

In church. James uses the same picture: the tongue is “a restless evil, full of deadly poison,” and “with it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God” (James 3:8–9). The mouth that sang in the service dismantles somebody in the car afterwards without changing gear. And our age has given the open grave a distribution network: words written in ninety seconds of irritation reach thousands and stay there for years.

A test. Don’t ask whether you swear. Think of one sentence this week that was perfectly polite, that nobody would have called unkind, and that you knew as you formed it would land somewhere tender. You may have called it honesty. That sentence is under your lips, and this verse is about it. Go and put it right.

The way out. Isaiah, seeing God’s throne, said, “I am a man of unclean lips,” and a coal from the altar touched his mouth and took his guilt away (Isaiah 6:5–7). The fire came not from his effort at better speech but from an altar where something had died — and then that mouth was sent to speak. The organ called an open grave in chapter 3 is, in chapter 10, the one you confess with and are saved (10:9–10).

verseByVerse.quote: "Their feet are swift to shed blood;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the mouth Paul moves to the feet: “Their feet are swift to shed blood” (from Isaiah 59:7; Proverbs 1:16). Sin does not stay inside; it moves, travels, and arrives at destruction with terrible efficiency.

Swift. The disturbing word is not “blood” but “swift.” Speed measures desire. Nobody hurries toward what he is reluctant about. The verse describes an eagerness, and the eagerness tells you what is in the runner.

Evil as belonging. The proverb Paul echoes describes a recruitment. A father warns his son about men who will say, “Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood… throw in your lot among us,” and then comments: “their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed blood” (Proverbs 1:11–16). The invitation is attractive: company, adventure, a share of the proceeds. Evil rarely presents itself as evil. It presents itself as belonging.

A line crossed. Until now the catalogue has been the inside of a man and the noise he makes. Now the body moves. Thought is private and speech can be taken back, but a man who has gone somewhere and done something has produced a fact in the world. Feet are how intention becomes history.

Not just other people. Jesus traced the sixth commandment to its root: “everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5:22). John: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). A harsh word is not equal to homicide in its consequences; the point is the substance — the desire to see someone diminished, silenced, humiliated, gone. Respectable people have it at their kitchen tables. Most never reach the deed for lack of opportunity, nerve or anonymity — a mercy, not innocence.

Clean hands. Bloodshed has always had its tidy forms. David never touched Uriah; he sent a letter and let the enemy do it. Ahab did not stone Naboth; a court was convened and false witnesses found. Pilate washed his hands in public and handed Jesus over anyway. Distance between decision and death keeps the feet unmarked. It soothes the conscience and does not deceive the Judge for a moment.

A test: what are you quick toward? When someone you resent is in trouble, how fast does the news reach you, and how fast do you pass it on? When there is a quarrel at church, how quickly are you in it? When a story confirms what you already thought about someone, how long before you believe it? Nobody has to drag you there. Your feet can hurry, and what they hurry toward is evidence. Slow down before you repeat the next story.

Beautiful feet. Scripture uses the same image the other way. Isaiah saw a runner on the mountains and called his feet beautiful because of what he carried — good news, peace, salvation — and Paul quotes it of gospel messengers: “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!” (10:15; Isaiah 52:7). Feet that ran to shed blood are not amputated. They are sent elsewhere, in a hurry, carrying something worth the speed.

parallels.desc: their feet run to evil

verseByVerse.quote: "in their paths are ruin and misery, and the way of peace they have not known."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“In their paths are ruin and misery, and the way of peace they have not known” (from Isaiah 59:7–8). Wherever people live without God, they leave wreckage behind them, and the peace every one of them wants is a road they have never found.

Behind, not ahead. The ruin is not a destination in front of them. It is in their paths — along the route, where they have already been. Every other line has examined the sinner’s throat, tongue, feet and eyes. This one steps back and photographs the road he walked.

We don’t see our own wreckage. We experience our lives from inside, as a series of understandable decisions. The damage is in other people: the child who learned to read his father’s mood before entering a room; the friend who stopped calling and was never asked why; the colleague humiliated in a meeting eleven years ago who still thinks about it; the marriage that did not end but went quiet. None of it appears on the sinner’s own account. All of it is in the path. Ruin is the breakage; misery is what it costs the people living in it. Sin always has a second address, and there is usually a person at it.

The way of peace. Peace here is shalom: everything in its place, whole, working. The charge is not only that people fight, but that they have never learned the road to what they all want. Not refused — not known. Every generation produces its confident method — better education, systems, technology, politics — and each leaves a fresh crop of ruin. Isaiah saw his nation groping for the wall like the blind, stumbling at noon (Isaiah 59:10).

A test you can’t run alone. Take the three people closest to you and ask honestly what it costs to be in a relationship with you. Not what you provide — what it costs. Where do they walk carefully? What subject do they avoid? What have they stopped expecting? Most of us can answer for others at once and go blank about ourselves. The braver version is to ask one of them. The answer will be small, specific, probably years old, and in your path.

Repair is part of repentance. Zacchaeus did not only confess; he worked out fourfold repayment (Luke 19:8). Jesus told a man to leave his gift at the altar and first be reconciled to his brother (Matthew 5:23–24) — interrupting worship for a repair. A guard: not every path can be walked back. Some people are dead, some unreachable, some would be harmed by your return, and then forgiveness is not withheld because the road is closed. But where it is open, walk it.

Peace is a Person. Because no one knew the way of peace, someone had to come and be it. “For he himself is our peace,” and he “came and preached peace to you who were far off” (Ephesians 2:14, 17), having made peace “by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20). He came looking for people leaving ruin in their paths, and he came “while we were still sinners” (5:8).

parallels.desc: the way of peace they do not know

verseByVerse.quote: "There is no fear of God before their eyes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list ends with its root: “There is no fear of God before their eyes” (Psalm 36:1). Everything above — speech, violence, ruin — comes from this. Sin is a failure of worship before it is a failure of morals.

Cause after symptoms. The body is now complete: throat, tongue, lips, mouth, feet, eyes. Paul moves from what a man is, to what he says, to where he goes, and last to what he is looking at. Five symptoms, then the cause.

What “fear of God” means. Not terror or cringing before a temperamental deity. We use the phrase correctly ourselves: “That boy has no fear of his father.” Nobody thinks we mean he should be frightened. We mean the father’s reality does not weigh with him; the boy behaves the same whether he is there or not. That is the charge: not that people are insufficiently scared, but that God makes no practical difference to them.

“Before their eyes.” It is about what a man keeps in view while deciding. Everyone knows the speed limit; a police car in the mirror changes behaviour instantly, though the belief has not changed — only what is in the frame. Almost nobody sins while consciously aware of God. The Christian’s problem is rarely unbelief. It is that at the moment of choosing, God is not in the picture.

Why it comes last. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Proverbs 1:7). So its absence explains the first charge too: verse 11 said no one understands; verse 18 says why. A man who reasons about life with God left out will reason, very cleverly, to conclusions that are reliably wrong.

Should a Christian fear God? John says “perfect love casts out fear” and adds, “fear has to do with punishment” (1 John 4:18). The dread of condemnation is gone (8:1). What remains, and grows, is reverence. A child of a good father is at ease on his knee and would go white to hear him spoken of with contempt. Both at once.

Where it comes from. Not from working yourself into reverence, which won’t last past Tuesday. It is a covenant gift: “And I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me” (Jeremiah 32:40). The fear is given as the thing that keeps you. It is part of how God holds on to his people. Ask him for it.

A test. What would you do differently in the next hour if Christ were visibly in the room? Not next year — the next hour. What would you not open, not say, not watch, not put off? That list measures how much of your day is lived with God out of frame. You already believe he is there; the gap is one of sight.

The cure in the same psalm. Psalm 36 opens with the man who has no fear of God before his eyes, and then turns: “Your steadfast love, O LORD, extends to the heavens… For with you is the fountain of life; in your light do we see light” (Psalm 36:5, 9). The psalm that diagnoses the eye supplies the light.

parallels.desc: there is no fear of God before his eyes

verseByVerse.quote: Now we know that whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may be held accountable to God. For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin. — Romans 3:19-20
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law speaks to those under it, “so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may be held accountable to God.” No one will be justified by doing what the law requires, because the law’s job is to show us our sin. It is a mirror, not a ladder.

What are “works of the law”? Scholars of the New Perspective on Paul argue that the phrase means chiefly the marks that set Jews apart from Gentiles: circumcision, the food laws and the Sabbath. Paul would then be saying that no one is put right with God by belonging to Israel. Those marks are part of what Paul means, and in vv. 29–30 the question of Jew and Gentile comes to the surface. But here the phrase must mean more. The verse ends “through the law comes knowledge of sin,” and the whole argument since 1:18 has been about guilt for wrongdoing, not badges of identity. Works of the law are everything the law commands, done in obedience to it; and by that road, because all have sinned, no one arrives.

No passing it on. Every passage Paul just quoted is from Israel’s own Scriptures, which invites an escape: the psalmist was describing the wicked elsewhere. Paul blocks it: the law speaks “to those who are under the law.” Scripture speaks first to the people who own it. The church instinct is the same — hearing a sermon on behalf of others: this would help my son; I hope he is listening. The word lands first on the people in the room.

Mouths stopped first. A man is not guilty because he stops arguing; he was guilty already. But until his defence ends, nothing can be given. A man still presenting his case is asking for a fair verdict, and grace has nothing to say to someone who thinks he might win.

The finding. At 2:7 Paul stated the standard: patient well-doing, eternal life. At 2:13: the doers will be justified. Both left one question: who has done it? Here is the verdict: “by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight.” Chapter 2 was the statute; this is the judgment. It does not say the law is bad, that obedience doesn’t matter, or that God lowered the standard. It says no one arrives by this road — reported impassable by the surveyor who laid it out.

Knowledge of sin. Paul’s word means full recognition, not vague awareness. Everyone knows roughly that he is not what he should be. The law turns that fog into an itemised statement — what Calvin called the first use of the law (see on 2:21–22). That is why an honest reading of the Ten Commandments helps an unconverted man more than encouragement: you cannot want a Saviour while your problem is only a mood.

A test. When Scripture shows you something true about yourself, where do you go next? Some go to despair — the law doing half its work and stopping. Some go to resolve — the law doing none of it; told he cannot climb, the man trains harder. The law has done its full work only when you stop climbing and look for rescue.

Not the end. This is the darkest sentence in the letter, and the next words are “But now.” Paul has demolished every refuge because what he is about to offer will only be received by people with nowhere else to stand. The silence in the courtroom is the pause before the Judge announces he has provided a righteousness of his own.

parallels.desc: no one living is righteous before you

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–31 — But Now: The Righteousness of God Through Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"But now" — nuni de. Two words in Greek that change everything. After three chapters of unrelenting diagnosis — the Gentile without excuse, the moralist self-condemned, the Jew convicted by his own scriptures, the entire world accountable to God — these two words open a door out of a sealed room. The righteousness of God has been manifested. Apart from the law. Through faith in Jesus Christ. For all who believe. Freely. By grace. Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.

This is the centre of Romans. This is the centre of Paul's gospel. This is the theological core of the Reformation. Every word of vv. 21–26 has been weighed and debated and celebrated for two millennia — and still it burns with the same fire. God put Christ forward as a propitiation — a mercy seat, a place of atonement — by his blood, to be received by faith. In this act, God demonstrated his own righteousness: He passed over former sins (under the patient forbearance of the old covenant) and he condemned the sin that deserved condemnation — in his own Son, at Calvary. The God who justifies the ungodly (4:5) is not a God who winks at sin. He is a God who bore its full weight in the person of his Son.

Boasting is excluded (v. 27). The person who is justified by faith through Christ has nothing to boast of but Christ. The Jew cannot boast in the Torah; the Greek cannot boast in philosophy; the moralist cannot boast in her record; the religious cannot boast in his devotion. The ground is level. There is one God, and he justifies the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith. The gospel is the great leveller — and the great glorifier, because it redirects all glory from the creature to the Creator.

Two things at the edges of the section should not be lost. The first is the sentence on which the whole offer rests, and it is the shortest in the passage: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (v. 23). It is not an insult dropped into a paragraph about grace; it is the reason there is a paragraph about grace, and everything from 1:18 onward has been written to make that sentence land as a plain description rather than an accusation. The second is the question Paul asks last, which is the one his critics had been asking loudly: do we then overthrow the law by this faith (v. 31)? He has just said righteousness comes apart from the law, and the obvious inference is that the law has been discarded — the very charge of 3:8. His answer is the strongest denial in his vocabulary, and then four words that will take him the whole of chapter 4 to prove: we uphold the law. Justification by faith does not abolish the Old Testament. It is what the Old Testament was about.
verseByVerse.theology:
Propitiation: The Heart of the Atonement

Romans 3:25 introduces one of the most important words in the New Testament: hilastērion — propitiation. This word carries the specific meaning of an offering that averts divine wrath by satisfying it. Leon Morris demonstrated exhaustively that this is the correct reading against C.H. Dodd's attempted substitution of "expiation" (which only removes sin, without reference to wrath). Christ's death on the cross was not merely a moral demonstration or a removal of guilt; it was the bearing of the holy wrath of God against sin, so that God could be both just (the sin was punished) and the justifier (the sinner is acquitted). The Reformed tradition has always insisted on this: without propitiation, justification has no foundation. If the wrath was not truly satisfied, the forgiveness is not truly free.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The language of vv. 24–25 deliberately echoes the Day of Atonement ritual of Leviticus 16: the mercy seat (hilastērion) where blood was sprinkled to cover the sins of the people. Paul is saying: what the Day of Atonement pointed to, Christ has accomplished — once for all, for all who believe. The entire sacrificial system of the old covenant found its fulfilment and its terminus in the cross. Now: Every human religion has some mechanism for dealing with the problem of guilt — sacrifice, ritual, moral achievement, reincarnation, denial. Romans 3:21–31 announces that the only mechanism that actually works is the one God provided: the substitutionary death of his own Son, received by faith. There is no other name, no other blood, no other righteousness that avails.

verseByVerse.quote: But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, although the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it—the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. For there is no distinction:
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But now” the light breaks. God has revealed a righteousness “apart from the law” — not earned by keeping it — yet witnessed by “the Law and the Prophets.” It comes “through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe,” with no distinction between Jew and Gentile.

His character, or his gift? Paul holds both together. It is a righteousness that comes “through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe” (v. 22), and so a status God gives: his verdict that a sinner is in the right with him (cf. Phil 3:9, “the righteousness from God that depends on faith”). Yet in vv. 25–26 the same cross shows God’s own righteousness, so that he is “just and the justifier.” Luther found the gospel when he saw that God’s righteousness in this letter is not only the standard that condemns us but the gift that clothes us.

The hinge. Since 1:18 everything has closed down: creation leaves no excuse, conscience convicts the man without the law, the law convicts the man with it, the moralist is condemned by his own standard, Scripture gives the verdict, every mouth is shut. Into that silence: “But now.” Not “therefore” — nothing in chapters 1–3 leads to grace. The gospel is not the conclusion of an argument but an interruption of it, news from outside the courtroom. And “has been manifested” is a completed act. It is not on offer pending conditions. It happened, in public, at a datable moment.

Apart from the law, yet witnessed by it. The law never produced this righteousness, but it pointed to it from the start: every sacrifice, every high priest on the Day of Atonement, every prophet who spoke of a servant “pierced for our transgressions” (Isaiah 53:5). A signpost is separate from the destination — you cannot live in it — and exists for nothing else. Paul is not founding a new religion. The old one has arrived at what it was for (cf. 1:2).

Faith in Christ, or Christ’s faithfulness? The Greek of “faith in Jesus Christ” could also mean “the faithfulness of Jesus Christ,” his obedience to death, and scholars divide. It matters little here, because Paul immediately adds “for all who believe.” Either way the righteousness rests on what Christ has done and reaches us by faith.

For all who believe — full stop. Not “all who believe and…” No probation, no minimum improvement, no requirement first to become the sort of person to whom such an offer could decently be made. Paul spent three chapters proving no such person exists, so that the offer could be phrased this way.

A test. Think of your worst week this year — the one with the failure you have told no one about. What happened to your standing with God that week? If the honest answer is that it dropped and has partly recovered, you are living under chapter 2, whatever you believe about chapter 3. A righteousness given apart from the law is not affected by your performance under the law. It never rested on it. Thank God for that today, by name, about that week.

The verdict fell elsewhere. “But now” is not a mitigation, a discount, or a decision to overlook the file. It is a righteousness from God held out to the very people the law had just finished condemning, priced at the life of the only innocent man who ever lived. The verdict did not soften. It fell on him.
verseByVerse.note: To be “justified” is to be declared righteous by God as judge.

verseByVerse.quote: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” — and all who believe “are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.” The universal diagnosis and the free remedy come in one sentence. Redemption means release bought at a price; Christ paid it.

To whom was the ransom paid? Some early Christian writers said it was paid to the devil, who held humanity captive. Scripture never says so. The debt was owed to God’s justice, which is why Paul goes straight on to propitiation (v. 25). The ransom picture tells us what our release cost and what it achieved; it is not meant to be pressed further.

One sentence. Verse 23 is usually quoted alone, as a verdict on the human race. In Paul it has no full stop: all have sinned… and are justified. The same “all” governs both halves. Paul built a list long enough to catch everybody — idolater, moralist, gossip, the man with four Bibles — so that this lands as a description, not an insult. Nobody is singled out.

Falling short of glory. This is not a moral score. People were made in God’s image — the one creature meant to show what he is like — and we don’t. That explains an ache everyone knows: the sense of falling short of yourself, of being meant for more — not more successful, more real. That is not vanity or neurosis. It is accurate, and this verse explains it. And the tense: “have sinned” is past, but “fall short” is present. It describes this morning, for Christians too.

A gift. “Justified” is also present: grace keeps working. “As a gift” translates a word meaning gratis, without cause. The same word appears in “They hated me without a cause” (John 15:25). Hatred with no reason in its object, grace with no reason in its object. There was nothing in Jesus to justify the hatred, and there is nothing in you to justify the gift.

Redemption. A marketplace word: the price paid to free a slave or a prisoner of war. It tells you your position — not a man with a poor record but a man owned. And it tells you grace was free to you and to no one else. A gift that cost the giver everything, given to someone who could contribute nothing — that is grace. Free is not cheap.

A test. Say it in the first person: “I have sinned and I fall short of the glory of God.” Many can affirm the doctrine and flinch at the pronoun. Then: “and I am justified freely by his grace.” Which is harder to say without qualifying? For most Christians, the second. We accept a diagnosis that puts us with everyone else more easily than a gift that puts us in debt to Someone. Say the second sentence aloud until you can say it without a “but.”

Not a slogan. Read alone, verse 23 makes Christianity a low view of people. Read as Paul wrote it, it says what no religion has said: the same “all” who are condemned are offered the gift, and the only qualification is one every human being already has.
verseByVerse.note: “Redemption” was the word for buying a slave’s freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: ...whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith. This was to show God’s righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins. It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. — Romans 3:25-26
verseByVerse.commentary:
What the word means. A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s just anger against sin by bearing it. Paul says God “put forward” Christ as that sacrifice: on the cross, the wrath that our sin deserved fell on him, so that none is left for those who trust him. And notice who acts. This is not a Son persuading a reluctant Father. The Father himself provides the sacrifice, because he loves us (5:8).

The picture. The Greek word Paul uses is the one the Greek Old Testament used for the “mercy seat” (also in Hebrews 9:5): the gold lid of the ark, in the innermost room of the tabernacle. Under the lid lay the tablets of the law Israel had broken; above it God met his people. Once a year, on the Day of Atonement, the high priest went in alone, in the dark, and sprinkled the blood of a sacrifice on it (Leviticus 16:14–16), and the next year he had to do it again. Paul says God has now set Christ out as the mercy seat — not hidden behind a curtain but in public, on a hill outside the city, once for all. Some translate the word “expiation” (the removal of sin). Sin is indeed removed, but Paul has spent three chapters on the wrath of God (1:18) and will say we are “saved by him from the wrath of God” (5:9). Sin is removed because wrath has been borne; “propitiation” says both.

What Paul is saying: God’s justice is on trial. Why did the cross have to happen? Paul’s answer starts with God’s own record. For centuries God had been forgiving people. David committed adultery and murder, and Nathan told him, “The LORD also has put away your sin” (2 Samuel 12:13). Yet “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4). So on what grounds were these sins let through? “In his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins” — held back the sentence without yet saying why. That made God look like a judge who lets the guilty walk free, and Scripture itself says, “He who justifies the wicked… [is] an abomination to the LORD” (Proverbs 17:15). The cross is God’s public answer. The sentence on sin was not waived; it was carried out in full on Christ. So God is “just” — sin has been punished — and “the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” — he can declare the guilty righteous without pretending. The question of Romans is not how a loving God can forgive, but how a just God can forgive and stay just.

All of this is “received by faith.” Faith does not earn it or add to it. It is the empty hand that takes what Christ has done.

In real life. Ask yourself why God accepts you, and listen to your answer. If it rests on God being kind, understanding your circumstances, or willing to overlook things, it will not hold at four in the morning — a God who overlooks could also change his mind. The answer this passage gives is firmer: God accepts you because the debt has been paid, and it would be unjust of him to collect it twice. The very justice you feared has become the ground you stand on. So when guilt rises over something you have confessed, do not argue that it was not so bad. Say what Paul says: it was that bad, and it has been paid for. At the cross “righteousness and peace kiss each other” (Psalm 85:10) — and the only one who paid anything was God himself.
verseByVerse.note: A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath. The same word is used in the Greek Old Testament for the “mercy seat,” the lid of the ark where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement.

parallels.desc: blood on the mercy seat

verseByVerse.quote: Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded. By what kind of law? By a law of works? No, but by the law of faith. For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So where is boasting? “It is excluded” — shut out — not by a law of works but by “the law of faith.” For “one is justified by faith apart from works of the law.” Faith is the hand that takes a gift, not labour that earns a wage, so there is nothing left to boast about.

Paul and James. James says “a person is justified by works and not by faith alone” (Jas 2:24). Do the apostles contradict each other? No. They answer different questions and use “justify” in different senses. Paul asks how a guilty sinner is put right with God: by faith, apart from works. James asks what kind of faith is real: “faith apart from works is dead” (Jas 2:26), and a person is shown righteous by what he does. Paul opposes works as the ground of acceptance; James opposes a faith that is only words. Paul agrees that true faith works — “faith working through love” (Gal 5:6) — and James agrees that Abraham “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness” (Jas 2:23). We are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

Locked out. “Excluded” is the word for shutting a door. Boasting is not discouraged or rationed. It is put out of the building. And what excludes it is not humility or a rule but the structure of salvation itself. A man told to stop boasting learns to boast more quietly. Paul’s point is that there is nothing left to boast about: you cannot be proud of a gift you did not choose, earn, deserve or contribute to. The impulse is not forbidden. It is unemployed.

Why God arranged it so. If any part of your standing rested on you, you would have grounds for comparison, and comparison is the seedbed of everything chapter 2 exposed. God closed off boasting because it is poison, and the only cure is a salvation in which nobody has anything to show.

“We hold.” Paul is not floating a proposal. After two and a half chapters this is the finding, entered into the record. (How this fits with judgment according to works: see on 2:7–8.)

“Alone.” Luther’s German translation added allein — by faith alone — and he was attacked for it all his life. The word is not in the Greek. But it is what the sentence means: if works are excluded, faith is the only thing left. Every opponent had to explain what else, besides faith, Paul had left in.

A guard. Some now worry about their faith instead of their works — the same disease at a new address. Is my faith strong enough, sincere enough, free enough of doubt? That treats faith as a work God rewards. Faith is not the payment; it is the receiving. A weak hand and a strong hand grasp the same rope, and the rope does the holding.

A test. What do you mention when you want someone to think well of you spiritually — years as a Christian, books read, things given up, service, hardship borne well? The currency varies by church: zeal, doctrinal precision, suffering, being relaxed about what others worry over. Whatever yours is, it is a boast, and the door it is trying to come through is locked.

A kindness. A religion of achievement makes you keep score — anxious when losing, insufferable when winning. Paul has removed the scoreboard. One boast is left: “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6:14). Not nothing to boast about — nothing of ours.

verseByVerse.quote: Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also, since God is one—who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is God the God of Jews only? No — of Gentiles too, “since God is one.” Israel’s own creed, “The LORD our God, the LORD is one,” means he is God of all, and so there is one way of being put right with him for all: by faith, for the circumcised and the uncircumcised alike.

The Shema turned outward. Every Jewish household said the Shema morning and evening. Its force had long been separation: the nations have many gods; we have the one true God. Paul turns the same words outward. If there is only one God, he is not our God as opposed to theirs. He is theirs too — and a God who belongs to everyone cannot have arranged a salvation only one group can use.

A question, not an assertion. No Jew would have said God was the God of Jews only; their Scriptures said otherwise, from the promise that all nations would be blessed in Abraham to Isaiah’s “house of prayer for all peoples” (Isaiah 56:7). Paul is not correcting their creed. He is showing that their practice had contradicted it — a more uncomfortable thing to be shown.

“By faith” and “through faith.” Paul varies the preposition for the two groups. Scholars debate whether he means a difference; the likeliest answer is that he refuses either group the standard phrasing. Same faith, same width of door, and neither is the tradesman’s entrance.

It was not settled then. Whether Gentiles had to become Jews first — circumcision, food laws, calendar — nearly tore the early church apart. It filled a council at Jerusalem (Acts 15), produced Galatians, and set Paul against Peter at Antioch over who would eat with whom (Galatians 2:11–14). Nobody denied Gentiles could be saved. The question was on what terms, and Paul saw that a gospel with a cultural entrance fee is not the gospel.

The modern form. No church teaches that outsiders must first become like us. It just turns out that those who thrive share the accent, education, politics, family shape, taste in music and ease with the vocabulary. Nobody voted for it; it assembles itself. The tell is not who may come but who is comfortable once they have.

A test. Look around the room on Sunday and ask who is missing who lives within two miles. Then think of the last person who came for a few weeks and didn’t return: did anyone find out why? A church that requires no circumcision but a hundred unwritten smaller things has reinvented the problem of Romans 3. Find out this week.

Comfort for individuals. If God justified people on anything a person can possess — nationality, upbringing, temperament, intelligence, moral aptitude, religious sensitivity — some would be nearer the door through no doing of their own. Faith levels every field because it is not an achievement. God is one, so there is one way in, the same width for everyone who ever lived.
verseByVerse.note: “God is one” echoes the Shema, Israel’s daily confession.

parallels.desc: the LORD is one

verseByVerse.quote: Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does faith overthrow the law? “By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law.” Faith takes the law seriously: it agrees that God is holy, sin is real, judgment is just, and we cannot save ourselves — and it receives the righteousness the law demanded but could never produce.

Answering the slander. At 3:8 Paul refused even to argue with the claim that he taught people to do evil. Now that the doctrine is fully stated, he faces it: if righteousness comes apart from the law, is the law thrown away? “By no means!” — his strongest negative again.

Making it stand. “Uphold” means to set something firmly on its feet. Not that the law survives the gospel, but that it was never standing properly until now.

How law-keepers lower the law. A man trying to be justified by the law must lower it to have any peace. He cannot live with “you shall not covet” meaning what it says, so he translates the commandments into achievable things: no adultery becomes no affair; no murder becomes no violence; honour your father becomes a phone call at Christmas. He has kept the law by redefining it to his own size — the deepest disrespect the law ever suffers, done by its admirers.

The gospel lets it stand at full height. “The law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good” (7:12). Nothing is discounted. The demand is met in full by Someone, the penalty paid in full by Someone, and the sinner justified without one letter adjusted in his favour. Only the man who no longer needs the law to be manageable is free to see how magnificent it is.

Abraham is coming. There is a second sense, which chapter 4 proves. The obvious objection is that Paul has invented a new religion. So he fetches Abraham, counted righteous by believing God before the law was given and before he was circumcised. Justification by faith is not smuggled in past Moses. It is the oldest thing in the book.

A guard. This verse is not mainly about how a Christian uses the commandments now; Paul gets to that in chapters 6, 8 and 12–13. Here he answers a charge about the doctrine. But the answer has the same shape: grace does not lower the standard. It produces people who begin, unevenly, to want it (8:4).

A test. Read the Sermon on the Mount slowly this week and watch your reaction. If your instinct is to soften it — “he can’t mean that literally, allowances must be made” — something in you is still trying to pass, because only a candidate needs an easier exam. If you can let it stand at full height, agree with every word, and not be frightened, you are upholding the law. The man not being examined can afford to admire the standard.

A mirror, honoured. The law cannot save anybody, and Paul has said nothing against it. Both are true. The law was always a mirror, and a mirror is not discredited because it cannot wash a face. It is honoured by the man who stops arguing with it and goes to be washed.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Then what advantage has the Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision?<sup>2</sup>Much in every way. To begin with, the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God.<sup>3</sup>What if some were unfaithful? Does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God?<sup>4</sup>By no means! Let God be true though every one were a liar, as it is written, “That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged.”<sup>5</sup>But if our unrighteousness serves to show the righteousness of God, what shall we say? That God is unrighteous to inflict wrath on us? (I speak in a human way.)<sup>6</sup>By no means! For then how could God judge the world?<sup>7</sup>But if through my lie God’s truth abounds to his glory, why am I still being condemned as a sinner?<sup>8</sup>And why not do evil that good may come?—as some people slanderously charge us with saying. Their condemnation is just.<sup>9</sup>What then? Are we Jews any better off? No, not at all. For we have already charged that all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin,<sup>10</sup>as it is written: “None is righteous, no, not one;<sup>11</sup>no one understands; no one seeks for God.<sup>12</sup>All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one.”<sup>13</sup>“Their throat is an open grave; they use their tongues to deceive.” “The venom of asps is under their lips.”<sup>14</sup>“Their mouth is full of curses and bitterness.”<sup>15</sup>“Their feet are swift to shed blood;<sup>16</sup>in their paths are ruin and misery,<sup>17</sup>and the way of peace they have not known.”<sup>18</sup>“There is no fear of God before their eyes.”<sup>19</sup>Now we know that whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be held accountable to God.<sup>20</sup>For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin.<sup>21</sup>But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, although the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it—<sup>22</sup>the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. For there is no distinction:<sup>23</sup>for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God,<sup>24</sup>and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,<sup>25</sup>whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith. This was to show God’s righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins.<sup>26</sup>It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.<sup>27</sup>Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded. By what kind of law? By a law of works? No, but by the law of faith.<sup>28</sup>For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law.<sup>29</sup>Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also,<sup>30</sup>since God is one—who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith.<sup>31</sup>Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law.

4.title: Abraham: The Father of All Who Believe
4.overview:
If justification is by faith and not by works of the law, Paul faces an immediate objection from Jewish readers: what about Abraham? Abraham is the father of the Jewish nation, the recipient of the covenant, the model of obedience. If he was justified by his works, then surely righteousness is earned, not given. Romans 4 is Paul's extended answer — and it is devastating in its exegetical precision and its theological reach.

The answer is simple and irrefutable: Abraham was justified by faith before he was circumcised (Genesis 15:6 precedes Genesis 17), and before the law was given (by four centuries). The very man whom Judaism claimed as the exemplar of covenant faithfulness is in fact the exemplar of justifying faith — and therefore the father not only of circumcised Jewish believers but of all Gentile believers as well.
