The gospel does not contradict the covenant with Abraham; it fulfils it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Abraham Justified by Faith, Not Works or Circumcision
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's argument from Abraham is both simple and lethal to the works-righteousness position. He goes directly to Genesis 15:6: "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness." The verb "counted" (Greek: logizomai; Hebrew: chashab) is an accounting term — to reckon to someone's account. God reckoned Abraham righteous — not because Abraham had earned it but because Abraham believed. The righteousness was credited; it was not achieved.

Paul then deploys a second argument from David. Psalm 32:1–2 speaks of the blessedness of the man whose sins are not counted against him. David was not speaking of a man who earned God's favour; he was speaking of a man who received forgiveness he did not deserve. Blessed is the man whose iniquity is forgiven — not whose record is clean. The whole Old Testament agrees: righteousness before God is received, not achieved.

The third and clinching argument concerns the timing of Abraham's circumcision. The justification of Genesis 15:6 precedes the circumcision of Genesis 17 by perhaps fourteen to twenty-four years. Abraham was declared righteous while still uncircumcised — which means circumcision was a sign and seal of a righteousness already received by faith, not the means by which that righteousness was obtained. This means Abraham is the father of all who believe, circumcised or not: his pattern is faith, not ethnicity.

And at the centre of it stands a phrase so shocking that Paul can only have chosen it deliberately: God “justifies the ungodly” (v. 5). Not the sincere, not the searching, not the imperfect but well-intentioned. The ungodly — the very people the God of the Old Testament had sworn he would not acquit, since his own law had called the justifying of the wicked an abomination. Paul is not softening the difficulty; he is naming it in the strongest available terms, because the cross has already answered it (3:25–26). This is the sentence the whole chapter is arranged around, and every reader who has ever wondered whether he is too far gone should notice which category is being justified here.
verseByVerse.theology:
Imputation: The Reckoning of Righteousness

The word logizomai (count, reckon, credit, impute) appears eleven times in Romans 4. This is deliberate. The doctrine of imputation — that God credits Christ's righteousness to the believing sinner's account — is the hinge of the doctrine of justification. Luther's language of the "wonderful exchange" captures it: Christ takes our sin; we receive his righteousness. Not infused into us (as Rome taught), but credited to us — declared righteous in Christ, clothed in a righteousness that is not ours by achievement but ours by gift. Luther called this the "alien righteousness" (iustitia aliena) — foreign to us by nature, ours by grace.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's appeal to Abraham was the ultimate trump card in Jewish theological discussion. If Abraham himself was justified by faith and not by works, the works-righteousness position has lost its founding father. Paul turns the Jewish trump card against itself. Now: Every form of religious merit-earning — "I'm basically a good person," "I attend church," "I pray every day," "I've never done anything really terrible" — collapses before Romans 4. Abraham, the father of the faithful, stood before God with nothing but faith in the promise. So must we.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul turns to Abraham, father of the Jewish people, to prove that justification by faith is not his invention but God’s original way. If Abraham had been justified by works, he would have something to boast about — “but not before God.” No human record, however impressive, counts in God’s court.

Why this chapter exists. Paul has just claimed that faith upholds the law (3:31). A claim like that must be proved from Scripture, so he calls the one witness no opponent could dismiss: the man the whole nation traced itself to. If Abraham was justified by faith, the argument is over. There is nobody further back.

A bold choice. In Paul’s day Abraham was celebrated as the great example of obedience — the man who kept God’s law before it was given and was tested ten times and found faithful. One well-known book of the period ties the very verse Paul will use to the binding of Isaac: “Was not Abraham found faithful when tested, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness?” (1 Maccabees 2:52). On that reading Genesis 15:6 rewards proven obedience — nearly the opposite of Paul’s point. Paul is taking the text back, and his tool will be the calendar: what Genesis 15 says, and when it happened.

The record was real. Paul does not belittle Abraham. He left city, family and inheritance on the word of a God he had not known. He refused the spoils of a war he won so no king could say he had made him rich. He pleaded with God for a wicked city and would not stop at fifty, or forty, or ten. He welcomed strangers who turned out to be more than strangers. He was willing to give up the son he had waited a lifetime for. Any tribunal would have decorated him. Scripture calls him God’s friend (Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23).

“But not before God.” Paul grants all of it and then adds four words. The record is real, and it belongs to a different court. Before people Abraham towers. Before God he is a man counted righteous because he believed a promise — the same position as everyone else who has ever been counted righteous. Boasting has not just been forbidden; its ground has been removed (see on 3:27), and here Paul shows it was never there even in the strongest case anyone could produce.

A test. Write down three things you would most like said at your funeral — the achievements or qualities you quietly hope will be mentioned. Then ask what weight they would carry in a court where the charge is that you have not loved God with all your heart nor your neighbour as yourself. Your list is probably genuinely creditable. The point is that everything on it is evidence in a different case. Stop presenting it to God.

Abraham left at full height. Paul does not hunt Genesis for Abraham’s failures to make room for grace. He leaves the man as tall as he is and observes that height was never what was being measured.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish teachers held up Abraham as the great example of a righteous man.

verseByVerse.quote: For what does the Scripture say? "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness." Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scripture says, “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness” (v. 3, quoting Genesis 15:6). “Counted” is a bookkeeping word: credited. A worker’s wages are not a gift but what he is owed. Abraham was not working; he was believing — and God was not paying a debt but giving a gift.

Paul and James. James quotes the same verse and says that Abraham was justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar (Jas 2:21). The order of events resolves it. Genesis 15:6 comes many years before Genesis 22. Abraham was counted righteous when he believed, long before he offered Isaac; the offering, James says, was the Scripture fulfilled (Jas 2:23), the proof that his faith was alive. Paul asks how Abraham was accepted; James asks how his faith was shown (cf. 3:28).

One nail, hammered. The verb “count” appears eleven times in this chapter. The whole argument turns on one question: how does righteousness get onto a person’s account? Answer: it is put there.

Wages or gift. A ledger changes in only two ways. Either a sum is earned — the employer who pays on Friday is not being kind but settling a debt — or it is credited from outside, and the recipient contributes nothing but an account number. Abraham’s righteousness came the second way. So if you ever feel God owes you something — after a hard season of faithfulness, after a sacrifice nobody noticed — you have moved yourself into the first column, and there is no grace in it anywhere. Wages and gifts exclude each other.

What believing looked like. Genesis 15 is not a man in a devotional mood. An old man with no children is taken outside at night and told to count the stars: “So shall your offspring be.” There is no child and no evidence — only a sentence spoken to him in the dark. “And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). Faith is taking God at his word when the word is all you have. And notice what was counted: not his obedience or character, but that he believed. Accepting a gift is not meritorious; the hand that takes a parcel has not contributed to its contents. Faith justifies because of what it takes hold of.

Imputation. Two things happen. God does not count Abraham’s sins (vv. 6–8), and he credits something positive: righteousness, a standing Abraham did not have. This is what the Reformers called imputation. The righteousness is not infused like a medicine that gradually improves you; it is credited like a sum entered in a book. If it were infused, your standing would rise and fall with your progress. Because it is credited, it is complete the day it is entered. A Christian ten minutes old and one of fifty years stand in exactly the same righteousness.

A test. Think of the last costly thing you did for God — the giving that hurt, the expensive forgiveness, years in an unglamorous ministry. What did you expect afterwards? Things to go better, the prayer to be answered, God to notice? That is nearly universal, and it is the arithmetic of wages. Catch it, because it is how grace quietly turns back into religion. Next time, give it and thank him that you owe him, not he you.

The account was empty. Abraham had no child, no land of his own and no evidence, and that night he was credited with a righteousness he did nothing to produce. What he is famous for came later and was never the ground of his standing.
verseByVerse.note: “Counted” is a bookkeeping word: credited to his account.

parallels.desc: he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness,
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the one who does not work but trusts the God “who justifies the ungodly,” his faith is counted as righteousness. God declares in the right people who in themselves are ungodly — because Christ has paid for their guilt (3:25–26).

A shocking phrase. God told Israel’s judges: “He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both alike an abomination to the LORD” (Proverbs 17:15), and “I will not acquit the wicked” (Exodus 23:7). Those were the working standard of Israelite justice. Paul takes the very phrase and makes it a description of God. It is as if he defined the Almighty by the one thing his own law calls an abomination.

Not softened. Paul does not say God justifies the weak, the struggling or the sincere-but-inconsistent. “Ungodly” is the word of 1:18, the thing God’s wrath is revealed against. He puts the same people in the dock and says they are the ones acquitted.

How it is just. The guilt was not overlooked; it was transferred and dealt with (see on 3:25–26). Justification is not God deciding the ungodly are not so bad. It is a verdict already paid for. The gospel is not that God is lenient. A lenient God would be a corrupt judge — and a judge who can be talked round can be talked round by your accuser too.

“To the one who does not work.” This is not a commendation of idleness. It describes what a man brings: nothing. The qualification for being justified is having nothing to offer. That is the hardest verse in the Bible for respectable people. If you have been decent all your life, attended faithfully, given generously and raised your children well, you come on exactly the same terms as the man who wrecked everything he touched. Many would rather be forgiven much than told their record is not currency.

Two readers. If you fear you are too far gone — that something in your past puts you outside the offer, that God saves people like you in general but not you — read the category again. He justifies the ungodly. Not the improved ungodly, not those who have sorted themselves out. If God justified only good people, your fear would be rational. He doesn’t. And if none of this feels urgent because you have never done anything to frighten a congregation, the word “ungodly” is yours too. There is one door, marked with a description you would not have chosen.

A test. Finish this sentence: “God accepts me even though I…” Most Christians can. Now say: “God accepts me even though there is nothing about me that recommends it.” If that brings a flicker of resistance — a wish to add something about your sincerity or effort — that flicker is exactly what verse 5 is written to remove, and it will keep coming back. Each time, say the sentence again.

Don’t wait to be fit. The only people ever justified are people who at that moment had nothing to bring. If you are waiting until you are in a fit state to come, you are waiting to be disqualified. A holy God declares right people who are demonstrably wrong, without telling a lie. The words stand because a cross holds them up.

parallels.desc: I will not acquit the wicked

verseByVerse.quote: just as David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works: "Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
David says the same: blessed is the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works — “Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered” (v. 7, quoting Psalm 32:1). The blessed man is not the one with no sins but the one whose sins are forgiven.

Two witnesses. “Only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15). Paul has called Abraham, founder of the nation, from before the law. Now he calls David, its greatest king, from under the law. Two men a thousand years apart, on either side of Sinai, both righteous by reckoning, not record. Nobody can now say Abraham was a special case from before the rules.

A harder question. Abraham shows God can credit a man who has done nothing. David shows God can credit a man who has done something — who had forfeited everything.

Blessed at the point of failure. Every religious instinct says the blessed man has a clean record. David says the blessed man’s lawless deeds are forgiven — so by definition he has lawless deeds. His blessing is not where he did well but at his worst failure, because that is where the forgiveness is. This psalm has no beatitude for anything David got right.

Two verbs, two fears. “Forgiven” means lifted and carried away — the load taken off your back. “Covered” means put out of sight by atonement, so that the Judge no longer holds it against you. One answers the weight; the other the exposure. If you cannot carry it, the first word is for you. If you cannot bear it being seen, the second is.

What “covered” does not mean. Not that God has agreed to look away, or that the file is lost, or that enough time has passed. That would be a fiction, and every honest person would know it. That is why the psalm describes life before the covering: while David kept silent his body wasted away, God’s hand was heavy on him day and night, his strength dried up like summer heat (Psalm 32:3–4). The relief is not of a man who decided to stop thinking about it. It is of a man who said it aloud and found it dealt with (32:5).

A test. Take the thing you would least want read aloud. Is it unmentioned or covered? Unmentioned means nobody knows and you are managing it, and the arrangement holds as long as nothing surfaces. Covered means you have named it to God without qualification and it has been dealt with at the cost of blood — and a covered sin is safe precisely because it has already been fully seen. If yours is only unmentioned, do what David did in Psalm 32:5 today.

Why David. The blessing is not the sigh of someone whose life went smoothly. It is the verdict of a man who wrecked what mattered most and found that God had removed his sin from the record — not by pretending, but at a price revealed a thousand years later.

parallels.desc: blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven

verseByVerse.quote: "blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin” (v. 8, quoting Psalm 32:2). The same verb used for crediting righteousness (v. 3) is used here for not charging sin. Our sin is not counted against us because it was counted to Christ, and his righteousness is counted to us.

Never. The Greek uses its strongest double negative: “will never, under any circumstances.” It is the form Jesus used in “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). This is not a statement of God’s current mood, which might change. It is a door welded shut. There is no future in which God reopens the ledger and enters the sin after all.

Future sins. Every honest Christian eventually asks, usually at night: what about the sins I haven’t committed yet? It is natural to think the past was settled at the cross and the future runs on account. But the promise faces forward: he will not count it. When Christ died, every sin you would ever commit was still future — no less known to him than last week’s.

Not back to zero. Most Christians are clear their sins are not counted. Far fewer live as if a positive righteousness has been counted to them. A man whose debts are cancelled has nothing; a man whose debts are cancelled and whose account is filled from someone else’s fortune is rich. Justification gives you a standing you did not have even before you sinned.

A test. After you have failed badly and confessed it, do you keep your distance for a few days — praying less, reading less, unable to sing on Sunday — until you feel you have re-established something? That interval is the tell. It is the behaviour of someone who believes his sins are forgiven but suspects his standing must be earned back. There is nothing to re-establish; the account was never yours. Next time, pray the same evening.

A guard. A verdict this absolute can be turned into permission: if the Lord will never count my sin, the arithmetic has changed in my favour. Paul answers that in chapter 6, not by weakening the promise but by pointing to what has happened to the person. A man pardoned at the scaffold does not spend the afternoon looking for another capital offence.

Where David stood. The man who wrote this had done two things his own law punished with death, had been caught, and had been confronted by a prophet in his own throne room with nothing to say. That man wrote “blessed” — the word that opens the Psalter (Psalm 1:1). Not tolerated, not merely relieved: blessed. And before the psalm ends he is telling other sinners where to come (32:6–11).

parallels.desc: blessed is the man against whom the LORD counts no iniquity

verseByVerse.quote: Is this blessing then only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? For we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness. How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? It was not after, but before he was circumcised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is this blessing only for the circumcised? Paul asks when Abraham was counted righteous: before or after his circumcision? Before. Genesis 15 (faith counted) comes at least fourteen years before Genesis 17 (circumcision). Abraham was justified while uncircumcised — as, in effect, a Gentile.

The calendar argument. This is what Paul promised (see on vv. 1–2), and it is quietly devastating. He disputes not one word of the text his opponents value. He just asks when. Genesis 15 comes before Genesis 17, and no theology can move it.

Fourteen years. Between that night and the day of his circumcision Ishmael was born (Abram was 86, Genesis 16:16) and grew to thirteen (Genesis 17:24–25). For about fourteen years the father of the nation walked around justified before God and physically indistinguishable from any pagan in Canaan. Had he died then, he would have died righteous with nothing anyone could inspect.

Justified as an outsider. Abraham came from a family of idolaters (Joshua 24:2), with no law, temple, priesthood, sign or religious community. The founder of the covenant people entered righteousness from outside, because there was no covenant people yet to be inside.

Is it house property? Paul has just quoted David’s beatitude, and beatitudes are the kind of thing people assume belong to their own kind. Is the forgiveness of Psalm 32 for insiders only, through proper channels? The answer is settled not by an appeal to God’s generosity but by a date.

The human instinct. This is not just a Jewish question. It is the assumption that blessing arrives through the arrangement — that the promises are really for people properly inside: baptised, on the roll, in the right church, taught by the right people. It is rarely said, so rarely examined. It shows in the quiet confidence of those who have the arrangement and the hesitancy of those who don’t.

A test. Think of a promise you find hard to apply to yourself — that God is near the brokenhearted, that nothing can separate you from his love, that he will not cast you out. What do you think stands between you and it? If the answer is anything like a credential — you came to faith too late, were never properly discipled, have the wrong background, are not the sort of person these things are written for — this passage is about you, and its answer is a date. Abraham had none of it either. He had a promise and believed it. Claim yours by name.

A guard. This does not make the sign worthless; Paul says so in the next verse. God commanded it and Abraham obeyed. The argument is about order, not value. The sign could not produce what its owner already had, and a man with the sign and nothing else has the receipt without the purchase.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham was declared righteous in Genesis 15 and circumcised in Genesis 17, some years later.

verseByVerse.quote: He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. The purpose was to make him the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them as well, and to make him the father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham received circumcision as “a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised.” So he is father of all who believe without being circumcised, and father of the circumcised who also “walk in the footsteps” of his faith. Both inherit through faith, not the sign.

A seal. In the ancient world a seal pressed into wax certified a document. It did not create the agreement; it authenticated one already made and showed whose the thing was. Nobody became owner of a field by acquiring a seal. A seal on an empty page certifies nothing.

What about baptism? Baptism stands to faith as circumcision stood to Abraham’s faith — commanded by God, genuinely meaningful, never the thing itself. Paul’s argument cuts equally against trusting circumcision and trusting baptism, and equally against treating either as nothing. A seal is issued by an authority. What it cannot do is manufacture what it certifies.

Does this support infant baptism? Many Christians believe it does. They reason that circumcision and baptism are signs of the same covenant of grace (Col 2:11–12), that the sign was given to Abraham’s infant sons, and that the households baptized in Acts (16:15, 33) carry that pattern into the church. Those are serious arguments. But the more likely reading is believer’s baptism, and this verse is part of the reason: Paul’s whole point is that Abraham’s sign followed his faith. Circumcision was given to all Abraham’s physical descendants, Ishmael as well as Isaac, believing or not. The new covenant is different. Its members “shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest” (Jer 31:34), and its sign belongs to those who have come to faith, as Colossians itself says: “buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith” (Col 2:12).

A real father. Because Abraham was justified before circumcision, he is not just an example Gentiles may study from a distance. He is their father. A believing Gentile is not like one of Abraham’s children; he is one. If you are the first Christian anyone in your family can remember, this verse hands you a lineage running back four thousand years to a man under the stars in Canaan — argued by Paul as fact from the order of two chapters in Genesis.

Footsteps. Abraham is father of the circumcised who are “not merely circumcised” but walk in his faith’s footsteps. The sign alone does not put a man in the family. And the picture is a child in a field placing his feet where his father’s prints already are. Sonship shows in the direction of travel, not the paperwork.

A test. Which of Abraham’s footprints is your life stepping into? He left security on a promise. He waited twenty-five years for what God had said with no evidence arriving. He believed something physically impossible. Where in your life are you actually depending on something God has said, in a way that would look foolish if he did not exist? If nothing comes to mind, that is worth knowing. You can hold all Abraham’s doctrines and stand in none of his footprints.

A guard. If your faith feels far too small for his footsteps: Paul describes a direction, not a standard of performance. He will soon say Abraham considered his own body as good as dead (v. 19). A child does not have to fill his father’s footprint. He only has to be going the same way. One man, two families, one door — and what makes believing Jew and Gentile brothers is not the sign that once divided them but the faith that came before it.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and confirmed that something was genuine.

parallels.desc: the sign of the covenant

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — The Promise Through Faith: Abraham's Hope Against Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now extends his argument to the promise God made to Abraham — that he would be heir of the world, that his offspring would be numberless, that through him all nations would be blessed. This promise, Paul insists, was given through the righteousness of faith, not through the law. The law cannot be the means of inheriting the promise, because the law can only pronounce wrath (it condemns those who fail to keep it); if the promise depends on law-keeping, the promise is void for everyone.

The portrait of Abraham's faith in vv. 17–21 is one of the most moving passages in the entire New Testament. Abraham — "as good as dead" at a hundred years old, Sarah's womb "dead" — hoped against hope. He did not weaken in faith when he considered the hopeless biological reality. He did not waver in unbelief but grew strong in faith, giving glory to God, fully convinced that what God had promised he was also able to perform. This is faith in its purest form: not faith in the circumstances, not faith in human possibility, but faith in the God who raises the dead and calls into existence things that do not exist (v. 17).

And then the connection to us: this was written not for Abraham's sake alone but for ours — for those who believe in him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead. Jesus was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification. The resurrection is not merely the proof that Jesus is who he claimed to be; it is the declaration that the justification he accomplished has been accepted. The empty tomb is God's receipt for a debt paid in full.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith and the Resurrection

Romans 4:24–25 ties justification directly to the resurrection of Jesus. Christ was raised "for our justification" — His resurrection is not merely the proof of his deity but the declaration that his atoning work was accepted by the Father. The resurrection is the Father's public vindication of the Son's sacrifice. This means that Christian faith is not merely belief in the ethical teachings of Jesus or even in his death; it is faith in the God who raised him from the dead. Easter is not the happy ending of a sad story; it is the announcement that the story of sin and death and wrath has been definitively answered.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The promise to Abraham that he would be "heir of the world" (v. 13) goes beyond what Genesis explicitly states but draws on the expansive reading of the Abrahamic covenant in Jewish tradition. Paul is claiming that the full scope of that promise — a redeemed humanity, a renewed creation — is fulfilled in Christ and received by faith. The Jewish hope for the world is the Christian gospel. Now: Abraham's "hope against hope" (v. 18) is the model for Christian faith in every situation where the circumstances shout impossibility. The God who gave life to Abraham's dead body and Sarah's dead womb is the same God who raises the dead today — physically at the last day, spiritually in every conversion. No situation is beyond him.

verseByVerse.quote: For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith. For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be the heirs, faith is null and the promise is void.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promised Abraham and his offspring that he would be “heir of the world,” and that promise came “through the righteousness of faith,” not through the law. If the inheritance depended on keeping the law, faith would be emptied and the promise void.

Does the land still belong to the Jewish people? Dispensational Christians hold that it does: God promised Canaan to Abraham’s descendants “for an everlasting possession” (Gen 17:8), and a promise of God cannot be cancelled. The more likely reading is that the promise has not been cancelled but enlarged. Paul says Abraham would be heir of the world; Hebrews says he “was looking forward to the city that has foundations” (Heb 11:10); Jesus says the meek “shall inherit the earth” (Matt 5:5). Canaan was the down payment; the renewed creation is the inheritance, and it belongs to all who are Christ’s, Jew and Gentile: “if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to promise” (Gal 3:29).

“Heir of the world.” Genesis does not use those words. God promised a land, countless offspring, and blessing for “all the families of the earth” (Genesis 12:3). Jewish writers of Paul’s time already read the promise broadly, and the seed is in the text: a blessing for all the families of the earth was never going to be exhausted by a strip of land.

Emptied and void. If the inheritance runs on law-keeping, faith is “null” — literally emptied, the verb used of Christ emptying himself (Philippians 2:7) — and the promise “void,” put out of use. Not weakened; cancelled. If the estate goes to those who perform, performance is the mechanism and trust has nothing to do. Faith would become a feeling alongside the deal, decorative rather than load-bearing. You cannot run one inheritance on two mechanisms.

Promise, not contract. A contract binds two parties, either can break it, and it is only as secure as the weaker signatory. A promise binds one party and names a recipient, whose conduct does not keep it in force because he never undertook anything.

God walked alone. In the very chapter Paul quotes, Abraham asked how he could know he would inherit. God told him to cut animals in half and lay the pieces opposite each other (Genesis 15:9–10). Everyone understood the ceremony: the parties walked between the halves, calling the same fate on themselves if they broke the agreement (cf. Jeremiah 34:18). Abraham prepared the pieces and waited. Then a deep sleep fell on him, and “a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces” (Genesis 15:12, 17) — God, alone. Abraham never walked. God swore by himself, took the whole liability, and left the other party asleep on the ground.

An heir. Nobody earns an inheritance; an heir only has to be named. And an inheritance takes effect by a death (Hebrews 9:16–17). The oath made between the pieces was finally carried out when the One who walked alone kept its terms in his own body.

A test: the size of your hope. Try to describe what you will inherit. Most Christians produce something vague and elsewhere — a good place after death. Paul says heir of the world: this creation healed, a body that works, work worth doing, the earth under a good King. If your hope is basically an evacuation, it is smaller than the promise. The Bible does not end with the saints leaving the world. It ends with the world handed to them. Let that shape how you spend this week — and what you fear losing.

verseByVerse.quote: For the law brings wrath, but where there is no law there is no transgression. That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring — not only to the adherent of the law but also to the one who shares the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The law brings wrath,” because it turns wrongdoing into lawbreaking. So the inheritance depends on faith, in order that it may rest on grace and be “guaranteed” to all Abraham’s offspring — Jew and Gentile who share his faith. Abraham is “the father of us all.”

No law, no transgression. Paul is not saying people without the law are innocent; chapters 1–2 proved the opposite. His point is narrower. “Transgression” means stepping over a drawn line. You can be lost without a map, but you can’t trespass until someone puts up a fence. The law does not create wickedness; it makes it a chargeable offence.

The law brings wrath. That was devastating for people whose hope rested on having the law. They thought it was the mechanism of the inheritance; Paul says it is the mechanism of the indictment. Giving the law to sinners is like installing a speed camera on a road everyone was already speeding on. Nothing got worse. Everything became explicit, and the fines started arriving.

Guaranteed. Paul states the goal first: a promise that is guaranteed. Working back, it had to rest on grace through faith, because there is no other way to build a promise that cannot fail. Any arrangement involving human performance is only as reliable as the human. Grace is not just the kinder option; it is the only one that produces certainty. The word for “guaranteed” comes from law and business: a title that stands when challenged. Not a warm hope but a valid deed.

The audit in the back of the mind. If your standing depends on performance, it moves, and you know where you are by how the last few days went. Some Sundays you can sing and some you can’t. A low-grade audit runs constantly, loudest when you most need to pray. That is not your temperament. It is the condition of anyone whose inheritance runs on law, and the cure is to change the instrument.

A test. Compare how you approach God after a week when you did well — prayed, resisted something, were generous — and after a week when you did none of it. If those feel very different, something is fluctuating, and it is not the promise. That doesn’t make you a hypocrite; nearly every believer lives with some of it. But it shows the work still to do — not more effort, but learning to believe the title is secure in both weeks. Come to God tonight on the same terms either way.

A guard. A guarantee is not an invitation to indifference. Your life is not the ground of the promise, but it is not irrelevant; Abraham’s offspring walk in his faith’s footsteps (v. 12). A man who knows his inheritance cannot be lost does not grow careless toward the Father who gave it. He is free to obey without bargaining.

A family. “The father of us all.” Not one nation with an annex for outsiders. An argument about law, promise and guarantee lands on a family — which a promise, unlike a contract, is able to produce.

verseByVerse.quote: as it is written, "I have made you the father of many nations" — in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist. In hope he believed against hope, that he should become the father of many nations, as he had been told, "So shall your offspring be."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God told Abraham, “I have made you the father of many nations.” Abraham believed in the God “who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist.” With no natural ground for hope, “in hope he believed against hope.” Faith is not optimism about circumstances; it is confidence in who God is.

Creation and resurrection. Paul picks two descriptions of God out of the whole Old Testament: he gives life to the dead and calls into existence what does not exist. Between them they cover the only two situations where a human being can contribute nothing: when there is nothing yet, and when what was there has died. A corpse cannot help raise itself, and nothing cannot assist in its own creation. Both applied to Abraham literally: the offspring did not exist, and the bodies they would come from were as good as dead.

“I have made you.” God does not say “I will make you” but “I have made you” the father of many nations (Genesis 17:5) — spoken to a childless old man with no evidence. God speaks of the not-yet as done, because for him it is. That is what it means to call into existence what does not exist. And Abraham’s new name — “father of a multitude” — was used by everyone he met before the son was born. Every introduction was a small act of faith or a small humiliation, depending on whether the One who named him could be relied on.

“In the presence of” God. Abraham was not reasoning about a distant deity. He stood before Someone. Biblical faith is not a calculation of probabilities but a posture before a Person, which is why it survives evidence a calculation could not.

Hope against hope. With nothing in the situation to hope for, he hoped. This is not positive thinking or refusing to face facts; the next verse says he faced them. Hope is a settled expectation resting on something said. The question is never how much hope you can generate but whether the One who spoke can do it.

Why Paul tells this. His readers must believe something at least as unlikely: that a man executed in a distant province is alive and his death has settled their account with God. So Paul gives them a father who was in the same position and whose faith rested not on a reason to expect a child but on a God who does this kind of thing.

A test. Take what you are praying for and can see no way through — the marriage, the son, the diagnosis, the part of your character that hasn’t moved in twenty years. Which category is it: something that doesn’t exist and would have to be created, or something alive that has died? Those are the two named here as God’s specialities. There is no third department for merely difficult cases.

A guard. This verse has been used to promise outcomes God never promised. Abraham had a specific word about a specific thing, and his faith was in that word, not in his own conviction that it should happen. Believing hard for a particular result is not this faith, and when it fails the collapse is severe. Where God has spoken plainly — that he forgives, keeps you, raises the dead, works all things for good — believe against every appearance. Where he has not spoken about your case, ask, leave the answer with him, and keep believing what he has said while you wait.

parallels.desc: the father of a multitude of nations
so shall your offspring be

verseByVerse.quote: He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah's womb. No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham faced the facts: his body was “as good as dead” at about a hundred, and Sarah was barren. Yet he did not weaken in faith or waver at God’s promise. He grew strong in faith “as he gave glory to God.” Mature faith does not refuse to see the facts; it refuses to let them have the last word.

He did the arithmetic. “Considered” means taking careful stock and reaching a conclusion. Abraham did not protect his faith by not thinking. He thought clearly and got the right answer: his body was finished, and so was hers. Much Christian teaching implies doubt comes from looking too hard at reality. Paul says the opposite. Abraham looked, named what he saw — as good as dead — and believed God anyway.

The exact category. Verse 17 said God gives life to the dead. Verse 19 says Abraham considered his body as good as dead. He was standing inside the very category God had just named. The deadness was not the obstacle to the promise but the material it would work with.

“No unbelief made him waver.” Read alone, this produces despair in many: my faith wavers weekly, so I am not what Abraham was. But look at Genesis. He lied about his wife to save himself, twice. He took Hagar because waiting became unbearable. When God repeated the promise, “Abraham fell on his face and laughed and said to himself, ‘Shall a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old?’” (Genesis 17:17). Sarah laughed too. Paul knew Genesis well. He is describing the direction of a life, not auditing every hour — the difference between a man who wavers and a man who defects. This is how God chooses to remember a believer.

A guard. If you think your faith is a different species from Abraham’s, look at his from the inside: twenty-five years of nothing happening, a wife past childbearing, two episodes of cowardice, a laugh — and one line in the New Testament saying he did not waver. That is what God does with a faith that staggers and keeps facing the same way.

Faith grows by worship. “He grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God.” Faith is not increased by trying to have more faith — like trying to fall asleep by concentrating. It grows by attention to its object. Giving glory to God means telling him what he is like — he keeps his word, nothing is too hard for him, he has never failed anyone — and the one who does it finds believing has become easier.

A prescription. When you catch yourself wavering, notice what you reach for. Most of us reach inward: we take faith’s temperature, worry about its size, and end up with a smaller faith more closely observed. Do the opposite. Take fifteen minutes and rehearse what God has actually done, in Scripture and in your life — name five things, aloud, specifically. The first ten minutes will feel mechanical. Then notice the size of what you were worrying about. Abraham looked at his dead body, then he looked at God, and the second look was the longer one.

verseByVerse.quote: fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham was “fully convinced that God was able to do what he had promised.” That is the simplest description of saving faith: not persuaded by circumstances, but resting its whole weight on the God who speaks and keeps his word.

A narrow conviction. Abraham was not sure he would enjoy the experience, or understand what God was doing, or that the waiting was reasonable. He was sure of one thing: God was able to do what he had promised. That is smaller and harder than general spiritual confidence, and it is all that is required.

Where our doubt really sits. Ask a Christian whether God could heal the illness, restore the marriage, save the son, break the habit, and the answer is immediate: of course. The doubt sits elsewhere, rarely said aloud: whether he will bother, whether he has noticed, whether he is inclined to, this time. The letter answers that question at 8:32: a God who “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” has already shown how he is disposed toward you.

Must I be “fully convinced” first? The word means filled to the full, like a sail. Most Christians don’t feel full of anything. But faith does not justify by reaching a certain intensity; it justifies by what it is attached to. Abraham lied and laughed; if full conviction were the entry requirement, he would not have qualified either. Paul describes the character Abraham’s faith settled into over twenty-five years. That assurance is the fruit of a long walk with God, not the fee for starting one.

“What he had promised.” Faith is never free-floating. It has a word behind it and goes exactly as far as that word, no further. Abraham was holding a specific sentence God had spoken about a specific thing.

When faith is thin. Don’t try to manufacture conviction; you can’t, any more than you can decide to find something funny. Go and find the promise. Get the actual words — “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5), “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6), nothing “will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (8:39) — and put your weight on them. Vague faith is thin faith because there is nothing in its hand.

A test. Name the promise you are relying on right now. Not a doctrine or a general sense that God is good — a sentence from Scripture you could say aloud that addresses what you are actually worried about. If nothing comes, that is not a verdict on your faith. It is the diagnosis of why trusting feels so hard: you have been trying to trust without holding anything. Find one today and write it down.

The freeing part. This verse does not ask you to be strong. It asks you to be convinced of Someone else’s strength. Abraham’s greatness was that he thought better of God than his circumstances did.

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: That is why his faith “was counted to him as righteousness.” But the words “it was counted to him” were not written for his sake alone, but for ours also. — Romans 4:22–24a
verseByVerse.commentary:
That is why Abraham’s faith “was counted to him as righteousness.” And those words were not written for his sake alone, “but for ours also.” Genesis 15:6 is not just biography. It is how God justifies everyone who believes: credited, not earned, by faith, through grace.

The words were for us. Paul is precise. He does not say Abraham’s life is relevant or inspiring. He says the specific phrase “it was counted to him” had a second audience from the start. Moses wrote a sentence about one man that was meant to hold your weight thousands of years later. It was fully true of Abraham that night, and it was also being written down for you.

How Paul argued. He has not asked anyone to accept a new doctrine. He asked them to read an old text carefully — what it says, in what order, with which words — and the doctrine came out of the reading. That is his answer to the charge of novelty: he did not get round the Old Testament; he found justification by faith in the founding story of the nation whose Scriptures they were.

How to read Old Testament stories. They are not mainly a gallery of moral examples. Many of us were taught them that way — be brave like David, faithful like Daniel, patient like Job. That reading exhausts you, because it asks for qualities you don’t have, and it is not what the texts are for. Paul does not say “be like Abraham.” He says the way God dealt with Abraham is the way God deals with you. The point is not the patriarch’s faith but the Lord’s reckoning. Moral lessons are real, but they rest on this.

A test. Take the last Old Testament passage you read. What did you come away with? If it was a resolution — I should be more like that — you read it as a moral example. Go back and ask: what does this show me about what God is like, and what he does with people who have nothing? That question is why a chapter about a man dead four thousand years can settle where you stand tonight.

Addressed to you. Paul does not say the words can be applied to us, as if we were borrowing something. They were written for us; the intention was in the writing (cf. 15:4). You are not reading someone else’s letter hoping some of it fits. It has your name on it, and it was addressed before you existed.

verseByVerse.quote: It will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification. — Romans 4:24b–25
verseByVerse.commentary:
Righteousness will be counted to us who believe in the God who raised Jesus from the dead — Jesus, “who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification.” His death dealt with our sins; his resurrection is God’s public declaration that the payment was accepted and we are acquitted.

The same God, the same work. Paul describes the God we trust as the one “who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord.” Abraham believed in the God who gives life to the dead (v. 17) and looked at a body as good as dead (v. 19). We believe in the God who gave life to the dead and look at a body that was actually dead, three days in a tomb. Not an analogy: the same God doing the same kind of thing, and the second time is what the first pointed to.

“Delivered up.” This is the verb that fell three times in chapter 1: God “gave them up” to their desires, to dishonourable passions, to a debased mind (1:24, 26, 28). There God handed sinners over to what they chose; here God hands his Son over to what they deserved (see on 1:24–25). The letter’s most terrible verb and its most merciful are the same word. One handing-over answers the other.

Read the parallel slowly. The same small Greek word stands in both lines: delivered up because of our trespasses, raised because of our justification. Our sins were the reason he went to the cross; our justification was the reason he came out of the grave. He was raised because the work was done.

Why the empty tomb matters. Imagine the case without it. A man dies claiming to bear the world’s sins, and stays dead. Then there is no way to know whether the payment was accepted or whether he simply died like everyone else, under the same sentence. Death holding him would mean the account was unsettled. Death releasing him is God’s public statement that there was nothing left to hold him for (cf. 1 Corinthians 15:17).

The receipt. Most of us rest our assurance on the cross, and rightly. But the cross is the payment, and a payment can be doubted at three in the morning: was it enough — for this, for me? The resurrection is the receipt: the Father’s own signature, given in public before witnesses who later died rather than deny it. The Father does not raise men whose work is unfinished.

A test. When you have sinned badly and the accusation comes — “you can’t be forgiven for that” — what do you reach for? If it is your repentance, how sorry you are, or a resolution, the accusation will win, because none of those is strong enough and you know it. Reach instead for an event you had nothing to do with: he was raised. Nothing you did this week can un-empty that tomb. Say it aloud the next time the accusation comes.

From Canaan to a garden. The chapter began with an old man in Canaan and ends outside a grave in Jerusalem, and one sentence covers both: it was counted to him; it will be counted to us. Between them stands the event that makes the accounting honest — a Son handed over by his Father, and handed back.

For we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness.<sup>10</sup>How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? It was not after, but before he was circumcised.<sup>11</sup>He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised.
